samples.result:
# The Office of Lost Time

The Office of Lost Time occupied the second floor of a building that had once sold pianos. On damp mornings, the staircase smelled faintly of felt and varnish. A brass plate beside the entrance listed the opening hours as NINE UNTIL SUFFICIENT, which newcomers generally took to be a joke.

It was not a joke, although the staff disagreed about what it meant.

Mara had worked there for eleven years. Her job was to receive claims, establish eligibility, and explain that certain kinds of time could not be returned.

“No,” she said to a man in a cycling helmet, “we cannot reimburse a marriage.”

“Not even part of one?”

“Not as a single claim.”

He considered this.

“What if I itemize?”

She slid the appropriate form across the counter.

There were rules. Time spent waiting for a late train could be recovered. Time spent looking for glasses already on your head could not, because the department classified that as an educational expense. Time lost to administrative error was fully refundable, provided the error had been made by another office.

Their own errors were handled upstairs.

There was no upstairs.

Mara did not make the rules. She knew this because she had once submitted a proposal to change one and had received a letter thanking her for her interest in local government.

At eleven each morning, her colleague Ivo brought tea in two unmatched cups.

“Anything interesting?”

“A marriage.”

“Again?”

“He may itemize.”

Ivo nodded. “Ambitious.”

***

Returned time arrived in small glass cylinders, sealed with gray wax. A cylinder containing seven minutes was no larger than a sewing needle. An hour could fit comfortably in a coat pocket. Anything beyond a day required collection by an accredited carrier.

The cylinders did not glow. People were often disappointed by this.

To use one, you broke the seal.

The world then continued without you for the specified interval, while you remained in a private allotment of ordinary time. You could sleep, read, peel potatoes, or sit on the edge of your bed and fail to decide what to do.

You could not travel backward. You could not bring anyone with you. Nothing you did could affect another living person until the interval ended.

These conditions appeared in bold print on every receipt.

Nevertheless, people asked.

“Could I see my mother?”

“Not through our office.”

“Could I finish a conversation?”

“Only your side.”

“Could I be young?”

“You would be exactly as old as you are.”

This last answer caused the most trouble.

People imagined that time, once recovered, would arrive with its original weather and the strength they had possessed when they lost it. Instead, a retired mason received the forty-three minutes he had spent outside a locked supply depot in 1968 and used them to take a bath.

He later wrote to say it had been an excellent bath.

Mara kept his letter in her desk. She had shown it to Ivo so often that he could recite it.

***

One Thursday in November, a woman brought in a cardboard box held together with blue string.

She was perhaps seventy, with the upright posture of someone who had spent years carrying things without assistance.

“My husband died in September,” she said.

“I’m sorry.”

“Yes,” the woman said, acknowledging this as one might acknowledge rain. “He left these.”

Inside the box were cylinders. Hundreds of them. Some were thin as fish bones; others had the solid dimensions of fountain pens. All remained sealed.

Mara lifted one carefully.

“Your husband made these claims?”

“Over forty years.”

“Did he ever use any?”

“Not that I know of.”

Mara checked the registry. The husband’s name was Emil Voss. There were six hundred and twelve approved claims under his account.

Delayed buses. Canceled appointments. A mistaken hospital admission. Eleven hours in a lift. Three days lost when a ferry company sent him to the wrong island.

“He was saving them,” the woman said.

“For what?”

“For when things settled down.”

The office grew quiet around them. Outside, someone was reversing a delivery van, its warning bell sounding at patient intervals.

“I’d like them transferred to me.”

Mara turned the cylinder between her fingers.

“Recovered time is nontransferable.”

The woman looked at the box.

“Well,” she said. “Of course it is.”

It was not an angry remark. Mara would have preferred an angry remark.

She gave the woman a claim review form, although she knew exactly how the review would end.

***

At lunch, Mara ate a pear over the wastebasket.

“Six hundred and twelve,” she told Ivo.

“How much altogether?”

“About nine weeks.”

Ivo stopped stirring his soup.

“Good grief.”

“He saved nine weeks and then died.”

“People save all sorts of things.”

“Not usually nine weeks.”

“My aunt had a cupboard full of wrapping paper. We buried her on a Tuesday. On Wednesday I used some of it for a wedding present.”

Mara looked at him.

“I’m not comparing them,” he said. “I’m saying the cupboard was full.”

After lunch, she went into the records room.

The oldest claims were written in brown ink on cards with softened corners. Before cylinders, the office had issued folded paper packets. Before packets, there had apparently been a system involving knots, although nobody still employed understood the filing method.

Mara searched for precedents.

She found a sailor whose unused time had been returned to the sea. A teacher had requested that hers be divided among her pupils, but the application had been rejected because several were already adults. One man had asked to be buried with his accumulated hours.

Permission granted, the record said.

Then, beneath that, in another hand:

Not recommended. Groundskeeper reported persistent knocking.

At four, Mara found a regulation headed DISPOSAL OF UNREDEEMED PERSONAL CHRONOLOGIES.

The relevant paragraph was short.

In the absence of an eligible beneficiary, recovered intervals may be released into the municipal commons.

There was no definition of municipal commons.

There was, however, a form.

***

Her supervisor, Mr. Pell, wore knitted waistcoats and distrusted questions that began with “technically.”

“Technically,” Mara said, “we can release Mr. Voss’s time into the municipal commons.”

“No.”

“You haven’t heard the proposal.”

“I’ve heard the first word.”

She put the regulation on his desk.

He read it twice.

“This refers to an obsolete practice.”

“It’s still a current regulation.”

“So is the requirement that we maintain a hitching post.”

“We do maintain a hitching post.”

“That is a bicycle rack.”

“It was reclassified in 1987.”

Mr. Pell removed his spectacles.

“What do you imagine would happen?”

“I don’t know.”

“That is not a strong opening.”

“We could find out.”

He looked through the glass partition toward the waiting room. Four people sat beneath a poster reminding them that impatience did not constitute additional loss.

“Public time is complicated,” he said.

“Private time seems complicated too.”

“Private time is administered by the individual. When they misuse it, they can hardly write to the council.”

“They do.”

“Yes, but the council forwards it to us.”

He handed back the regulation.

“Get written consent from the widow. Get a location. Get a statement of risks.”

“What risks?”

“That,” said Mr. Pell, “is what the statement must establish.”

As Mara reached the door, he added, “No public announcements.”

She turned.

“We are not advertising free time,” he said. “Can you imagine the queue?”

From the waiting room came the sharp sound of someone tearing up a form.

Mr. Pell shut his eyes.

***

Mrs. Voss lived above a bakery on a street where the trees had lifted the pavement into ridges.

She served coffee in cups so small that Mara worried she might swallow hers accidentally.

“Release it where?” Mrs. Voss asked.

“A public place. A square, perhaps. A park.”

“And then?”

“We’re not certain.”

“Would people get younger?”

“No.”

“Would they notice?”

“Possibly.”

Mrs. Voss looked toward the window.

Below them, a baker in a floury apron was smoking beside a stack of delivery crates. He held the cigarette away from his body, as though hoping to establish that it belonged to someone else.

“Emil hated waste,” she said. “He cut the mold off cheese until there was hardly any cheese left. He kept screws in jam jars. Every time we bought a new kettle, he saved the old flex.”

“Was he happy?”

The question escaped before Mara could make it more professional.

Mrs. Voss considered.

“Frequently. But he rarely admitted it until afterward.”

She stood and took a photograph from the mantelpiece. A younger Emil was sitting in a deck chair, holding a peach. His expression suggested that the photographer had interrupted something important.

“That was the wrong island,” she said.

“The ferry claim?”

“We had a lovely time.”

Mara studied the photograph.

“He claimed three days.”

“He had principles.”

Mrs. Voss returned the frame to its place.

“There’s a little square behind the old market. Emil used to eat his lunch there. Would that do?”

“I think so.”

“Then do that.”

***

The square behind the old market contained four benches, a dry fountain, and a tree whose roots had broken the fountain’s supply pipe twenty years earlier.

The council had decided that repairing the pipe might damage the tree. Removing the tree might damage the fountain. Leaving both alone had eventually become policy.

Mara visited on Friday afternoon.

A courier ate noodles from a paper carton. Two schoolgirls shared earphones. A man in a dark overcoat sat with a shopping bag between his shoes, doing nothing Mara could identify.

She tried to imagine nine weeks entering the square.

Would every person receive nine weeks? Would the time divide itself among them? Would the pigeons qualify? What about the tree, which was already very good at occupying time without appearing to spend it?

She wrote these questions in her notebook.

Under STATEMENT OF RISKS, she wrote:

Uncertain distribution.

Then:

Potential effects on wildlife.

Then, after some thought:

Possibility of disappointment.

On Monday, Mr. Pell read the statement.

“You cannot list disappointment as a risk.”

“It seems like the main one.”

“If we listed disappointment as a risk, we would never do anything.”

Mara waited.

He sighed and signed.

They scheduled the release for Wednesday at twelve seventeen. This was not a significant time. It was simply when Ivo could cover the counter.

Mrs. Voss said she would come.

“Should I bring anything?”

“No.”

“I’ll bring sandwiches.”

Mara nearly said they would not be necessary, but found herself asking for cheese.

***

The cylinders made a surprisingly heavy burden.

Mara carried them in the original box, with the blue string replaced. Mrs. Voss brought sandwiches wrapped in greaseproof paper.

They sat beside the fountain.

“How do we do it?” Mrs. Voss asked.

Mara unfolded the instructions she had found attached to the old regulation.

“We open them.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

“This could take a while.”

It did.

The wax was brittle on the older cylinders, stubborn on the newer ones. Mara used a small knife. Mrs. Voss employed a hairpin with impressive efficiency.

Nothing happened.

They opened delayed trains, missed connections, a printer’s error that had cost Emil an afternoon. They opened the lift and the hospital and the wrong island.

A breeze moved through the square.

The courier arrived with his noodles. The schoolgirls passed along the far side of the fountain. Somewhere behind the market, bottles crashed into a recycling bin.

Mara broke the final seal.

Mrs. Voss looked around.

“Is that it?”

“I don’t know.”

They waited.

The man with the shopping bag came and sat on the opposite bench.

A pigeon approached Mrs. Voss with the brisk entitlement of a minor official.

“Well,” she said, opening the sandwiches, “we might as well.”

Mara took one.

It was cheese, with pickle cut into small uneven pieces.

She had not realized how hungry she was.

For a little while, neither woman spoke.

Then Mrs. Voss said, “He always ate the crusts first. Emil. Did you know anyone else who did that?”

***

Mara returned to the office at one eleven.

Ivo looked up.

“You’re early.”

“I’m late.”

“It’s twelve nineteen.”

The wall clock agreed with him.

Mara checked her watch. Twelve nineteen.

She looked back toward the stairs.

“What happened?” Ivo asked.

“I’m not sure.”

That afternoon, three people missed appointments because they believed the clocks had stopped. A market porter completed an entire crossword during his smoking break. The courier reported that his noodles had remained hot for what seemed an unreasonable length of time.

The schoolgirls returned to the square after lessons and sat until dark.

No official complaints were filed.

Over the following weeks, the effects became harder to document.

People who sat in the square sometimes found that they had enough time to finish things. Not large things. A letter. An argument. An orange.

A woman who worked at the pharmacy went there between shifts and discovered she could remember a dream from beginning to end.

The fountain remained dry.

The tree lost its leaves.

Nobody grew younger. Nobody met the dead. The pigeons, so far as anyone could tell, experienced no administrative difficulties.

Mr. Pell requested a report.

Mara wrote six pages, then reduced them to one.

“How long will it last?” he asked.

“I don’t know.”

“Can we repeat it?”

“Possibly.”

“Can we measure it?”

“Not yet.”

He read her conclusion.

“You’ve written, ‘People seem less hurried.’”

“Yes.”

“That is not a unit.”

“No,” Mara said. “It isn’t.”

He left the sentence in.

***

In December, Mara found a cylinder in the back of her own desk.

Seventeen minutes. A canceled dental appointment, years earlier.

She had forgotten it completely.

At lunchtime, she took it to the square.

Mrs. Voss was there, feeding crumbs to a pigeon.

“You shouldn’t,” Mara said.

“I know.”

Mara showed her the cylinder.

“Another contribution?”

“Perhaps.”

But Mrs. Voss shook her head.

“You keep that one.”

“What for?”

“How should I know?”

Mara laughed and put it in her pocket.

They sat together beneath the bare tree. A delivery van rattled past the mouth of the square. Somewhere a radio was playing a song neither of them could quite identify.

After a while, Mrs. Voss began describing a shelf she wanted put up in her kitchen.

“Emil left plenty of screws,” she said.

“I can help on Saturday.”

“Morning?”

“Yes.”

The pharmacy woman arrived and sat down with her eyes closed.

Mara checked her watch, then tucked her hand back into her pocket around the cylinder. She would have to leave soon. There was time to hear about the shelf.

# A Map of Small Repairs

On the morning the city decided to remove the public benches from Halden Square, Mara found a teaspoon inside the municipal photocopier.

It was a good teaspoon, heavy and silver-colored, with a small rose pressed into the handle. Someone had laid it on the glass and closed the lid. The machine had produced forty-seven pictures of it before running out of paper.

Mara stood holding the spoon while the maintenance request blinked on her screen.

**HALDEN SQUARE: REMOVE SIX BENCHES. INSTALL STANDING RAILS.**

Under “Reason,” someone had written: **Discourage extended occupancy.**

She read this twice. Then she put the spoon in her desk drawer, beside a dead battery, three keys that opened nothing she knew of, and the retirement photograph of a man whose name she had forgotten.

At nine, her supervisor called.

“Simple job,” he said. “We need dimensions, access requirements, cost estimate. Thursday?”

“Why standing rails?”

“That’s what’s been approved.”

“Approved by somebody standing up?”

He sighed without hostility. His name was Daniel, and he had the worn patience of someone who spent his working life forwarding messages he had not written.

“Just survey the site,” he said. “We can discuss recommendations afterward.”

Mara worked in Public Realm Assets, a department whose title suggested fountains and statues but mostly meant broken bollards. She had been there eleven years. She knew which paving stones turned treacherous in winter, which drain swallowed wedding rings, and which bicycle rack had been installed backward in 2008 and remained backward because correcting it required consultation.

At thirty-eight, she was good at distinguishing things that could be fixed from things that could only be reported.

Lately, the second category had grown.

Her father had died in February. Since then, she had become irritated by small defects: a loose handle, an uneven chair leg, the whistle of a window that would not shut. His house was full of such things. He had repaired other people’s homes for forty years and left his own in a state of permanent negotiation.

On his kitchen table was a notebook she had not yet opened.

She went to Halden Square at lunchtime.

The square occupied an awkward wedge between the library, a pharmacy, and the back wall of a supermarket. There were four plane trees, six benches, and a bronze plaque commemorating a mayor remembered principally for having been mayor.

Five benches were occupied.

On the first, two teenagers shared headphones. On the second, a man in paint-spattered trousers ate an orange with the concentration of a surgeon. On the third, a woman held a sleeping child across her knees.

The fourth bench was empty.

On the fifth sat an elderly man wearing a bicycle helmet. He had no bicycle.

The sixth belonged, in some unspoken but evident sense, to a woman surrounded by shopping bags. She was feeding crumbs to a pigeon with one damaged foot.

Mara measured the empty bench.

“Are we getting new ones?” the man in the helmet asked.

“Possibly.”

“Good. That one catches your trousers.”

He pointed at the slat beside her hand. A screw had risen from the wood by perhaps four millimeters.

Mara wrote it down.

“What sort?” he asked.

“We’re still assessing.”

He watched her extend the tape measure.

“My wife’s in the pharmacy,” he said. “I wait here.”

Mara looked toward the pharmacy, though there was nothing to see but a poster advertising vaccinations.

“She likes to do it herself,” he added.

Mara wrote that down too, then felt foolish. It was not an asset condition.

***

That evening, she went to her father’s house to clear a cupboard.

The house had become less like a house and more like a difficult question. Every object asked whether she would keep it, sell it, give it away, or admit that nobody wanted it. Even the ordinary things had acquired an unreasonable gravity.

She had spent twenty minutes on a plastic measuring jug the previous Sunday.

The notebook lay where she had left it, under an electricity bill.

On the cover her father had written, in block capitals:

**THINGS TO GO BACK TO**

Mara sat down.

The first pages were what she expected: names, addresses, estimates, dimensions. A gutter at number twelve. A kitchen drawer that stuck in damp weather. Mrs. Vale’s gate.

Then, halfway through, the entries changed.

**Bus stop outside clinic. Seat loose. Ask council.**

**Library steps. Bottom edge hard to see when wet.**

**Halden Square. Bench near pharmacy. Screw up. Take driver.**

Mara touched the page.

There were dates. The bench entry was from November.

Her father had still been working then, though he had begun telling her he was cutting back. She had imagined fewer ladders, fewer boilers, fewer drives across town with lengths of timber sticking out of his van.

She had not imagined him maintaining a private list of public inconveniences.

Further on, she found:

**Woman at number 8 says crossing too quick. Time it.**

And:

**Little path behind school floods. Children walking in road. Photograph after rain.**

The final entry was unfinished.

**Square. Ask man with helmet about—**

Nothing followed.

Mara closed the notebook, opened it again, and checked the pages after that one. She had become familiar with this impulse during the hospital weeks: the conviction that if she looked properly, someone would have written down what to do next.

The following morning she took a screwdriver to Halden Square.

It was technically improper. Repairs required a logged work order, appropriate allocation, and confirmation that the asset had been inspected. Mara understood why. Someone had once “helpfully” repaired a playground gate with a latch that trapped two fingers.

She checked the wood for rot, examined the screw, and tightened it.

The man in the helmet arrived while she was testing the slat.

“You’ve fixed it.”

“Yes.”

“Quick service.”

“Don’t spread that around.”

He sat cautiously, then shifted his weight.

“Excellent.”

Mara put the screwdriver away.

“Did you know a man called Peter? Gray beard. Blue van.”

The man considered.

“Used to come with sandwiches?”

“Yes.”

“He fixed my wife’s walking stick. The rubber bit had worn through.”

“That sounds like him.”

“How is he?”

Mara looked at the screw she had just tightened.

“He died.”

“Oh,” the man said.

For a while they watched a delivery driver reverse badly toward the supermarket.

“Kind fellow,” he said at last. “Never made a production of it.”

***

By Wednesday, Mara had completed the survey and failed to write the report.

Instead, she returned to the square at eight, twelve, and four, recording what happened.

At eight, a cleaner from the library sat down to change her shoes. At twelve, three construction workers ate lunch. At four, a girl practiced reading aloud to a woman who corrected her without looking up from her knitting.

The woman with the shopping bags was called Sal. She had once worked in the supermarket bakery. Now she rented a room above a takeaway, where the window opened onto an extractor fan.

“Can’t hear yourself think till midnight,” she said.

“Do you come here every day?”

“Not if it rains properly.”

“What counts as properly?”

“When it comes through the tree.”

Mara asked whether Sal knew the benches might be removed.

“Of course.”

“How?”

“People measure things before taking them away.”

On Thursday, Mara brought Daniel a report twenty-three pages longer than he expected.

He turned the pages slowly.

“What’s this?”

“A usage study.”

“I asked for dimensions.”

“They’re on page two.”

He looked at a table.

“Average seated occupancy?”

“Yes.”

“Rest intervals?”

“People stop here between the bus station and the clinic.”

“And you’ve counted them.”

“For three days. It needs a longer study.”

Daniel leaned back.

“Mara.”

She disliked the careful tone. Since February, people had begun saying her name as though setting down a full glass.

“The benches aren’t being removed because nobody uses them,” he said.

“I know.”

“There have been complaints.”

“About what?”

“Drinking. Litter. Arguments. Someone sleeping across two seats.”

“Were there complaints about the broken light?”

“That’s a separate team.”

“And the bin that disappeared?”

“Waste services.”

“And the public toilet that’s been locked since August?”

“Facilities.”

Daniel rubbed his forehead.

“I know what you’re saying.”

“Then put it in the recommendation.”

He looked again at the report.

Through his office window, Mara could see a man replacing the paper in a parking meter. He had opened the machine like a cabinet and was working with extraordinary delicacy.

“I can delay procurement,” Daniel said. “For a month. No promises after that.”

It was less than she wanted and more than she had expected.

“What do you need?”

“Evidence that doesn’t all come from you.”

She left before he could qualify this.

For the next two weeks, Mara spent her lunch breaks in the square with a clipboard.

Some people were eager to talk. Others regarded her with suspicion. A boy asked if signing her sheet meant he would receive emails forever.

“No emails.”

“That’s what they always say.”

A shop owner supported removal.

“I clean up bottles every morning,” he said. “You people come here at lunchtime and see pensioners. Come at ten at night.”

So she did.

There were bottles. Two men were shouting near the library. Somebody had burned a small black crater into a bench slat.

Sal sat beneath the pharmacy awning, looking exhausted.

“Still counting?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Count the light.”

Mara looked up. Above them, the lamp was dark.

***

She began calling departments.

At first she received reference numbers. Then she received explanations of why the reference numbers belonged elsewhere. She made a spreadsheet and called again.

Her father would have hated the spreadsheet. He would also have admired its vindictiveness.

The lamp was repaired on a Tuesday.

A bin arrived the following Monday.

The toilet remained closed because of a cracked waste pipe beneath the building, which was not, as Mara had hoped, a simple failure of willingness. The repair would require excavation. Facilities sent photographs. She added them to her folder and stopped mentioning the toilet as though someone merely needed to turn a key.

Meanwhile, the benches became briefly famous.

The library displayed her survey. Someone posted a photograph online. A local reporter called the proposal a “war on sitting,” which made Daniel close his eyes when Mara showed him.

At the public meeting, twenty-seven people attended.

The shop owner came with photographs of litter. The woman from the pharmacy came with her husband, who removed his helmet indoors and held it in his lap.

Sal did not come.

“I’ve been discussed in rooms before,” she told Mara.

The meeting was untidy. People interrupted. A man who never used the square spoke for eleven minutes about civic decline. The teenagers said they needed somewhere to wait for the bus, and an older woman asked why they could not wait standing.

“Why should we?” one of them said.

It was the most useful question of the evening.

In the end, the committee approved keeping four benches. Two would be replaced with seats with armrests. Lighting would be reviewed. Cleaning would increase for a trial period.

Nobody was satisfied enough to applaud.

Outside, Daniel stood beside Mara beneath the library canopy.

“You got most of it.”

“Sal won’t be able to lie down on the new seats.”

“No.”

“Was that the point?”

“Partly.”

Rain ticked against the metal roof.

“I don’t want you to think I’m calling this a complete victory,” he said.

“I don’t.”

“But four benches are still four benches.”

She knew. She was tired enough to resent him for being right.

The next Saturday, she returned to her father’s house.

She cleared the cupboard she had intended to clear a month earlier. It contained jam jars, electrical fittings, three unopened packets of biscuits, and a small cardboard box labeled **USEFUL BRACKETS**.

She kept the brackets.

Then she took his notebook into the garden and read it from beginning to end.

Between the repairs were other things. A bread recipe. The telephone number of an old customer’s daughter. A reminder to ask Mara whether she had booked her car service.

On one page he had drawn a rough map of the town.

There was no scale. Several streets were missing. He had marked the clinic, the library, the river path, and a café where he liked the soup. Little crosses showed places to revisit.

She recognized some from his notes. Others meant nothing to her.

***

The benches were installed in June.

Mara went to inspect them with the contractor. He checked the bolts while she checked the clearance around each seat. They filled out separate forms, leaning on the same clipboard.

The man in the helmet watched.

“Comfortable?” Mara asked.

“Not bad.”

His wife emerged from the pharmacy carrying a paper bag.

“Come and try this, June,” he called.

She sat beside him. He moved his helmet to make room.

Mara waited until the contractor had gone, then walked to the bench beneath the largest tree.

Sal was there, sorting receipts.

“How’s the room?” Mara asked.

“Still above a takeaway.”

Mara sat down.

For a minute neither spoke.

Then Sal held out a receipt.

“Look at that. Four pounds for washing powder. Used to be two.”

They discussed washing powder. Then the supermarket. Then a pigeon that had learned to land on the automatic door sensor and walk inside.

Mara stayed through her lunch break.

Before leaving, she opened her father’s notebook to a blank page and drew the square. She marked the lamp, the bin, the six seats, the pharmacy door. Beside the toilet she wrote the repair reference number.

“What’s that for?” Sal asked.

“So I remember.”

“Put the tree roots in. People trip there.”

Mara added them.

Back at the office, she found the teaspoon while searching for a pencil. She washed it in the staff kitchen and put it beside the kettle.

The next day somebody used it.

That evening, she took the longer route home, past the clinic. At the crossing she pressed the button and started the timer on her phone. A woman with two heavy bags stepped into the road beside her.

Halfway across, the signal changed.

Mara finished timing before opening the notebook.

# Things That Hold

On the morning the city decided to remove the bench, Arthur arrived with a screwdriver, a thermos of tea, and the wrong pair of glasses. The glasses belonged to his late wife. He had put them on in the kitchen without thinking, and now the world possessed the strange, underwater softness it acquired whenever he made this mistake. He could have gone home. Instead, he lifted them onto his head and knelt beside the bench, because the left armrest had been loose for three weeks and there were still things a person could do without seeing clearly.

The bench stood halfway up Bell Street, where the hill briefly relented before continuing toward the hospital. Nobody had planned this mercy. According to the plaque, the bench commemorated a former alderman whose chief accomplishment, as far as Arthur could discover, had been owning several laundries. The alderman’s name was almost illegible. People called it the halfway bench, or the red bench, although it had not been red for years. Arthur thought of it as Number Seventeen. He had maintained forty-three benches before retiring, and he remembered their numbers more reliably than the birthdays of his surviving relatives.

He was tightening the second screw when a woman in a fluorescent jacket stopped beside him.

“You work for the council?”

“Not anymore.”

“Then technically you shouldn’t be doing that.”

“Technically, it shouldn’t wobble.”

She considered this, holding a paper cup near her chin. She was young enough that Arthur initially mistook her weariness for impatience. Her name badge said PRIYA, and below that, in smaller letters, PUBLIC REALM. He had never liked the phrase. It made the pavement sound like a kingdom whose citizens had disappointed their monarch.

“It’s coming out on Thursday,” she said.

“The screw?”

“The bench.”

Arthur sat back on his heels. Across the street, a delivery driver was carrying flowers into the hospital entrance, upside down, with the blossoms brushing his trousers.

“Why?”

“There’s a streetscape improvement.”

“What’s improving?”

She glanced uphill, as if the answer might be arriving by bicycle.

“Accessibility. Pedestrian flow. Some planting.”

“People sit here.”

“I know.”

“People going there.” He pointed toward the hospital.

“I know,” she said again, and this time he believed her. She looked at the screwdriver in his hand. “You can finish that, if you like. I won’t report you.”

At home, Arthur found the consultation leaflet beneath a supermarket flyer and an invitation to have his hearing assessed. The proposed design showed Bell Street as a clean white channel, bordered by green circles representing trees. There were six illustrated pedestrians. All were upright, slender, and traveling somewhere with purpose. None appeared to have knees. The bench had vanished. In its place stood a rectangular planter, which Arthur recognized from a procurement catalogue. It cost more than his first car, even allowing for inflation, and could accommodate neither a tired person nor a particularly ambitious tree.

His wife, June, would have known what to do. She had possessed the rare ability to complain without making complaint her occupation. Once, after the pharmacy installed a step too high for her mother’s walker, June had arrived with her mother, the walker, a folding chair, and sandwiches. They stayed outside until the manager came down. By the following week there was a ramp. Arthur, meanwhile, had always believed that competent work should explain itself. If a hinge stopped squeaking, surely someone would notice. June used to kiss his forehead and say, “Darling, silence doesn’t submit an invoice.”

He telephoned the number on the leaflet. After a recording thanked him for his patience before he had demonstrated any, he spoke to a man who explained that comments on the scheme had closed in February.

“It’s April,” Arthur said.

“Yes.”

“The bench is still there.”

“The consultation has closed.”

“Has the pavement closed?”

“I’m not sure what you mean.”

Neither was Arthur, entirely. He thanked the man, because the man had not personally invented the situation, and put down the telephone. Then he returned to Bell Street with a notebook and a folding stool.

He began at nine the following morning. For the first twenty minutes nobody used the bench, which made him feel both foolish and obscurely betrayed. A pigeon inspected a crust beneath it. Two schoolchildren stepped across the seat rather than around it. Then a woman wearing hospital slippers beneath a long coat lowered herself carefully onto the middle slat. She sat with her eyes shut, holding a little clear bag containing keys and a telephone. After eleven minutes, she stood and continued downhill. Arthur wrote: 9:24. Woman. Rested. Eleven minutes. He disliked how little this said.

At ten, a man with a walking stick sat down to change the hand in which he carried a shopping bag. At ten seventeen, two nurses shared a pastry. At eleven, a father tied his daughter’s shoelace while she rested one foot on the seat. A courier stopped to answer a call and remained after it ended, staring at his gloves. Arthur recorded them all. Beside the courier’s entry he wrote: Perhaps bad news. Then he crossed it out. A notebook, he felt, ought not to claim knowledge it did not possess, particularly about strangers.

Around lunchtime, Priya appeared carrying another paper cup.

“Are you conducting a survey?”

“I’m sitting.”

“With a clipboard.”

“It’s a notebook.”

“That may be an important legal distinction.”

He showed her the pages. She read without smiling, which he appreciated. Twenty-three people had used the bench. Four had walking aids. Three were accompanied by small children. One had cried, though Arthur had recorded only that she had stayed for seventeen minutes.

“You need to send this to the project manager,” Priya said.

“Will it matter?”

“It will be something they have to answer.”

It was the first useful sentence anyone had offered him.

By Wednesday, the notebook had become a minor neighborhood attraction. The bakery owner brought Arthur a cheese roll and asked whether he was collecting signatures. When he said no, she seemed disappointed, so he drew a line down a fresh page and let her sign. A taxi driver signed while double-parked. A teenager added his name, then returned to ask whether signing meant he might have to attend something. Arthur assured him it did not. The teenager signed again for his brother, which Arthur crossed out. He was beginning to understand why democracy required so many pencils.

Not everybody agreed with him. A woman with a double buggy said the pavement was too narrow, and the bench made it worse. Arthur almost told her there was plenty of room. Then he watched her negotiate a lamppost, a rubbish bin, his folding stool, and him.

“You’re right,” he said, moving.

She looked surprised.

“It should be farther back,” he added.

“There isn’t a farther back.”

Behind the bench stood a low brick wall. Behind the wall was a strip of weeds belonging to the hospital.

Arthur turned around. He had looked at that wall for twenty-eight years without properly seeing what lay beyond it.

The hospital estates office occupied a prefabricated building behind the ambulance bays. Arthur knew this because he had once repaired its door closer during a rainstorm. He also knew that the man responsible for the grounds was called Dennis and disliked being contacted through official channels. Dennis answered his extension on the sixth ring.

“No,” he said, after Arthur explained.

“I haven’t asked yet.”

“You’re asking about land. The answer’s no.”

“It’s eighteen inches.”

“Eighteen inches of land.”

“For a bench.”

“Then eighteen inches of liability.”

Arthur looked at June’s photograph beside the telephone. She appeared amused by something outside the frame.

He brought Dennis a measured drawing anyway. The hospital wall had a recess where a gate had once stood, filled in with newer brick. Remove the infill, set the bench into the recess, and the pavement would gain nearly two feet. The weeds could become the planting the council wanted. Arthur had even marked the underground service cover, because he knew what happened when enthusiastic people drew gardens over things that occasionally needed opening. Dennis studied the paper for a long time. Then he asked whether Arthur had obtained the wall dimensions from existing records.

“Measuring tape.”

“That’s not an approved survey.”

“Has the wall changed size?”

Dennis rubbed his face.

“You can’t just make a hole in a hospital wall.”

“It used to be a gate.”

“It used to be lots of things. This place used to have a smoking room.”

But he kept the drawing. As Arthur left, Dennis called after him.

“If this goes anywhere, there’ll need to be proper clearance.”

“Of course.”

“And I’m not maintaining it.”

“Of course.”

“And don’t tell anyone I said it might go anywhere.”

Arthur promised nothing on that point.

Thursday morning brought rain and a council truck. Arthur was already at the bench, not chained to it or standing in front of it, but sitting under a black umbrella that had lost one rib. He had considered a protest sign. Everything he thought of sounded either too grand or too cross. SAVE OUR BENCH made it seem as though the bench were an endangered animal. PEOPLE GET TIRED was accurate but insufficiently specific. In the end he had brought the notebook, wrapped in a shopping bag, and a spare cup in case anyone wanted tea.

The two workers climbed out. Arthur knew one of them.

“Morning, Lee.”

“Arthur.”

“Your mum all right?”

“Hip’s much better.”

“Good.”

Lee looked at the bench, then at the sheet on his clipboard.

“They told us there might be an obstruction.”

“There’s me.”

“Yeah.”

“I can move.”

“Right.”

Neither man did anything for a moment. Rain drummed on the truck roof. Then Lee’s colleague said they had another job near the station, and perhaps they should do that first. Lee telephoned someone. Arthur poured tea into the spare cup, and the younger worker accepted it with both hands.

Priya arrived twenty minutes later, wet from the shoulders down and angry in a tightly organized way. The removal had been paused, she said. Not canceled. Paused. There would be a site meeting on Monday involving highways, hospital estates, accessibility, and the contractor.

“Will anyone who sits on it be there?” Arthur asked.

“You will.”

“I don’t sit on it much.”

“You have recently.”

He could not dispute that. She took the tea Lee had declined and stood beneath the damaged side of the umbrella. Water ran from its exposed rib onto her sleeve, but she did not mention it.

The meeting took place around the bench because nobody could find a room all six organizations were allowed to book. There were eight people, nine including Arthur. They discussed sightlines, turning space, gradients, ownership, drainage, and whether moving an existing asset across a property boundary constituted disposal. Arthur listened carefully. Some of it was nonsense, but less than he had expected. The accessibility officer, a broad-shouldered man using a wheelchair, demonstrated exactly where the route narrowed. The engineer found a drainage problem in Arthur’s drawing. Dennis pointed out that the wall supported nothing except several generations of ivy.

Then the contractor asked why they could not simply install a new bench elsewhere.

Arthur opened his mouth and closed it again. He had been preparing to defend the old wood, the familiar shape, the almost invisible alderman. But the question was reasonable. A better bench could be a good thing.

“Where?” he asked.

They walked uphill together. The proposed location was thirty yards away, on a steeper section beside the hospital doors. It had more space and less shelter.

The accessibility officer tried the slope, came back, and said, “Here is where people need the rest. Not after they’ve managed it.”

The revised design took six weeks. During that time, Arthur learned that a pause could become a remarkably busy condition. Emails arrived asking him to confirm things he had already confirmed, sometimes in documents containing his earlier confirmation. Priya translated whenever necessary. Dennis obtained permission for the recess, provided the council accepted maintenance responsibility. The council accepted, provided the hospital repaired the brickwork. The contractor offered a price. Everyone became unhappy with the price. Then the bakery owner mentioned that her brother was a bricklayer, producing immediate concern about procurement and eventual agreement that he could quote like anyone else.

When work began, Arthur stayed away. He told himself this was courtesy. Nobody liked a retired man supervising from the pavement. In truth, he was afraid they would discover some insurmountable pipe or regulation, something that had been waiting underground to make the whole effort ridiculous. He cleaned his kitchen cupboards instead. At the back of one he found June’s old thermos, the smaller green one she took on walks. Inside its cup was a peppermint sweet wrapped in translucent paper. He sat down at the table with it in his palm until the kettle switched itself off.

The bench returned on a Tuesday. The workshop had replaced three slats, tightened the joints, and painted it dark red. Set into the new recess, it looked simultaneously unfamiliar and exactly right. There was room to pass in front of it. Behind it, in the hospital’s narrow strip of soil, somebody had planted rosemary and two tough little grasses. The plaque had been cleaned. The alderman emerged from obscurity as EDWIN PELL, 1908–1981. Arthur hoped he had been kind to the people who worked in his laundries. It seemed possible. There was no need to decide.

No ceremony had been planned, which suited nearly everyone. Priya came during lunch. Dennis inspected the brickwork and found a minor flaw he was pleased to mention. The bakery owner brought six buns in a paper bag, though eight people arrived, requiring a knife and some negotiation. Lee sat on the left side and tested the armrest with a theatrical shove.

“Solid,” he said.

Arthur nodded.

A woman coming down from the hospital stopped nearby, breathing hard. They moved aside. She sat, not knowing she had interrupted anything, and rested her hands on her knees.

The others stood about for a moment, then began to disperse. Dennis went back through the hospital gates. Lee took the remaining bun for his colleague. Priya asked Arthur whether he wanted his notebook returned from the project office, and he said yes, though there was no hurry. When they had gone, he sat at the other end of the bench. The woman asked him the time. He checked his watch and told her. Across the road, the flower shop driver was unloading buckets, keeping them upright this time. Arthur poured himself some tea and watched until she felt ready to leave.

# The World Is Held Together by Small Repairs

The most important object in a room is often the one nobody notices. Not the painting, not the bright screen, not the vase arranged to suggest that someone has a coherent life. It might be the small felt pad beneath a chair leg, preventing a daily scrape across the floor. It might be a washer inside a tap, holding back the patient ambition of water. It might be the screw that someone tightened six months ago and has not thought about since.

We tend to tell stories about beginnings. The first stone laid, the first page written, the first rocket rising on a column of fire. Beginnings have excellent publicity. They come with ceremonies, photographs, declarations of purpose. Maintenance rarely receives such treatment. Nobody gathers beneath a banner to celebrate the fifteenth year in which a bridge has remained, uneventfully, a bridge. Yet that continued existence is an achievement, renewed through inspections, cleaning, calculations, budgets, and the unglamorous replacement of tired parts.

A beginning happens once. Keeping something going happens over and over, usually without applause. There is a kind of courage in that repetition, although it does not look much like courage in the usual pictures. It looks like checking a seal. Returning a call. Labeling a wire before disconnecting it. Remembering which neighbor needs help carrying groceries upstairs. Perhaps a civilization should be judged not only by what it can invent, but by what it can keep in good condition without making a spectacle of the effort.

***

Consider a public bench.

At first, it seems too simple to deserve consideration. Some slats, some bolts, a pair of supports. A place to sit while waiting for someone who said they were almost there. But a bench is a small agreement between strangers. It says that a person may occupy a little space without buying anything. It says that tiredness is a sufficient qualification for stopping. A bench acknowledges that people have bodies, and that bodies do not move through a city at a uniform speed.

Then rain enters a crack in the wood. A bolt loosens. Someone scratches a name into the paint. The ground beneath one support begins to settle. None of these changes is dramatic. That is how deterioration prefers to work: in increments too small to provoke a meeting. Eventually the bench becomes uncomfortable, then unreliable, then unusable. One day it disappears. The absence may never become news, but someone’s walk has become harder.

Somebody could have repaired it. That sentence contains more politics than it first appears to. Who was responsible? Who noticed? Who had the tools, permission, time, and money? Did the city consider the bench an amenity or an obligation? Did the person making the budget ever need somewhere to sit? Repair is not merely a technical activity. It is a decision about what deserves to remain available, and to whom. A tightened bolt can be a modest expression of public respect. The person resting there afterward need never know the name of whoever turned the wrench.

***

Much of the knowledge required to sustain ordinary life is difficult to put into a manual. A manual can tell you the recommended torque for a fastener. It has a harder time explaining the faint wrongness an experienced mechanic hears before anyone else hears anything unusual. A recipe can specify heat and duration. It cannot entirely substitute for the cook who recognizes when an onion has crossed from softened to sweet, or when the pan needs to come off the flame.

This knowledge is sometimes called intuition, which can make it sound magical. Often it is accumulated attention. A person has encountered enough variations to recognize a pattern without narrating every step of recognition. The skill lives partly in memory, partly in the senses, partly in muscles trained by repetition. An experienced cleaner knows which stain will yield and which solvent will damage the surface. A nurse notices that someone who says they feel fine is answering half a second too slowly.

When such people leave an organization, the loss is not fully represented by a vacancy. A whole unofficial library may go with them: the door that sticks in humid weather, the supplier who answers urgent calls, the machine that needs a pause between cycles. Institutions often discover this library only after it has vanished. They thought they employed a person to perform a list of tasks. They actually depended on someone who understood the gaps between the tasks, and quietly prevented those gaps from becoming failures every working day of the year.

***

There is, however, a danger in making repair sound inherently virtuous. Not everything should be preserved. Some systems are cruel, some objects unsafe, some arrangements kept alive chiefly because changing them would inconvenience the people who benefit. A patched roof is useful; a patched excuse may not be. The question is not simply whether something can be maintained. It is whether its continued operation serves a purpose worth the cost, and whether that cost is being fairly shared.

An old appliance may be repairable but consume far more energy than a replacement. A beloved building may contain hazards that affection cannot neutralize. A workplace may praise resilience while requiring employees to compensate endlessly for deliberate understaffing. In such cases, the language of maintenance can become a trap. People are asked to keep the wheels turning when the wheels are rolling over them. Their ingenuity conceals the design failure, allowing those responsible to mistake endurance for evidence that everything works.

Good repair therefore requires judgment, not merely persistence. Sometimes the right action is to replace the pipe. Sometimes it is to redesign the whole plumbing system. Sometimes it is to stop pumping. There is no universal romance in keeping an old thing alive. The useful commitment is to the life the thing supports: warmth rather than the boiler, mobility rather than the vehicle, learning rather than the administrative machinery of a school. Objects and institutions are means. Forgetting that makes preservation a form of captivity, however attractive the old building or familiar its daily routines.

***

Human relationships also require maintenance, though the mechanical metaphor becomes unreliable if pushed too far. People are not devices, and affection is not a substance that can be topped up according to a service schedule. Still, there are recognizable patterns of neglect. An unanswered message becomes two. A small resentment is stored rather than discussed. Someone keeps assuming that the other person knows they are appreciated. The relationship continues to function, apparently, while some essential connection slowly loosens.

Often the necessary repair is embarrassingly ordinary. A specific apology. A question asked without preparing a defense against the answer. A change in behavior small enough to be credible and consistent enough to matter. “I’m sorry you felt that way” is usually less useful than “I interrupted you, and I will let you finish.” The first statement describes an unfortunate atmosphere. The second identifies an action and accepts a task. Repair becomes possible when responsibility stops wandering around looking for somewhere else to live.

But here too, maintenance has limits. No one is obligated to preserve a relationship through endless self-erasure. Mutuality matters. Safety matters. A repair attempted by only one person may become another name for carrying the whole structure. The humane goal is not to make every bond last forever. It is to treat people honestly, including when honesty requires an ending. Sometimes care means rebuilding trust. Sometimes it means leaving without inflicting an extra wound merely to prove that the departure was justified, or that the departing person was right about everything.

***

The strangest feature of successful maintenance is that it erases evidence of its own importance. If a technician prevents an outage, there is no outage to explain the value of the technician. If a vaccination campaign prevents illness, the missing illness cannot walk into a budget hearing and testify. If careful editing removes a confusing sentence, the reader never experiences the confusion that justified the edit. Prevention produces an absence, and absences are notoriously bad at competing for attention.

This creates a recurring institutional temptation: to cut the work whose benefits are hardest to see. The system has been reliable for years, so perhaps reliability no longer needs funding. The archive has suffered no major loss, so perhaps preservation is excessive. The staff have managed every emergency, so perhaps staffing is adequate. In each case, success is misread as proof that the effort producing it was unnecessary. The umbrella is thrown away because the person underneath it has remained dry.

A more intelligent culture would learn to represent avoided harm without pretending that every prediction is certain. It would keep records, listen to experienced workers, and understand that slack is not always waste. Spare capacity can be what allows a hospital, a power grid, or a family to absorb a difficult day. A system operating permanently at its limit may appear efficient, right up to the moment when anything unexpected happens. And something unexpected, by definition, does not wait until the schedule becomes convenient, the accounts improve, or everyone has had enough sleep.

***

Maintenance has its own relationship with time. A neglected problem often becomes more expensive in a nonlinear way. A little water under the sink is not merely a small version of a ruined floor; it is an opportunity to prevent the ruined floor from existing. The difficulty is that the early problem rarely arrives wearing its future consequences. It appears as a damp patch, a faint smell, a sound that can probably be ignored until the weekend after next.

Attention must therefore reach beyond the immediate inconvenience. To clean a gutter is to respond to rain that has not fallen yet. To back up a file is to care about a future person who has just discovered that the original is gone. That future person may be oneself, but the gesture still requires imagination. Present effort is being exchanged for a benefit that might never become visible. The task is easy to postpone because the person who will suffer the postponement has not yet arrived.

There is tenderness in this form of foresight. Someone leaves clear instructions for the next shift. Someone marks the shutoff valve. Someone puts a spare key where it can actually be found. These are messages sent forward through time: I knew you might have a difficult moment, so I made part of it easier. They lack the grandeur of monuments, yet they may be more directly generous. A monument asks the future to remember us. A well-maintained system helps the future get on with its own concerns, whether or not we are remembered.

***

Repair also has an aesthetic dimension, although preferences differ about what a repair should look like. Some people want it invisible: the seam matched, the surface restored, the interruption erased. Others prefer the evidence to remain. A patched jacket can display its history. A repaired bowl can make its fracture part of its appearance. Neither approach is automatically more honest. Sometimes seamless restoration honors the original intention. Sometimes a visible patch acknowledges that survival has changed the object, and that change need not be disguised.

What matters is resisting the idea that only untouched things can be beautiful. A staircase worn slightly hollow by generations of footsteps has acquired a shape no designer could have specified exactly. A cookbook with notes in several hands contains more than recipes. The penciled instruction to use less salt, the substituted ingredient, the date beside a successful birthday cake: these additions turn an object into a record of participation. Its value has grown through use rather than remaining intact despite it.

Yet wear is not the same as neglect, and damage should not be romanticized merely because it photographs well. A cold apartment is not made charming by peeling paint. A dangerous staircase does not become acceptable because its wood is old. Beauty and responsibility need not be enemies. The best repair can preserve evidence of life while removing obstacles to living. It lets an object have a past without demanding that the next person suffer for the authenticity of experiencing it exactly as found, broken step and all, in the present.

***

Imagine a neighborhood room devoted to small repairs. Not a polished showroom, not a place organized around selling replacements, but a bright room with sturdy tables and enough chairs. People arrive with lamps, torn sleeves, bicycles, and toys whose silence has become a household grievance. Some repairs prove simple. Others require parts. A few are impossible or unsafe. The point is not that every object leaves restored. The point is that each one receives informed attention before being declared finished.

Around the tables, knowledge changes hands without becoming a performance of superiority. Someone learns to thread a needle. Someone discovers that the mysterious failure was a loose connection. A child sees an appliance opened and finds not magic but an arrangement of understandable parts. This does not mean everyone becomes an expert. Expertise remains important, especially where electricity, structural safety, or hazardous materials are involved. But a little understanding can replace helplessness with discernment: knowing what to attempt, what to ask, and when to stop.

Such a room would repair more than objects, though that claim should remain modest. It would not dissolve inequality or substitute for reliable public services. Still, it could create encounters that ordinary commerce rarely encourages. People would have a reason to cooperate without needing to agree about everything. They could admire a useful skill. They could lend a tool. They could leave with a functioning toaster and the name of someone three streets away. Community might begin there, not as an ideal, but as something useful they had done together.

***

None of this requires turning every moment into a duty. A life devoted entirely to preventing deterioration would become its own kind of damage. There must be time to use things, enjoy places, and inhabit relationships without constantly inspecting them. The purpose of maintaining a garden is not to achieve a state in which no leaf is ever out of place. It is to make room for growth, shade, food, scent, insects, conversation, and afternoons in which nothing particularly productive occurs.

Maintenance serves freedom when it reduces the number of emergencies that govern our days. A reliable bus gives someone choices. A sharp kitchen knife makes cooking easier. A clear agreement allows friends to relax instead of guessing what is expected. Good upkeep recedes into the background, not because it is unimportant, but because its purpose is elsewhere. The floor is clean so a child can play on it. The instrument is tuned so somebody can make music.

Perhaps that is enough to remember the next time a small necessary task feels beneath notice. Tighten the handle. Send the clarification. Mend the pocket before the keys fall through. Thank the person whose work made the morning uneventful. These actions will not usually produce a story worth telling at dinner. They will simply leave something ready for use: a door that opens, a coat that holds what it carries, a person who knows where they stand. Tomorrow, someone will reach for the handle and find that it works.

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

The museum stood between a locksmith and a bakery, in a building so narrow that visitors sometimes walked past it sideways without noticing. Its sign had been painted by someone who got as far as THE MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED and then apparently remembered an appointment. For thirty-one years, nobody had added the final word. Rain had softened the lettering. Pigeons nested behind the M. On sunny mornings, the baker propped open his door, and the whole first gallery smelled of bread.

Lena arrived on a Tuesday carrying a cardboard box and wearing the expression of someone who had rehearsed a practical question to avoid asking an emotional one.

“Do you accept donations?” she asked.

The man behind the desk was repairing a pencil sharpener. Small brass pieces lay on a cloth before him. He wore a green cardigan with three different buttons.

“Sometimes,” he said. “What have you brought?”

“A ship.”

He looked at the box.

“A modest ship,” she added.

Inside, wrapped in a tea towel, lay a wooden model of a three-masted schooner. Its hull was painted blue. Two masts stood upright; the third rested loose along the deck. Threads hung from the rigging like the roots of a plant pulled out too soon. There were six tiny cannons, a coil of rope, and a captain no taller than a fingernail, still attached to the plastic frame in which he had been manufactured.

“My father made it,” Lena said. Then, because accuracy had become important since his death: “He made most of it.”

The man did not touch the ship.

“Was he planning to finish?”

“For twenty years.”

“That isn’t quite what I asked.”

Lena looked toward the door. Across the street, a woman was persuading a reluctant dog to pass a drainpipe.

“I think he liked planning to finish.”

The man smiled, not triumphantly, but as if she had supplied an essential measurement.

“That,” he said, “is something we understand here.”

His name was Ansel. He gave her a donation form on which the usual questions—name, address, description—were followed by several unusual ones.

*Was the object abandoned, interrupted, or released?*

*Does anyone still expect it to become something else?*

*Would its maker be relieved to know where it is?*

Lena tapped the second question with the pen.

“How could I possibly know?”

“You may write that.”

She did. In the next blank, after thinking for a while, she wrote it again.

While Ansel made tea, she wandered into the museum. The first room contained a sweater with one sleeve, a chessboard on which a game had stopped after eleven moves, and a stack of pages titled *A Brief History of Everything Important*. The stack was not especially large. Beside it stood a violin whose maker had carved the body but never attached the neck. The wood had darkened to the color of honey held against a window.

Every object had a label. None included a monetary value.

*Wedding speech, never delivered. The speaker decided, correctly, that the joke would hurt his brother.*

*Garden plan, abandoned after the discovery that the supposedly dead pear tree was alive.*

*First chapter of a detective novel. Donated by the author upon beginning a different detective novel.*

Lena stopped before a pair of small red mittens joined by a long string. One mitten lacked a thumb. Its label read simply: *No further information requested.*

In the second room, a woman was sitting beside a half-completed jigsaw puzzle of the sea. All the edge pieces were in place. The center was a scattering of blue.

“Are visitors allowed to work on things?” Lena asked.

“No,” the woman said.

“Then what are you doing?”

“Looking.”

“Sorry.”

“People always ask.”

The woman studied a piece near her elbow, turned it once, and put it down without trying to fit it anywhere. Lena found this unexpectedly irritating.

Ansel brought the tea in two cups that did not match.

“Why preserve any of it?” she asked him. “There must be millions of unfinished things.”

“There are millions of finished things. People preserve those.”

“Yes, but they’re—”

She stopped.

“Better?” he suggested.

“Easier to explain.”

“That’s true.”

He sat on a bench beneath a map of an imaginary country. The western coast was elaborately inked; the east dissolved into pencil marks and a note that said *mountains, perhaps*. Lena noticed that somebody had drawn a railway to the uncertain mountains.

Her father had kept the ship on a table in the spare room. Every winter he announced that this would be the winter. He bought glue, finer brushes, a magnifying lamp. He subscribed to a magazine about model boats, although he had no interest in actual sailing and disliked water deeper than his knees. When Lena visited, she would ask about his progress. He always said, “Getting there.” In later years, she had begun answering, “Where, exactly?”

Now she wished she hadn’t. Not because he had seemed hurt—he had usually laughed—but because the joke had hardened into her account of him. Her father, who could never finish anything. Her father, with his loose cupboard handles and stacks of unread books. She had repeated it so often that she had forgotten he worked for forty years in a hospital laundry, where everything had to be finished by six.

“I don’t want it in my flat,” she said.

“All right.”

“But I don’t want to throw it away.”

“All right.”

“And I don’t want you to pretend it’s a masterpiece.”

Ansel glanced into the box.

“The second mast is noticeably crooked.”

Lena laughed. She had not expected to, and it came out roughly.

“We can keep it,” he said. “But not as evidence against him.”

She looked up.

“Objects are sometimes donated in that spirit. We try to discourage it.”

She returned the following Saturday. She told herself she wanted to see where they had put the ship, but it was still in the little office behind the desk, waiting for a stand. Ansel was on the telephone, saying, “No, an unpaid electricity bill is unfinished in a different sense.”

When he hung up, he asked if she could hold two pieces of wood together while he measured them.

“I’m not volunteering,” she said.

“Of course not.”

She held them for twenty minutes.

By the end of the month, she had a key.

The work was less romantic than she had imagined. There were floors to sweep, emails to answer, and a damp patch in the ceiling that looked increasingly like an accusation. Ansel kept the accounts in a ledger whose columns never quite agreed. Lena, who managed invoices for a wholesaler, found this intolerable. She made a spreadsheet. He regarded it with polite suspicion until it revealed that the museum had been paying for two telephone lines, one of which ended in a cupboard.

Donations came in irregularly. A retired bus driver brought a papier-mâché moon. A student offered thirty-seven seconds of an animated film in which a fox opened a door. A man carried in a stone he had intended to sculpt into his wife’s likeness.

“Does she know?” Lena asked.

“She told me to get it out of the garage.”

They accepted the moon and the fox. The stone, after discussion, went into the little courtyard, where it became a place to sit.

Not everything belonged. Ansel refused a collection of letters someone had stolen from an ex-lover.

“But they’re unfinished,” the man protested.

“They’re also hers.”

A woman wanted to donate her daughter’s sketchbooks because the daughter had decided to become an electrician.

“Ask her first,” Lena said.

“She doesn’t care about them.”

“Then asking should be easy.”

The woman left offended and returned two weeks later with her daughter, who donated one sketchbook and took the rest home.

In April, Ansel fell on the bakery steps and broke his ankle. From his hospital bed, he gave Lena elaborate instructions about feeding the courtyard birds, though none about the museum itself.

“Shouldn’t we close until you’re back?”

“Would you like to?”

She thought about her evenings, which had become crowded with dusting and label writing. She thought about the ship, now resting on its stand between a half-woven basket and an unfinished translation of a poem.

“No,” she said.

“Then don’t.”

Without him, visitors asked her questions she could not answer. Why had the violin maker stopped? Had the red mittens belonged to a child who died? Was the chess game interrupted by war?

Sometimes the records supplied ordinary explanations. The violin maker developed an allergy to the varnish. The chess players got hungry, and one knocked the board over while reaching for his coat. Sometimes there was no explanation at all.

“Surely you could find out,” a visitor said.

Lena looked at the mittens.

“Possibly,” she replied.

The first school group arrived in May. Twenty-three children entered with the collective momentum of a dropped tray. Their teacher apologized before anybody had done anything.

Lena had prepared a talk about creativity and perseverance. Three sentences into it, a boy pointed at the sweater and asked, “Why didn’t they just make the other sleeve?”

“We don’t know.”

“Maybe they only had one arm,” another child said.

“Maybe,” Lena replied.

The teacher began to correct them, then thought better of it.

They spent half an hour inventing explanations for the exhibits. The imaginary country had lost funding. The fox behind the animated door was waiting for a parcel. The ship’s captain refused to sail until someone released him from his plastic frame.

At the end, a quiet girl stayed beside the jigsaw puzzle.

“My mum says I have to finish every book I start,” she said.

“What does your teacher say?”

The teacher, collecting coats nearby, suddenly became very interested in a zip.

In June, a letter arrived from the building’s owner. He intended to sell. The museum could purchase the premises at a price so far beyond its means that Lena initially assumed a decimal point had been omitted.

Ansel read the letter twice.

“Well,” he said.

“That’s it?”

“I’m waiting to see if another word helps.”

She paced the office. They could apply for grants, start a fundraiser, contact newspapers. There must be foundations interested in overlooked cultural institutions.

“There are,” Ansel said. “They receive many applications.”

“So we write a good one.”

They spent three weeks on the application. Lena described the collection as an archive of interrupted creative practice. Ansel crossed out “interrupted” and wrote “unfinished.” She restored “interrupted” because the foundation’s guidelines used it.

They counted visitors. They photographed the galleries. They attached testimonials, a budget, and a plan for expanding educational outreach.

Under *Demonstrated outcomes*, Lena wrote three sentences, deleted them, and went to look at the ship.

The loose threads had gathered dust. Carefully, she cleaned them with a soft brush.

The foundation declined. So did another. A local newspaper ran a cheerful article under the headline MUSEUM MAY NEVER BE FINISHED, which produced forty-six visitors, twelve donations, and enough money to pay the electricity bill.

Lena began staying late. She made lists at home. She woke thinking of people she might contact.

One evening, she found Ansel removing labels from an empty display case.

“What are you doing?”

“Planning.”

“For closing?”

“For what happens next.”

She felt a sharp, unreasonable anger.

“You could try harder.”

He set down the label.

“Yes,” he said. “I could.”

The simplicity of his answer stopped her.

“I’ve been here thirty-one years, Lena. I wanted somewhere these things could be kept without apology. For thirty-one years, there has been somewhere. I’m not sure losing the building makes all of that a failure.”

She wanted to argue. Instead, she sat beside him.

Beyond the wall, the baker was dragging racks across his floor. The locksmith’s bell rang. Someone outside laughed so loudly that they both turned toward the sound.

“What will happen to everything?” she asked.

“We’ll ask.”

And they did. They wrote to donors and their families. Some wanted their objects back; others did not. A library offered space for the imaginary map and several manuscripts. The local school adopted the papier-mâché moon. The animated fox went online, where viewers supplied hundreds of theories about what stood behind the door. The woman who watched the jigsaw puzzle took it home.

“Will you finish it?” Lena asked.

“Perhaps. I’ve retired.”

The answer pleased her more than she expected.

On the final Saturday, the museum was crowded. People moved slowly through rooms that had seemed too small when full and now looked smaller as they emptied. The baker brought rolls. The locksmith fixed the office latch without being asked.

Lena packed her father’s ship. Beneath its stand she found Ansel’s label, which she had somehow never read closely.

*Model schooner, worked on intermittently over twenty years. According to the donor, its maker enjoyed having it to look forward to.*

She wrapped the loose mast separately.

At home, she put the ship on a low shelf near the window. It occupied the space where she had intended to keep a houseplant, once she found a kind she could reliably keep alive. In daylight, the blue paint revealed small variations: darker beneath the rail, thin near the stern. One cannon pointed inward. Her father must have noticed. Perhaps he had meant to fix it. Perhaps he had decided nobody would come aboard from that direction.

A week later, Lena bought a small pair of cutters. She sat at her kitchen table, lifted the plastic frame from the box, and carefully freed the captain. Then she placed him on the deck. He leaned slightly, but stayed upright. She carried the ship back to the shelf, washed the tea towel, and put it in the drawer with her others.
