samples.result:
# The Museum of Unfinished Things

On the morning the museum appeared, every clock in town was seven minutes slow. This was not immediately considered a miracle. The town had suffered worse inconveniences, including a mayor who collected ceremonial scissors and a winter during which all the pears tasted faintly of onions. People adjusted their watches, missed their buses, and blamed the power station. Only Ada Vale noticed the new building between the pharmacy and the locksmith, where an alley had been the evening before. It had narrow windows, a green door, and a brass plaque that read: MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS. Admission was free.

Ada was sixty-three and had recently become unemployed in a manner everyone described as retirement. For thirty-eight years she had repaired clocks in the shop her father had opened after the war. Now the landlord wanted a wine bar, and her knees objected to the cellar stairs. She had packed her tools into six wooden boxes and brought them home. Each morning she still woke at half past six, dressed, and waited for the day to explain itself. That morning, carrying a loaf of bread she did not particularly want, she stood before the museum and tried its door.

Inside, the air smelled of pencil shavings, raincoats, and the dusty warmth behind a television. A woman sat at a desk, knitting something gray. Her needles moved steadily, but the fabric remained the same length. Above her hung a sign: PLEASE DO NOT COMPLETE THE EXHIBITS. Beneath that, in smaller letters: Even if you know how. Ada approached the desk. “Is this new?” she asked. “To you,” the woman said. She had a friendly face, though Ada could not later have described it. “Do I need a ticket?” “Only if you intend to leave.” Ada put down her bread.

The woman handed her a pale blue ticket with no number on it. “What sort of things do you collect?” Ada asked. “The unfinished sort.” “Buildings?” “Occasionally. They’re difficult to dust.” The woman pointed toward an archway. “Start wherever you like. Most visitors begin with the objects. Please leave your bread here. We had trouble once with a sandwich.” Ada considered asking what kind of trouble, then decided she would rather not know. She tucked the ticket into her coat and entered the first gallery, where a hundred glass cases stood beneath a ceiling painted to resemble an ordinary ceiling.

The first case held a red mitten with three fingers. Its label read: Made by Emil S., aged nine, for his younger brother. Abandoned upon discovery that mittens generally require fewer fingers. Beside it lay a shopping list ending with the word something. There was a half-carved horse, a crossword with every answer filled except DOWN 14, and a jigsaw puzzle depicting a stormy harbor. The puzzle lacked one piece of sky. Ada bent closer. Through the opening she saw a seabird pass, very far away. She straightened, waited, and bent again. This time there was only blue.

She had expected the place to be melancholy. Instead, the first gallery felt almost cheerful. Someone had given up knitting a scarf and used the needles to support a tomato plant. A manuscript titled A Complete History of Human Civilization stopped on page four, halfway through an argument about turnips. An elaborate machine designed to peel grapes had been abandoned after its inventor fell in love with someone who preferred apples. Under each object was a small account of interruption: boredom, illness, employment, embarrassment, a change in weather. Some labels said simply: The maker found something else to do.

In the second room, the exhibits became less easily contained. A sentence hovered above a velvet cushion: What I should have told you was—. Every few seconds its final dash lengthened, as if listening. In a shallow bowl lay the silence after an unanswered question. It looked like water until Ada noticed that reflections entered it but did not return. A wedding speech occupied three shelves. Its speaker had died before the ceremony, and the unwitnessed jokes occasionally laughed at themselves. Ada passed these things more carefully. Here the museum’s polished floor seemed unusually loud beneath her ordinary shoes.

At the far end of the room stood a kitchen table set for two. One chair was pushed back. On the other rested a cardigan Ada recognized before she understood why. It was brown, with leather buttons and a burn on the cuff. Her father had worn it for twenty years. She reached toward the sleeve, then stopped. A label stood beside the sugar bowl. Breakfast, 17 October. Conversation interrupted at 8:12 a.m. Below that: Property of Arthur Vale and his daughter. Ada read it twice. Her father had been dead for eleven years. She had forgotten the cardigan.

She remembered the breakfast. That was the trouble: she remembered it perfectly. Her father had wanted to discuss selling the shop. His hands shook, and customers had begun to notice. Ada had mistaken his weariness for surrender. She had spoken sharply about responsibility and the family name. He had stirred his tea long after the sugar dissolved. “You think I kept it open because of the name?” he had asked. Then the telephone rang. Ada answered it. A customer needed a carriage clock delivered. When she returned, her father had gone upstairs. They never resumed the conversation afterward.

“People usually recognize something,” said the woman from the desk. She had arrived without her knitting. Ada kept looking at the empty chair. “Did he mean to say more?” “Presumably.” “Can I hear it?” “There’s nothing here to hear. He never said it.” Ada turned. “Then what is this for?” The woman looked at the table as though the answer might be underneath it. “I don’t know that it has a use,” she said. “Things arrive. We give them somewhere to stand.” Ada disliked this answer. She had spent her working life making objects justify their place in the world.

“Who brings them?” she asked. “Mostly nobody.” “And you’re the curator?” “On Tuesdays.” “It’s Thursday.” The woman glanced toward a window. “Then I’m probably covering.” Ada would have preferred a proper explanation, ideally one involving a delivery entrance and a system of records. She asked whether there was a catalog. The woman nodded toward a large book on a stand. Its pages turned by themselves, too quickly to read. “We’ve been meaning to finish it,” she said. Ada almost smiled, which annoyed her. She returned her attention to the cardigan. The little burn seemed more terrible than any ghost.

Her father had made it while reaching across a soldering iron. Ada had been fourteen. He had looked at the smoking cuff and said, with immense gravity, “Your grandmother must never know.” For years afterward, whenever anything broke or burned or went missing, they had repeated the phrase. Then her grandmother died, and somehow the joke became impossible, though neither of them had decided to stop. Standing beside the table, Ada realized how much of a life disappeared without ceremony. A joke went unused. A route home changed. Someone bought a new kind of tea. Eventually, almost everything was different.

She returned the next morning. The museum was still there, though the locksmith insisted the neighboring building had always been a dry cleaner. This time Ada brought no bread. She went directly to the kitchen table and sat opposite the cardigan. Nothing happened. After a while she described the sale of the shop, then corrected herself. “Not the sale. The landlord took it back.” She explained the boxes of tools and the mornings. It embarrassed her to speak aloud. It embarrassed her more to stop. Finally she said, “I thought you wanted me to prove it had all been worthwhile.”

The sugar bowl did not tremble. No spoon rose into the air. Her father, who had disliked dramatic displays, made none. Ada sat for another ten minutes, then stood. Before leaving, she noticed that the table had a small wobble. One leg was shorter than the others. She folded an old receipt and crouched to slide it underneath. “Careful,” called the woman. Ada froze. “I’m not completing anything.” “I know. But some visitors begin with the furniture.” Ada removed the paper. On her way out, she asked whether the woman had a name. “Nell,” she said. “For practical purposes.”

Over the following weeks, Ada learned the museum’s geography, though geography was perhaps too confident a word. The staircase sometimes led to a mezzanine and sometimes to a room filled with abandoned New Year’s resolutions, which smelled strongly of unused trainers. Behind the cloakroom was an unfinished tunnel whose far end opened onto a summer afternoon in 1926. Ada was forbidden to enter it because of mosquitoes. A door marked STAFF ONLY contained a field. Another, marked FIELD, contained the staff lavatory. Nell seemed unsurprised by everything except the kettle, which regularly boiled before anyone had switched it on.

There were other visitors. A young man came to look at the first eight pages of a novel and always left furious. Two sisters stood for an hour beside a holiday they had never taken. A boy in a school uniform inspected a model airplane with one wing, then asked whether its owner might still want it. Nell said she hoped so. An elderly couple visited separately, on different days, to sit beside the same apology. Ada noticed that nobody was encouraged to forgive, resume, or let go. Nell offered chairs. Sometimes she offered tea. She never offered a conclusion.

By the fourth week, Ada had begun helping. She repaired a loose hinge on a display case and replaced the felt beneath a sculpture of an unmade decision. She was permitted to mend the museum, Nell explained, but not its contents. This distinction became difficult when a half-built mechanical bird began clicking in distress. Ada could see the problem: a spring pressed against the wrong tooth. One small adjustment would free the mechanism. She stood with her screwdriver ready. “It sounds uncomfortable,” she said. Nell listened. “Yes.” “We could help.” “We could change it,” Nell replied. “That’s not necessarily the same.”

Ada put the screwdriver away, but the clicking followed her home. That night she opened the first of her wooden toolboxes. Beneath the oil bottles lay a watch her father had never repaired. She remembered the customer: a tall woman who laughed when told the damage was extensive. “Keep it,” she had said. “My husband gave it to me when he was still trying.” The watch had remained in a drawer for thirty years. Ada wound it carefully. Nothing. She opened the back and found the broken pivot almost at once. By midnight, the watch was ticking on her table.

The next morning, the museum had no front door. Ada found a blank wall between the pharmacy and the locksmith. She knocked on the bricks. The pharmacist came outside and asked whether she needed assistance. “There was a museum here,” Ada said. He looked at her with a kindness she found insulting. She went home, carrying the repaired watch in her pocket. All afternoon its ticking seemed excessively self-satisfied. At six, someone knocked. Nell stood on the doorstep holding Ada’s loaf of bread, now hard enough to serve as a structural support. “You forgot this,” she said. Ada let her in.

“I broke a rule,” Ada said. Nell placed the loaf on the kitchen counter. “Did you?” Ada produced the watch. “It was unfinished.” “So are most things.” “Then why did the museum disappear?” Nell looked around the kitchen. Six toolboxes stood against the wall. Only one was open. “Perhaps you were expected somewhere else.” Ada frowned. “That sounds like an answer designed to avoid being checked.” “It is,” said Nell. “I’ve found them useful.” She accepted tea and examined the watch. “Nice work.” “My father could have done it.” “Probably.” “He just didn’t.” Nell handed it back. “Apparently not.”

For several minutes they drank in silence. Outside, a delivery van reversed with three apologetic beeps. Ada said, “I thought if I kept the shop going, I could finish what he started.” Nell brushed a crumb from her sleeve. “Did he start a shop, or did he run one?” Ada looked up. The distinction irritated her first, then settled somewhere she could feel it. Her father had opened the shutters every morning. He had argued with suppliers, repaired clocks, eaten sandwiches over the sink, and gone home. The shop had been his livelihood. It had also made him tired.

“What happens to the exhibits?” Ada asked. “Do they stay forever?” “Some do. Some leave.” “When someone finishes them?” “Sometimes. Others stop belonging to us.” Nell stood and carried her cup to the sink. Ada wanted to ask about the breakfast, but Nell was already putting on her coat. At the door she paused. “There’s a loose handrail on the upper stairs. If you happen to be passing.” “Will there be an upper staircase?” “One hopes.” After she left, Ada sat listening to the repaired watch. Then she opened the second toolbox and began sorting its contents into the kitchen drawers.

The museum returned on Monday, slightly narrower. Ada fixed the handrail. She visited the kitchen table only briefly, long enough to notice a tea stain she had missed before. Then she spent an hour talking to the boy with the airplane. His name was Leo, and he wanted to build something that actually flew. Ada knew little about flight, but she understood balance and the stubborn behavior of small parts. They arranged to meet at the public library. Nell lent them a pencil, making them promise to return it unfinished. Leo thought this was the funniest thing anyone had ever said.

Spring came. Ada began repairing clocks at her kitchen table, two mornings a week. She charged enough to discourage people who wanted miracles cheaply. On Saturdays, Leo brought balsa wood, glue, and occasionally his little sister, who believed every aircraft should have curtains. The first plane crashed. The second flew into a pond. The third remained airborne for eleven seconds, which they celebrated with cake. Ada still visited the museum. Sometimes she sat beside her father’s cardigan. Sometimes she walked past it. She never heard the end of his sentence, though she stopped trying to supply the words herself.

One Thursday, the kitchen table was gone. Ada stood before the space it had occupied. There was no label, only a slightly paler rectangle on the floor. She fetched a cloth and a small tin of polish from the cupboard beneath Nell’s desk. Kneeling took some effort. She worked along the edge, testing whether the difference would come out. By noon she was hungry. Nell brought her bread and cheese on a plate, and Ada ate sitting on the floor, with her shoes off. Then she put them back on, washed her hands, and went to meet Leo at the library.

# The Office of Unclaimed Hours

When the railway station closed, the town converted it into a library, except for the room where passengers had once complained about delays. That became the Office of Unclaimed Hours. Nobody remembered voting for it. One Monday there was simply a brass plaque beside the door, a clerk behind the glass, and a notice explaining that time lost through no fault of one’s own might, under certain circumstances, be recovered. The notice was printed in very small type. People assumed this was a government service and therefore probably useless. For the first three weeks, nobody went inside.

Mara entered on a Thursday because it was raining and the library had not opened yet. She repaired umbrellas for a living, which meant rain was both her livelihood and a professional embarrassment. The umbrella she carried had a broken rib. She had intended to fix it for months. Behind the glass sat a narrow man in a green cardigan, eating a pear with the thoughtful concentration of someone reading a difficult letter. He looked up when she came in, then down at the umbrella dripping on his floor.

“You can leave it in the stand,” he said.

The stand contained a walking stick and a sword.

“I’m only waiting for the library.”

“That’s perfectly acceptable. We don’t recover time lost willingly.”

He slid a form through the opening beneath the glass anyway. It asked for her name, address, and the approximate duration of the loss. Under Cause, the available boxes were Mechanical Failure, Administrative Error, Deception, Weather, and Other. Mara thought of the afternoon she had spent waiting for a plumber who never arrived. She thought of her marriage. She checked Weather, because it seemed impolite to enter a strange office and immediately become complicated.

“How much?” the clerk asked.

“Twenty minutes, perhaps.”

“Perhaps won’t do.”

He gave her a pencil and pointed toward a clock above the door. It had three hands, none of which moved.

“What does that tell you?”

“How certain I am,” he said.

Mara looked again. The shortest hand trembled.

She put down the pencil. “I don’t think I understand what this office does.”

“Most people lose time in small, ordinary ways. A late bus. A locked gate. Instructions that send them to the wrong building. Usually it disperses. Occasionally it collects.”

“Where?”

“In the vicinity.”

He said this as though describing damp.

“Can you give it back?”

“If we can establish ownership.”

Mara laughed. The clerk waited without smiling, which made her feel she had laughed at someone’s medical condition.

He introduced himself as Vale. Then he brought out a wooden tray holding several glass objects. They resembled the cloudy marbles children found in gardens, except each contained something moving. In one, a curtain billowed. In another, a little patch of sunlight crawled across a wall. A third held nothing Mara could see, though when Vale set it down she heard the distant sound of someone clearing a throat.

“Seven minutes at a dental surgery,” he said. “Unclaimed since April.”

“What would I do with seven minutes?”

“Use them.”

“Would I become younger?”

“No.”

“Could I go back?”

“No.”

He lifted the marble with the curtain inside.

“This belonged to a woman whose train was delayed outside the town where her sister lived. She recovered forty-three minutes. Spent them sleeping.”

“That sounds disappointing.”

“She had a newborn.”

Mara stayed until the rain stopped. Before leaving, she asked whether Vale could recover time someone had wasted deliberately.

“Whose intention?” he asked.

“Mine.”

“No. Though people are often mistaken about what they chose.”

She did not like this answer. It sounded expensive, even though a second notice explained that all services were free.

Her shop occupied the ground floor of a house that leaned toward the canal. The sign above its window read MARA VENN: UMBRELLAS, PARASOLS, MINOR REPAIRS. The last phrase had expanded over the years to include lampshades, handbags, folding chairs, and, once, a stuffed heron with a damaged leg. People brought whatever they could not bear to throw away and hoped she would understand its mechanism. Usually she did. Objects were generous that way. They broke in specific places.

On her workbench lay a blue umbrella with a silver handle. Its owner had died six weeks earlier.

His daughter had come to settle his account.

“You can keep it,” she said. “Or give it away.”

But the repair ticket was still attached, and Mara could not bring herself to remove it. The man had visited every autumn, whether the umbrella needed attention or not. He wore a brown hat and smelled faintly of oranges. It troubled her that she could remember the precise shape of his hands but not his name.

That evening, she took the umbrella to the office. Vale was watering a plant with no leaves.

“Is this yours?” he asked.

“No.”

“Then we’ll need permission.”

“He’s dead.”

“Ah.”

Vale put away the watering can.

Mara expected condolences. Instead, he asked whether she knew the man’s name. She admitted she did not. He turned the repair ticket over. There, in her own handwriting, was Arthur Bell.

“I stopped reading it,” she said.

Vale nodded, not unkindly.

From a filing cabinet he extracted a drawer much longer than the cabinet itself. It extended across the room until its far end touched the opposite wall.

Mara decided not to comment.

“Bell,” he murmured, moving through folders. “Arthur. There are several.”

“He had a daughter. He used to work at the foundry.”

“That helps.”

Vale removed a little paper envelope.

Inside was a pale disk like a slice of onion.

“Eleven minutes,” he said. “He waited outside your shop last November. You were late opening.”

“I had a hospital appointment.”

“Then it wasn’t your fault.”

“Can his daughter have them?”

“No. They were his.”

“What happens to them?”

“They remain here until they can no longer be distinguished from ordinary time.”

Mara looked at the envelope in his hand.

“May I see?”

Vale hesitated. “Seeing is not the same as using.”

He placed the disk on the counter.

The office grew cold. Through the glass, Mara saw her own shopfront, the shutters down, the canal dark behind her. Arthur Bell stood beneath the awning, holding his umbrella across his body. He checked his watch. A girl passed carrying a violin case. He stepped aside for her, although there was ample room.

Nothing else happened.

After a while he took an orange from his pocket and began peeling it in one long ribbon. He saved half in a paper bag.

Then the office returned.

“That’s all?”

“That’s all.”

Mara went home irritated with him, though she could not have said whether she meant Vale or Arthur Bell. She had wanted something more useful than a man eating an orange. At the shop she cut the old ticket from the blue umbrella and wrote a new one: REPAIRED. She stood it beside the door, where a customer might notice it. Then she searched her ledger for his daughter’s address.

Word spread slowly. The butcher recovered half an hour lost during a power cut and used it to sharpen every knife in his kitchen. A schoolboy reclaimed nine minutes from a jammed locker and spent them looking at a beetle. Mrs. Pell, who chaired three committees, applied for fourteen years. Vale asked her to itemize them. She returned with six binders, and the office closed early that day.

Some people accused him of favoritism. Others said the service undermined the value of punctuality. The newspaper requested an interview. Vale answered its questions by post, enclosing a leaflet that explained very little.

Mara began bringing him lunch on Fridays.

It was not entirely charitable. His office remained warm without a visible stove, and he listened carefully when she described difficult repairs. He was particularly interested in hinges.

“A good hinge is surprisingly hard to make,” she told him.

“So I’ve gathered.”

“Have you tried?”

“No. But I see a great deal of time lost because of bad ones.”

She brought a spare hinge the following week. He kept it beside his blotter.

They became friends, although Mara would have preferred a more precise word for someone whose age, home address, and ordinary evening activities she did not know.

In January, a letter arrived from her brother.

He had written to tell her that their mother’s house was finally sold. There were papers to sign, a small amount of money to divide, and three boxes he thought she might want. His letter was courteous. Mara read it twice, looking for an accusation, then a third time because she had found none.

She and her brother had not spoken in eight years.

The quarrel had begun over their mother’s care and widened to include childhood, money, which of them always left, and which of them made leaving necessary. Mara could no longer reconstruct the sequence. She remembered saying something cruel with the deliberate clarity of a person setting down a glass she intends to break.

That Friday, she asked Vale about eight years.

He took off his spectacles.

“Were they taken from you?”

“It feels that way.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

She stood to leave. He did not stop her, but as she reached the door he said, “You can apply. I can’t promise anything.”

The form was the same as before.

Under Cause, she checked Other.

The office requested supporting documents. Mara supplied the letter, two photographs, and an account of the quarrel that she rewrote four times. In the first version her brother was selfish. In the second they were both exhausted. In the third she described the hospital corridor, the paper cup burning her fingers, and the way he had kept looking toward the lift. In the fourth she admitted that she did not know why he had been looking.

Vale accepted all four.

“Will this take long?”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“I’m afraid that time isn’t recoverable.”

She nearly smiled, then saw he was serious.

For several weeks she heard nothing. She repaired a wedding parasol and twenty-three umbrellas after a storm. She tried to answer her brother’s letter. Dear Thomas looked too formal. Tom seemed presumptuous. She wrote the address on an envelope and left the paper blank.

In February, Arthur Bell’s daughter collected the blue umbrella.

“I thought you’d sold it.”

“I meant to write.”

The woman opened it carefully in the shop. One panel had faded more than the others.

“He always stood with his left side toward the sun,” she said.

Mara waited while she examined the handle.

Then, without planning to, she told her about the orange.

The woman laughed.

“He used to bring me half. Said he couldn’t finish a whole one, but he never bought smaller oranges.”

She closed the umbrella. Mara did not explain where she had seen him. There seemed no way to do so without making the visit harder.

After she left, Mara sat behind the counter for a while.

That afternoon she wrote to her brother.

She began with the practical matters. Yes, she would sign the papers. Yes, she wanted the boxes. Then she wrote that she was sorry for what she had said in the hospital.

She did not add an explanation.

Vale’s decision arrived three days later.

Her claim was approved in part.

Mara took the notice to his office before opening the shop. She had not slept well. All night she had imagined years stacked somewhere, ready to be handed over.

“How much?” she asked.

“Six seconds.”

He said it gently, which was worse.

“Out of eight years?”

“Most of those years were lived. You worked. You ate. You went places. Your brother did too. They aren’t held here.”

“And the six seconds?”

Vale laid a small clear bead on the counter.

“After he asked whether you wanted him to stay at the hospital. Before you answered.”

“I remember answering.”

“Yes.”

“Can I change it?”

“No.”

“Then what earthly use is this?”

He folded his hands.

“I don’t know.”

She disliked him more in that moment than she ever had.

He let her take the bead home in a matchbox.

It weighed almost nothing. Beside the claim number, the instructions said to hold it firmly and allow the recovered interval to elapse. Mara put it in a drawer.

Her brother answered on Tuesday. He thanked her. He was sorry too. Would Saturday suit for bringing the boxes?

She spent the intervening days cleaning parts of the shop he would never see. On Saturday morning she bought biscuits he had liked as a child, then wondered whether he still liked them. She put a plate on the counter and immediately moved it upstairs.

At noon a car stopped outside.

Mara watched him get out. He had grown heavier. His beard was gray. For a moment she was angry that he had changed without her, then embarrassed by the thought.

He opened the boot.

She took the matchbox from the drawer.

There was still time to leave it there.

Instead, she pressed the bead between finger and thumb.

Six seconds passed.

She heard the hospital lift arrive. Her mother coughed behind a curtain. Thomas stood beside her, younger and frightened, holding two cups of tea. His question had been ordinary.

Do you want me to stay?

She had heard an offer made from duty. She had heard his wish to escape. Now she could hear the question, and she still did not know what he had wanted.

The bead was gone. Outside, Thomas lifted the first box.

Mara went to open the door.

“Hello, Tom.”

“Hello.”

“Let me take that.”

“It’s heavy.”

“I’ve got it.”

They carried the boxes upstairs together. She made tea. He noticed the biscuits and ate three before she had finished pouring. For the first half hour they discussed the house, the sale, and a damp patch the surveyor had found. Then Thomas opened a box and took out their mother’s kitchen scales.

“Do these work?” he asked.

Mara cleared a space on the table. One pan hung lower than the other. She examined the little brass pivot, then fetched her tools.

While she worked, he held the lamp closer.

Neither mentioned the hospital. There would be time for that later. For now, the pivot needed cleaning, and her brother had the light exactly where she needed it.

# The Department of Unclaimed Time

On her first morning at the Department of Unclaimed Time, Mara was told never to open a container that was humming.

“Whistling is harmless,” said Mr. Vale. “Ticking is expected. If it sounds like someone quietly clearing their throat, put it beside a window until Thursday.”

“And humming?”

“Come and get me.”

He gave her a brass key, a ledger, and a desk whose previous occupant had worn two pale hollows into the wood with her elbows.

The department occupied the basement of the central railway station. Above them, trains carried people toward marriages, interviews, operations, seaside holidays, and jobs they intended to leave. Below, in six long rooms, the time those people mislaid was collected, measured, and stored.

There were seconds dropped while searching for tickets already held in the hand. There were afternoons lost to waiting for plumbers. There were the peculiar, brittle minutes between deciding to say something and deciding against it.

Those came in narrow blue bottles.

Mara’s first assignment was to label seventeen minutes found in a telephone queue.

“Do we give them back?” she asked.

“If someone claims them.”

“How would they know?”

Mr. Vale looked troubled.

“There used to be a poster.”

***

Twenty-three years later, Mara was head of the department, and the poster had still not been replaced.

Mr. Vale had retired to a village where, according to his Christmas cards, nothing happened at a manageable pace. Mara now had his office, his pension calculations, and his responsibility for humming containers.

She had opened one only once.

Inside was the summer a nine-year-old boy had expected to last forever.

For three days afterward, everything smelled of warm bicycle tires.

The work had changed less than the station overhead. Paper tickets disappeared. The station café became a pharmacy, then a café again, but one where the cups had lids and nobody brought the coffee to your table.

The lost time arrived just as steadily.

A morning spent refreshing a tracking page could fill a biscuit tin. An hour in a meeting that should have been a note arrived flattened and gray, like felt. Whole weekends misplaced in the vague intention of doing something worthwhile were too heavy for one person to lift.

Mara handled them with a trolley.

She was careful not to think of the owners.

Thinking of them slowed the work, and there was already so much work that her lunch usually went uneaten until four.

At home, her son Daniel telephoned on Sundays.

He lived three hundred miles away and designed drainage systems.

When she asked about his work, he said, “Water still goes downhill.”

When he asked about hers, she said, “People are still careless.”

They had worn these remarks smooth enough to pass between them without effort.

One Sunday he told her he and his wife were separating.

Mara stood beside the kitchen window with a tea towel over her shoulder.

“Oh,” she said.

Then, because the silence frightened her, she asked whether they had considered counseling.

“Yes.”

“And you’re certain?”

“No.”

She could hear traffic at his end. He was outside somewhere.

“Have you eaten?”

“Mum.”

“I only meant—”

“I know.”

Afterward, while washing a clean plate, she found forty-three seconds in the sink.

They looked like a small, transparent fish.

She put them in a jam jar and took them to work.

***

The closure notice arrived on a Tuesday.

It was delivered by a young man wearing a coat too expensive to look new. He introduced himself as Adrian Bell, from Municipal Efficiencies, and apologized for coming in person.

“We usually do these remotely,” he said. “But your department isn’t on the system.”

“We’re under it.”

He smiled uncertainly.

Mara read the notice twice.

The department was to be consolidated. Its premises would become commercial storage. Its holdings would be transferred to an approved contractor for productive redistribution.

“What does that mean?” she asked.

Adrian glanced toward the shelves.

“The accumulated resource will be reintroduced where demand is highest.”

“Where?”

“Workplaces, primarily. There’s a pilot scheme.”

Mara considered a biscuit tin containing the Saturday a man had spent waiting for his daughter to call.

“What kind of workplaces?”

“I don’t have those details.”

“And the owners?”

“Ownership is considered to have lapsed after a reasonable period.”

“How reasonable?”

He looked at the notice.

“It doesn’t specify.”

She showed him the storage rooms.

There were cabinets of misplaced mornings, drums of unused patience, and drawers holding the seconds people lost when they saw someone they loved coming toward them.

Adrian stopped beside a glass case containing something that flickered green.

“What’s that?”

“Eleven minutes from a school sports day.”

“Someone bored?”

“Someone happy. It’s not only unpleasant time people lose.”

He bent closer.

Inside the glass, small shadows ran across grass.

“Can you watch it?”

“Only from the outside.”

He straightened and took out his phone, then seemed to reconsider.

At the door, he said the decision was not personal.

Mara had never understood why people thought that helped.

***

The following morning, she began the transfer inventory.

She listed each container by weight, duration, condition, and provenance. The contractor had requested that personal associations be omitted.

By lunchtime, she had reduced a widow’s first Christmas to:

**3 hours, 12 minutes. Stable. Domestic.**

She put down her pen.

In the oldest storeroom, behind a cabinet of railway delays, she found a door she had never opened. Its paint matched the wall. The key hung from a nail above the frame.

Inside were wooden crates packed in straw.

The dates on them went back eighty years.

Mara lifted a lid.

The container within was not glass or metal but something like thick ice. It gave off neither cold nor heat. Through it, she could see a kitchen table laid for four.

There were only three chairs.

The label read:

**TIME THAT NEVER BELONGED TO ANYONE.**

Underneath, in Mr. Vale’s handwriting:

**Do not confuse with time that has merely been wasted.**

She telephoned him that evening.

He answered on the seventh ring.

“I was watching a fox,” he said.

“In the garden?”

“On television. What’s happened?”

She told him about the closure, the contractor, and the room.

For a while he said nothing.

Then he asked, “How much is there?”

“Years.”

“Yes. I suppose there would be.”

“What is it?”

He sighed.

“You know when a room is ready before anyone arrives? Or when an appointment is canceled and nobody fills the gap? There are intervals that don’t quite attach themselves to a life.”

“Surely someone owns them.”

“Not always.”

Outside Mara’s kitchen window, a bus stopped. One passenger got off carrying a tall plant in a paper sleeve.

“What do we do with it?”

“We were meant to release it.”

“When?”

“There was a procedure. Then there was a review of the procedure. Then the official authorized to approve releases died.”

“And nobody replaced him?”

“His post was absorbed into parking.”

Mara closed her eyes.

“Could it go to the contractor?”

“Anything can go to a contractor if the form is badly enough designed.”

She heard him settle more heavily into his chair.

“There’s a valve behind the station clock,” he said.

***

On Friday, Daniel called at half past eleven in the morning.

She nearly let it ring. There were forms spread across her desk, and Adrian was due at noon.

“Are you busy?” Daniel asked.

“Yes,” she said. Then: “But go on.”

He had gone back to the house to collect some clothes. His wife had left them in bags beside the door.

“She put the blue jumper in,” he said.

“Is that bad?”

“No. I don’t know. She hates that jumper.”

Mara waited.

“It was thoughtful,” he said. “That’s what’s awful.”

She looked at the jam jar on her desk. The forty-three seconds turned slowly inside.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“I know you are.”

She wanted to tell him that people sometimes came back, that things often improved, that he was young enough to begin again. Each sentence presented itself complete and useless.

So she asked where he was.

“In the car.”

“Are you driving?”

“No.”

“All right.”

For a while she listened to him breathe.

At noon Adrian knocked and opened the door. Mara held up one finger.

He sat outside until twelve twenty.

***

The release apparatus occupied a narrow chamber behind the station’s great clock.

To reach it, Mara climbed a staircase that grew steeper as it rose. Adrian followed, carrying a torch.

She had told him only that there was a piece of municipal equipment absent from his report.

“That happens quite often,” he said.

Behind the clock face, daylight entered through the translucent numerals. Machinery worked in patient increments. The minute hand moved with a sound like a boot dragged across gravel.

The valve was waist-high, painted red, and attached to a pipe descending through the floor.

A brass plate read:

**PUBLIC DISPENSATION — LOCAL ONLY.**

Beneath that:

**ENSURE ADEQUATE RECEPTION.**

“Reception?” Adrian said.

“People, I think.”

“Is this safe?”

“Mr. Vale remembers it being safe.”

“How old is Mr. Vale?”

“Eighty-six.”

Adrian inspected the pipe.

“What exactly happens?”

“Time enters the station.”

“Extra time?”

“Unclaimed time.”

“Will the trains be late?”

“I don’t know.”

He laughed once, without amusement.

“That seems like a significant thing not to know.”

Mara agreed.

They went downstairs and found the original operating instructions in a drawer labeled **CATERING**.

The release would affect the station concourse and platforms. Clocks beyond the premises would continue normally. People inside would experience an additional interval without corresponding external passage.

The recommended maximum was one hour.

There were warnings against release during fire, flood, structural instability, or periods of insufficient ventilation.

Adrian read everything twice.

“We can’t just do this.”

“No.”

“We’d need authorization.”

“The authorized post was absorbed into parking.”

He looked up.

“You’re joking.”

“I wish I were.”

He sat down at Mr. Vale’s old desk.

From above came the rolling thunder of a train pulling out.

“If we apply,” Mara said, “they’ll seal the equipment before answering.”

Adrian traced a scratch in the desktop.

“My mother used to come here early,” he said. “For every train. Forty minutes early, sometimes.”

Mara waited.

“I thought it was because she was anxious. After she died, my father told me she liked sitting somewhere nobody could ask her to do anything.”

He stood.

“That doesn’t constitute authorization.”

“No,” Mara said.

“But I’ll check the ventilation.”

***

They chose Wednesday at five forty.

The station was full but not crowded. A light rain had brought people indoors. On platform three, a child in yellow boots stamped at the thin water running beneath a bench.

Mara connected the oldest containers to the intake beneath the basement ceiling. Their contents moved reluctantly at first, then flowed like clear oil.

Adrian stood in the clock chamber with his phone.

“Ready?” he asked.

She thought of the table laid for four.

“Yes.”

Nothing dramatic happened.

No great bell sounded. No light swept through the building.

On the concourse, a woman looked up from the departure board and frowned at her watch.

A porter stopped beside his trolley.

The rain outside hung beyond the entrance in slanting silver threads.

Mara climbed the stairs.

For the first minute, people were frightened.

They shook their phones and walked toward the doors. At the threshold they stopped, uncertain of the stillness beyond.

Adrian used the public-address system.

His voice emerged too loudly, and several people flinched.

“Please remain calm. The station is experiencing a temporary additional interval.”

He looked helplessly at Mara.

She took the microphone.

“You have some time,” she said. “Nothing is required of you. Normal service will resume shortly.”

This did not reassure everyone.

A man demanded compensation before determining what had happened. A woman began to cry. Two teenagers discovered that their phones still took photographs and photographed each other jumping.

The café manager locked his till.

Then, after a moment, he unlocked it again.

Mara walked through the concourse.

At first people did what they had been doing already. They scrolled through pages that would not refresh. They checked messages that could not arrive. One man continued typing furiously into a laptop.

Then the station began to change.

A nurse took off her shoes.

Two strangers finished the argument they had begun over a seat and found themselves discussing a town where both had lived.

The child in yellow boots lay flat on the floor to inspect the underside of a luggage trolley.

His father started to tell him to get up, then sat beside him.

Not everyone became kinder. Three people quarreled at the café. Someone stole an unattended sandwich. A man who had been drinking fell asleep and missed nearly the whole interval.

Mara was relieved by this.

She had not wanted to improve anybody.

Near the ticket barriers, an elderly woman opened a paperback. She read two pages, looked up suspiciously, then read another.

Adrian sat beneath the departure board.

“What should we do?” he asked.

Mara sat beside him.

Her feet hurt. She had not noticed until then.

For several minutes they watched the suspended rain.

***

There was an investigation afterward.

Adrian received a formal warning. Mara retired three months earlier than planned.

The department closed, but the remaining time was not transferred. An argument about its legal status continued through winter.

Some called it dangerous. Some called it fraud. A newspaper printed a photograph of the sleeping man beneath the headline **FREE HOUR WASTED**.

Mara clipped it out.

Daniel came to stay in March. They spent Saturday repairing her garden gate, badly. On Sunday he asked if she wanted to walk.

She left the washing up.

Outside, he stopped to tie his shoe, and she waited beside him in the sun.

# The Museum of Almost Nothing

On the morning the museum was scheduled to close, a woman arrived carrying a teaspoon wrapped in a blue sock.

She stood outside until I unlocked the door, although it had been raining for twenty minutes and the awning offered no shelter.

“Are you still accepting things?” she asked.

“Until six.”

She nodded as if this confirmed an appointment. Then she followed me inside, leaving dark footprints on the floorboards.

The museum occupied the ground floor of what had once been a dentist’s house. We still had the dentist’s little porcelain sink in the room where we kept unfinished letters. Nobody knew how to remove it without damaging the plaster, so we displayed a toothbrush beside it and called the arrangement *Something Left Behind in a Hurry*.

The woman unwrapped the teaspoon.

It was stainless steel, ordinary except for a slight bend in the handle.

“What’s its story?” I asked.

“My husband used it to check whether the kitchen table was level.”

“Was it?”

“Never.”

She placed the spoon on the counter.

“He could have used a marble. He could have bought a spirit level. But he liked the way the spoon slid. Every few months he’d say the table had gotten worse, though it hadn’t moved.”

I took out an accession form.

“His name?”

She considered this.

“Does it need his name?”

“No.”

“Then just put: He kept checking.”

***

The Museum of Almost Nothing had begun with a mitten.

Not an ancient mitten, not a mitten belonging to a president, not one recovered from a glacier beside a body preserved for five thousand years. It was a child’s red mitten I found on a bus in November.

Someone had tucked it between the window and the seat, making it stand upright as though the bus itself had grown a small woolen hand.

I carried it home because it seemed impossible that nobody wanted it.

For a week it sat on my kitchen counter. I considered putting up a notice, but notices need useful particulars. A lost dog has a name. A stolen bicycle has a make. The mitten had only redness, smallness, and an astonishing capacity to make me feel late for something.

Eventually I put it in a box.

On an index card I wrote:

*One hand was cold.*

My sister found it when she came over for dinner.

“That’s either very sad or very funny,” she said.

“I haven’t decided.”

“You should put it somewhere.”

“It’s in a box.”

“Somewhere other people can see.”

My sister believed most problems were caused by insufficient circulation. Air, money, soup, grief: whatever it was, she thought it improved by being passed around.

Three months later she rented the dentist’s ground floor for almost nothing because the ceiling leaked and the landlord wanted someone to notice if the pipes burst.

We opened on a Saturday.

Seven people came. Two were looking for the dentist.

***

By the end of our first year, we had acquired a button that had waited eleven years to be sewn back on, a receipt for a disappointing anniversary dinner, and a stone a man had carried across three continents without remembering where he had found it.

We refused anything expensive.

This was less a principle than a practical necessity. We could not afford insurance, and neither of us liked the idea of spending our days protecting objects from people.

People were what we were trying to protect the objects for.

There were rules, though we invented most of them after something went wrong.

Nothing alive.

Nothing likely to explode.

No anonymous powders.

No teeth after the incident with the envelope.

Objects did not have to be small, but they had to fit through the door. We made one exception for a park bench, which came through the window in pieces and was reassembled by its donor, a retired carpenter who had proposed marriage on it and been turned down.

“Why keep it?” I asked.

“Beautiful joinery.”

He came every Thursday afterward to sit on it.

My sister made the labels. Her handwriting was clearer than mine, and she had a talent for knowing where to stop.

A cracked green mug:

*The one everyone knew was hers.*

A hotel key:

*He found it after unpacking.*

A paper crown:

*Worn all the way home.*

Sometimes visitors laughed and then became quiet. Sometimes they stayed quiet until the very end and laughed at something that wasn’t meant to be funny.

We learned not to correct them.

***

The museum never became popular, but it became necessary to a small number of people.

A nurse visited after night shifts and fell asleep on the proposal bench. A boy came every month to see the red mitten, though he insisted it had never been his. Two women who had stopped speaking to each other met in the room of unfinished letters and read in silence for forty minutes.

Then they went out for lunch.

We had no admission fee. There was a biscuit tin by the entrance, with a slot cut in the lid.

Some days it held coins. Some days buttons. Once, a folded note that said, *I needed somewhere to be for twenty minutes.*

My sister kept that one.

She died in the museum’s ninth winter, after an illness that turned every calendar in my house into a set of instructions.

For months afterward, I could not make a label.

Objects arrived with their little histories, and I wrote everything down in a ledger, but whenever I tried to reduce a life to three or four lines, the words seemed cruel.

A woman brought in her father’s shopping list.

Milk. Pears. Batteries. Something nice.

“What did he buy?” I asked.

“We don’t know.”

I put the list in a drawer.

There were thirty-seven unlabeled objects by spring.

I would open the drawers each morning and look at them. Then I would make tea, wash the mug, and open the museum.

***

The trouble began, as trouble often does, with a letter written by someone who had never been inside.

The dentist’s house had been sold. The new owner intended to turn it into furnished apartments for people who described themselves as being between places.

We had ninety days.

I applied for grants, wrote to the newspaper, and attended a meeting where a man in expensive shoes asked whether we had considered increasing our digital presence.

“We have a website,” I said.

“When was it last updated?”

I thought about it.

“The museum’s eighth birthday.”

“And how old is the museum now?”

“Fourteen.”

He wrote something down.

A cultural development officer suggested that we emphasize our unique value proposition.

I told her about the paper crown.

She asked how many visitors it attracted annually.

I did not blame these people. They had forms to complete, budgets to defend, reasons for needing numbers instead of stories.

But I had never counted how many people stood before the crown. I knew only that one woman had reached toward it, stopped herself, and tucked both hands beneath her arms.

You could not put that in the box marked projected growth.

We received two sympathetic refusals and one invitation to apply again next year.

I began collecting cardboard boxes from the grocer. At first I flattened them and kept them in the cellar. Eventually there were too many, and I stacked them beside my desk.

***

By noon on the final day, seventeen people had arrived.

That was a large crowd for us.

The retired carpenter came wearing a tie. He stood beside the bench and ran his thumb along its back.

“I can take this apart again,” he said.

“I know.”

“Whenever you’re ready.”

The nurse brought sandwiches. The boy who visited the mitten was now tall enough to duck beneath the low doorway. He came with a young woman and showed her the display without looking at me.

I liked that. I liked being briefly unnecessary to something I had made.

The woman with the teaspoon stayed.

She walked slowly through the rooms, pausing over labels, sometimes going back to read one again.

At one, she called me over.

“Who gave you this?”

It was a small brass bell with no clapper.

“A schoolteacher.”

“Why?”

“She said it had been in her classroom for thirty years.”

“Did it break?”

“No. She took the clapper out herself.”

“Why?”

“She preferred to raise her hand.”

The woman smiled.

“My husband taught geography.”

“Did he use a bell?”

“He used chalk. Threw it with remarkable accuracy.”

She returned to the teaspoon, which I had placed beneath a temporary card.

*He kept checking.*

“It looks smaller in there,” she said.

“Things often do.”

She leaned closer.

“I don’t mind.”

***

At two, a reporter arrived.

She was young and apologetic and carried a notebook with a bent cover. She asked for my age, the museum’s history, a photograph beside something meaningful.

I stood beside the mitten.

“Why does a place like this matter?” she asked.

I had answered versions of that question for fourteen years. Usually I said something about ordinary lives, or attention, or the things that official history forgot.

That afternoon I was tired.

“I don’t know if it matters,” I said.

She lowered her pen.

“People come here,” I continued. “They look at something. Sometimes they tell me something I wouldn’t otherwise know.”

“Such as?”

I pointed to a cheap plastic comb in a shallow tray.

“A man brought that in six years ago. It belonged to his mother. Every morning she combed her hair before opening the curtains.”

“Why?”

“He said she didn’t want to look surprised by the day.”

The reporter wrote that down.

Then she asked what would happen to the collection.

“I’m still deciding.”

This was a lie, although not an ambitious one. I had stopped deciding three nights earlier. I simply had not yet told anyone.

She took her photograph. Before leaving, she spent several minutes beside the shopping list I had finally put on display.

“Something nice,” she read aloud.

Then she shut her notebook and went out.

***

At three, I brought the empty boxes upstairs.

People assumed they were for storage.

“Do you have somewhere to put everything?” the nurse asked.

“Yes,” I said. “I think so.”

I set a box on the counter and took down the cracked green mug.

For fourteen years, I had been careful with that mug. I had dusted around its fracture with a soft brush. I had moved it away from the window after someone told me sunlight could fade the glaze.

Now I held it out.

“Would you take this?”

The nurse looked at me.

“Home?”

“If you want it.”

“But it belongs here.”

I looked around the room.

The familiar shelves seemed oddly bare already. There was a pale square where the mug had stood.

“It needs somewhere else now.”

She took it with both hands.

I gave her its card.

“The story goes with it,” I said. “If you pass it on, pass that on too.”

The carpenter asked whether I was serious.

“Yes.”

“Everything?”

“Everything people want.”

For a while nobody moved.

Then the woman who had brought the spoon approached the brass bell.

“Could I?”

“Yes.”

She lifted it and gave it an experimental shake. It made no sound.

The carpenter laughed. She shook it at him again.

***

Giving away a museum takes less time than building one, but more time than you might think.

People do not simply choose. They hesitate. They feel chosen and distrust the feeling. They ask whether someone else might have a better claim.

A bus driver took the hotel key because his father had worked in that hotel’s kitchens.

A university student took the button that had waited eleven years. She said she might finally sew it onto something.

“Would that be allowed?”

“There’s nobody left to prohibit it.”

The young man who visited the mitten stood before it for a long time.

“I used to come here when my parents were getting divorced,” he said.

I had not known.

“My dad would drop me off while he talked to my mum at the café.”

“Why the mitten?”

He shrugged.

“I liked knowing where it was.”

I opened the case.

His companion watched as he picked it up.

“It’s lighter than I thought,” he said.

Before leaving, he wrote his name and address in the visitor book. He underlined the address twice.

The shopping list went to a baker. The stone went to someone traveling the following week. The proposal bench returned to the carpenter in six pieces.

At five, the woman with the teaspoon approached me.

“What about mine?”

“Would you like it back?”

“No.” She paused. “Would you keep it?”

I wrapped it in its blue sock and put it in my coat pocket.

***

By six, the museum was almost empty.

Dusty rectangles marked the shelves. Hooks stuck out from walls with nothing to hold. In the room of unfinished letters, the dentist’s sink remained stubbornly attached.

I turned on its tap.

For years we had used it only to rinse dust cloths and fill the kettle when the kitchen pipe froze. Water sputtered into the basin, then settled into a clear stream.

The building was going to be apartments. Someone would sleep where the paper crown had stood. Someone would complain about the water pressure without knowing how relieved I had been whenever those old pipes survived a winter.

The last visitor was a child who arrived with her father just as I reached for the sign.

“Are we too late?” he asked.

“Nearly.”

She looked at the empty cases.

“Where’s the museum?”

“It’s gone to stay with people.”

She considered that, then pulled something from her pocket.

It was a small gray pebble, smooth on one side, rough on the other.

“I was going to give you this.”

“What’s its story?”

“I found it.”

“Where?”

“Outside.”

She seemed troubled by the inadequacy of this answer.

I crouched down.

“You can keep it until it has another one.”

She closed her hand around it.

Her father thanked me, though I wasn’t certain what for.

After they left, I locked the door and slipped the key through the landlord’s letterbox upstairs. Then I stood beneath the useless awning and felt for the teaspoon in my pocket.

The rain had stopped.

I went home to my uneven kitchen table, unwrapped the spoon, and laid it on the polished wood. It did not move at first.

I waited. Then, very slowly, it began to slide toward me.

# The Office of Unclaimed Weather

On her first morning at the Office of Unclaimed Weather, Mara was given a brass key, a wool cardigan, and a warning about the cupboard beneath the stairs.

“If you hear birds in there,” said Mr. Vale, “don’t open it.”

“What’s in it?”

“April, mostly.”

He said this without humor, but also without the satisfaction of someone being mysterious. He was a tired man showing a new employee where things belonged.

The office occupied the ground floor of a narrow municipal building between a dentist and a shop that sold only lampshades. Its windows were clouded from the inside. Behind the front counter stood filing cabinets labeled with years, districts, and conditions: DRIZZLE, LOCALIZED; FROST, PREMATURE; WIND, NO FIXED ADDRESS.

Mara had applied because the advertisement promised regular hours and no sales targets. After eleven years selling bathroom fixtures, she wanted work in which nothing was described as aspirational.

“People lose weather?” she asked.

“Constantly,” said Mr. Vale.

He handed her a ledger.

***

Weather became unclaimed when the person it was meant for failed to meet it.

A man died on Thursday, leaving behind the cool Saturday morning in which he would have painted his fence. A woman moved inland before the sea fog she had waited all summer to photograph arrived. A child grew too old, abruptly and without warning, for the first snowfall to mean what it had meant the year before.

Most unused weather dispersed naturally. But certain conditions persisted, especially when someone had expected them very strongly.

These were collected by municipal workers.

“Street sweepers find most of it,” Mr. Vale explained. “Occasionally the parks department. Once, a traffic warden brought in six minutes of perfect rainbow folded inside a parking ticket.”

“What happened to it?”

“Claimed by a schoolteacher. Proper documentation. Very straightforward.”

“And if nobody claims it?”

“We retain it.”

“For how long?”

He looked toward the back of the office, where a corridor extended farther than the building appeared to allow.

“That has become an issue.”

***

Mara’s duties were simple enough.

She logged arrivals, checked claimants’ identification, and maintained suitable distances between incompatible conditions. Thunderstorms could not be shelved beside dry lightning. Fog was stored below eye level. Hail required a locked drawer and a felt-lined scoop.

The cardigan was for cold fronts.

During her first week, she processed a jar of seaside wind, two envelopes of sleet, and a low gray afternoon recovered from a hospital car park.

A porter delivered the afternoon in a covered laundry basket.

“Found it by the payment machine,” he said. “Wouldn’t shift.”

Mara lifted the cover. Inside lay a dimness so dense that the office lights seemed to move farther away.

Mr. Vale gently replaced the cloth.

“Not yet,” he said.

She entered it into the ledger without asking.

There were rules about curiosity. She was beginning to learn them.

***

Most claimants were elderly.

They arrived carrying photographs, old addresses, or pieces of clothing whose relevance they found difficult to explain.

A retired bus driver wanted the frost from the morning he first drove the number sixteen alone. A woman in a green coat came every month to ask about a particular hot wind that had blown through her kitchen in 1974.

“It lifted the recipe off the table,” she said. “He caught it before it touched the floor.”

“Your husband?”

“My first husband.”

The woman smiled.

“The second one would have let it fall.”

Nothing matching her description had been found, but Mr. Vale always searched the drawers. Mara noticed that he never pretended to search. He checked dates, pressure readings, collection sites. Once he spent forty minutes following an incorrect reference into the basement.

“Wouldn’t it be kinder to tell her it’s unlikely?” Mara asked afterward.

“She knows it’s unlikely.”

“Then why does she keep coming?”

Mr. Vale slid the drawer shut.

“I think she likes telling someone about him catching the recipe.”

***

Mara had moved back to town six months after her mother died.

She disliked the phrase moved back. It made the intervening years sound like an errand.

Her mother’s house stood on Bellwether Street, with a shallow front garden and a kitchen window that swelled in damp weather. Mara slept in her childhood bedroom because changing rooms would have required decisions about furniture.

She had emptied the refrigerator immediately. Everything else was taking longer.

There were drawers of rubber bands, appliance warranties, birthday candles, and keys to locks that might no longer exist. In the cupboard above the washing machine, she found fourteen empty glass jars arranged by height.

Her mother had never worked for the weather office. The jars had held marmalade.

Still, Mara examined each one before recycling it.

***

In November, Mr. Vale showed her the returns process.

Occasionally, weather could be released without a claimant. A mild breeze might be assigned to a public garden. An undistinguished shower could water municipal trees.

“You must be sure it’s unattached,” he said.

“How?”

“Usually, unattached weather doesn’t resist.”

He selected a bottle from a shelf labeled MISCELLANEOUS, FAIR.

Inside it, a faint brightness moved like a reflection from water.

They took it to the courtyard behind the office, where a bicycle rusted beneath an elderly climbing rose.

Mr. Vale removed the stopper.

Warm air brushed Mara’s face. For a moment the bricks brightened and the rose gave off a little scent. Then the bottle was empty.

“Late September,” he said. “Nothing complicated.”

Mara found herself smiling.

“Could we do more of that?”

“When appropriate.”

He replaced the stopper.

“People assume pleasant weather is harmless. That isn’t always true.”

***

The cupboard beneath the stairs began singing on a Tuesday.

Not birdsong exactly. More the impression of birds heard from bed, when you have nowhere to go and someone else is making breakfast.

Mara was halfway through an intake form when she recognized a sound she had not heard in twenty-three years: the squeak of her mother opening the kitchen window.

She stood up.

At the far desk, Mr. Vale looked over his glasses.

“Don’t.”

“That’s my house.”

“No. It’s what you’re hearing.”

The cupboard smelled of wet soil and buttered toast.

Mara put her hand on the brass knob.

“Mara.”

His voice was not loud. It stopped her anyway.

He came around the counter and placed a folded towel along the gap beneath the door.

The smell faded.

“What is it?” she asked.

“Spring that never happened.”

“How much?”

“A considerable amount.”

She returned to her desk and found that she had written her mother’s old telephone number in the box marked COLLECTION AUTHORITY.

***

In January, the council announced a property review.

The announcement arrived in an email calling the building an underutilized asset and the office’s contents a legacy accumulation.

Mr. Vale printed it.

He read the page twice, then placed it facedown on his desk.

“Are they closing us?” Mara asked.

“They’ve appointed a consultant.”

This turned out to be a woman called Ms. Kestrel, who wore waterproof boots and asked sensible questions.

How many claims did they fulfill each year?

How much of the stock was identifiable?

Was there a fire plan?

Mara liked her until the final question, and then disliked herself for having no answer.

Ms. Kestrel walked the corridor with a measuring device. It stopped displaying numbers halfway past the room of coastal overcast.

She tapped its screen.

“That’s unusual.”

“Yes,” said Mr. Vale.

“Is there a floor plan?”

“Several. They disagree.”

Ms. Kestrel put the device away and took out a notebook.

***

Her proposal arrived three weeks later.

The building required repairs. The stock was growing. The office served fewer than sixty people annually, not counting repeat visits.

There would be a six-month identification period, followed by a managed release of unclaimed conditions. The lampshade shop next door wanted room to expand.

“A managed release?” Mara said.

Ms. Kestrel had returned to discuss the report. She sat opposite them with a paper cup of tea.

“In suitable locations. Under supervision.”

“You can’t just empty it all somewhere.”

“Then we need another recommendation.”

Mr. Vale was silent.

Ms. Kestrel turned to him.

“I’m not asking you to make it disappear. I’m asking you to help me explain what keeping it requires.”

He looked older than he had when she arrived.

After she left, Mara expected him to be angry.

Instead he said, “I should have written a fire plan.”

***

They began with the basement.

The oldest stock had labels written in violet ink. Some parcels bore street names that no longer existed. Several contained weather from gardens now buried beneath the ring road.

Mara opened a tin marked AUGUST, POSSIBLY 1936, and heard a cricket.

She closed it again.

Near the back wall, behind a stack of unused collection baskets, she found a shallow wooden box.

The label read:

BELLWETHER STREET  
17 MAY  
16:10–16:24  
COLLECTED FROM REAR GARDEN

The year was the one in which her mother had died.

Mara carried the box upstairs.

Mr. Vale glanced at the label and removed his glasses.

“You knew?”

“I knew something had come from that street. I didn’t know the number.”

“There isn’t a number.”

“No.”

“What’s inside?”

“We can examine it.”

She held the box against her chest.

“Not now.”

“All right.”

***

At home, she put it on the kitchen table.

On 17 May, Mara had been in a showroom ninety miles away, trying to persuade a couple that a freestanding bath could fit into their bathroom.

Her mother had called at four.

Mara had silenced her phone.

At four fifteen, there was a message.

Nothing urgent, love. Ring me when you’re free.

Her mother died that night, before Mara rang.

For months, Mara had returned to the message, listening for something she had missed. A breathlessness. A hesitation. Some small irregularity that would explain what she should have known.

Eventually the recording had begun to sound unfamiliar. Her mother’s ordinary voice had become a thing she studied.

Mara deleted it in October, by accident or on purpose. She was still not sure which.

Now there was a box on the table.

At half past eleven, she lifted the lid.

***

It contained rain.

Not dramatic rain. Fourteen minutes of steady, mild rain falling through sunlight.

It rose from the box in a small bright column, touched the kitchen ceiling, and vanished. The room smelled of paving stones and tomato plants.

Through it Mara could see the garden as it had been in May: bean poles leaning against the shed, the blue bowl her mother used for weeds, an old towel pegged over the back of a chair.

There was no one in it.

Mara waited.

The rain continued.

“Hello?”

A drop struck her wrist.

She had not realized, until then, that she had expected an answer.

She stood at the table for almost the full fourteen minutes. Nothing appeared except the garden, and nothing sounded except rain striking leaves.

Before it could finish, she closed the lid.

***

“I thought there might be more,” she told Mr. Vale.

They were in the courtyard. He had brought out two mugs of tea.

“Sometimes there’s an impression,” he said. “A room. A sound.”

“A person?”

“Not a person.”

She watched a pigeon inspect the gutter.

“Was she waiting for it?”

“Possibly.”

“Could she have been waiting for me to call?”

“I can’t tell you that.”

Mara was grateful that he did not try.

After a while he said, “You can claim it. Your address is enough.”

“What would I do with it?”

“Keep it. Release it. Take some time.”

“Is that what you do?”

Mr. Vale looked into his tea.

She thought he would refuse to answer.

Then he said, “There’s a snowfall upstairs. I’ve been meaning to take it home for nineteen years.”

***

They worked through February and March.

Mara made a public notice that did not use the phrase legacy accumulation. She put copies in the library, the hospital, and the supermarket.

HAVE YOU BEEN EXPECTING CERTAIN WEATHER?

Beneath that, she listed the office hours.

People came.

Some misunderstood. A builder wanted compensation for rain damage. A little boy asked for a tornado and was offered a pamphlet about wind safety.

But there were claims.

The woman in the green coat found her hot kitchen wind. It had been filed under DOMESTIC DRAUGHT, ORIGIN UNKNOWN.

She took it away in a biscuit tin.

A young man claimed a cold clear night meant for his father, who had bought a telescope and never unpacked it.

He brought the telescope as evidence.

Mara carried it out to his car while he held the night carefully in both hands.

***

Ms. Kestrel returned in April.

The office was busier now, but it was still full.

She reviewed the new records, examined the fire plan, and listened to Mara’s proposal for a public weather garden.

“A what?”

“A place for releases. Sheltered sections, drainage, seating. People could claim weather without having to take it home.”

“And the unidentified stock?”

“Some could be released there. If it’s safe.”

“What would it cost?”

Mara had expected this question. She pushed a folder across the desk.

Mr. Vale had worked out the operating requirements. Parks had suggested an unused nursery behind the library. A roofer who had claimed three mornings of dry weather had offered to repair the office guttering at cost.

Ms. Kestrel read for a long time.

“I can put this forward,” she said.

She did not promise anything else.

Mara had come to trust her promises.

***

The cupboard beneath the stairs was their last major inventory problem.

They opened it together, with Ms. Kestrel present and the courtyard door propped wide.

There were birds, but not actual birds.

There were kitchen windows, school holidays, seedlings, washed sheets, open roads. There were thousands of mornings intended for people who had imagined being younger, healthier, somewhere else, or with someone who had not stayed.

Mara heard the kitchen window squeak.

Beside her, Mr. Vale began to cry.

Ms. Kestrel took a handkerchief from her pocket and passed it to him without looking away from the cupboard.

Inside, the light shifted.

“How do we separate it?” Mara asked.

Mr. Vale wiped his face.

“One collection at a time.”

It took seven weeks.

***

The weather garden opened in June with two benches, an accessible path, and a storage shed that Parks insisted on painting green.

There was no ceremony. Ms. Kestrel cut a piece of string across the gate because nobody had brought ribbon.

The first release was a sea breeze.

It moved through the lavender, disturbed the council papers, and lifted a little girl’s hair. She laughed and ran after it, though it had already gone.

Mr. Vale sat on a bench with his snowfall beside him.

“Not today?” Mara asked.

“Not today.”

She nodded.

Her own box waited in her bag.

***

She took it home that evening.

Before opening it, she went into the garden and brought in the old towel from the shed. She had found it while clearing a shelf: stiff, faded, still smelling faintly of dust.

She put it in the wash.

Then she rang her brother.

They talked about nothing urgent. His boiler. Her work. Whether either of them wanted the dining table.

Afterward, Mara carried the box outside.

The rain fell over the small garden. It darkened the fence and gathered along the bean poles she had finally put upright. Sunlight shone through it from an angle the actual sun no longer occupied.

She could see the old blue bowl near the shed.

When she reached for it, her hand passed through.

So she stood still.

Fourteen minutes was longer than she expected. Long enough to become cold. Long enough to hear a neighbor shut a window and a bus pull away on the next street. Long enough for the ordinary evening to continue around her.

Then the rain stopped.

The bowl was gone. The garden was her garden again, neglected in places, growing anyway.

Mara tipped the empty box to drain the last drops from one corner. She left it open on the back step.

In the kitchen, the washing machine had finished.

She carried the towel outside and pegged it to the line before the light went.
