# The Department of Lost Afternoons

The letter arrived on a Tuesday, which seemed appropriate. Nothing extraordinary had ever happened to Mira on a Tuesday, and she had begun to suspect the day of concealing something.

It was a narrow envelope the color of weak tea. Her name and address were written in blue ink, in handwriting that resembled her own but looked more rested.

Inside was a single sheet.

> Dear Ms. Vale,
>
> Our records indicate that you have accumulated a substantial balance of unused afternoons.
>
> Please attend our office at your earliest convenience to discuss collection.
>
> Bring identification and something you have been meaning to mend.
>
> Department of Lost Afternoons  
> 14 Bellwether Lane  
> Window hours: whenever the light is suitable

Mira read it twice, then checked the envelope for a company name, a demand for payment, or the tiny gray print in which disappointments usually announced themselves.

There was none.

She put it beside the kettle.

For three days, she tried not to think about it.

***

At sixty-three, Mira had become skilled at arranging days so that nothing unexpected could get a foothold.

She rose at seven. She washed her breakfast cup before drinking a second cup of tea, which prevented the morning from feeling extravagant. On Mondays she shopped. On Thursdays she cleaned the bathroom whether it needed cleaning or not.

Until the previous autumn, she had scheduled buses for the city transport office. For thirty-one years she had helped ensure that people she would never meet arrived at places she would never see.

Retirement had been described to her as freedom.

Mostly, it was a large room into which she had moved too little furniture.

On Friday, while searching for a receipt, she found a cardigan with a loose button. It was green, or had been green before years of washing persuaded it toward gray.

She held it against herself.

Then she put it in a shopping bag and went to Bellwether Lane.

***

Number 14 stood between a locksmith and a bakery that had closed so recently its window still promised hot cross buns.

Mira had walked down the lane before. She remembered the locksmith. She remembered the bakery. She did not remember the narrow building between them, although its bricks looked old and a dandelion had established itself beneath the door.

A brass plate read:

**DEPARTMENT OF LOST AFTERNOONS**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**No appointments before lunch.**

Inside, the air smelled of dust warmed by sunlight.

There were three wooden chairs, a rubber plant, and a counter behind which a young man was eating a pear over a wastepaper basket.

He swallowed.

“Ms. Vale?”

“How did you know?”

“You’re holding the letter.”

She looked down. She was.

“Identification?”

She gave him her driving license.

“Item for mending?”

She showed him the cardigan.

“Excellent. Some people bring relationships. We’re not equipped.”

***

The young man introduced himself as Ellis and led her down a corridor.

On one side were filing cabinets. On the other were windows looking onto places that could not all have been outside the same building.

One showed a field in late summer. Another showed rain striking a red-tiled roof. Through a third, Mira saw a café terrace where every chair was empty except one, on which a large black dog slept.

She stopped.

“Are those screens?”

“No.”

“What are they?”

“Mostly Thursdays.”

Ellis continued walking.

His office contained a desk, two chairs, and a clock without hands. On the desk lay a folder thick enough to concern a solicitor.

He opened it.

“You have two hundred and eighteen afternoons in recoverable condition.”

Mira sat down carefully.

“I don’t understand.”

“That’s normal.”

“Have I forgotten them?”

“Some. Others you remember perfectly. Forgetting isn’t the criterion.”

“Then what is?”

Ellis considered her.

“An afternoon goes missing when you’re in it, but keep insisting you’re somewhere else.”

***

He turned the folder so she could see.

Each page contained a date, a place, and a brief description.

**17 April, age 24. Kitchen table. Waiting to hear whether the interview went well. Pear tree flowering outside. No observation recorded.**

**9 August, age 38. Seaside. Thinking about Monday. Daughter requests assistance with moat. Assistance deferred. Tide intervenes.**

**22 November, age 51. Bus shelter. Rain. Belief that proper life will begin after current difficulties resolved.**

Mira looked away.

“This seems judgmental.”

“It’s administrative.”

“It feels judgmental.”

“Yes. Administration often does.”

He closed the folder halfway.

“We don’t collect ordinary boredom. Boredom can be a perfectly good use of time. Nor do we collect rest, daydreaming, or sitting quietly because you’re tired.”

“What do you collect?”

“Time you repeatedly asked to be over.”

Mira folded her hands around the handles of the shopping bag.

Outside the nearest window, someone was mowing a lawn. The sound came and went.

“Everyone does that,” she said.

“Which explains the cabinets.”

***

“What happens if I collect them?”

“You may re-enter selected afternoons.”

“And change things?”

“No.”

The answer came quickly.

Ellis leaned forward.

“You can’t prevent an accident, buy a winning ticket, persuade someone to stay, or tell your younger self which investments would have worked. You can attend. That’s all.”

“Attend?”

“Notice things. Listen. Finish being there.”

“And then?”

“Then you come back.”

Mira thought of the beach. Her daughter, Lucy, had worn a yellow swimsuit and dug with a plastic spade whose handle broke before the holiday ended.

Could she remember the moat?

She could remember saying, *In a minute.*

“How much does this cost?”

“No money.”

“Then what?”

“One present afternoon for each afternoon recovered.”

Mira glanced toward the handless clock.

“How do you take it?”

“You spend it here. There’s a room downstairs. You wait without any way of keeping yourself occupied.”

“I’m sixty-three,” she said. “I’ve done plenty of waiting.”

Ellis gave her a doubtful look.

***

She chose the seaside afternoon.

Ellis wrote something on a form, stamped it, and took her to a blue door.

“Stay until you hear the bell.”

“What bell?”

“You’ll know.”

Beyond the door was August.

Heat settled on her shoulders. The sea shone with the harsh brilliance she had forgotten seaside photographs never quite captured. Somewhere, a radio played a song through static.

Lucy knelt in the sand.

Not adult Lucy, who sent photographs of her own children and apologized for being busy. This Lucy was six, with wet hair plastered to her cheeks and a fierce brown line of concentration between her eyebrows.

“Mum,” she said, “the water keeps coming in wrong.”

Mira tried to speak.

Her younger self sat on a striped towel nearby, staring at a diary.

Mira understood, without being told, that Lucy could not see her.

She knelt beside the moat.

The castle was terrible. Its towers slumped. Shells had been pressed into the walls at odd angles. One feather stood upright in the courtyard.

Lucy poured water into the trench.

It vanished into the sand.

“Oh,” she said softly.

Then she tried again.

***

Mira stayed beside her.

She noticed how Lucy first filled the bucket too full, then learned to carry less. She noticed the solemn care with which her daughter removed a beetle from the path of an approaching wave.

She noticed her younger self rubbing her forehead.

Mira had remembered that woman as selfish. Watching her now, she also saw how exhausted she was. There had been money trouble that summer. Her husband had begun sleeping in the spare room. The diary on her knees contained figures that would not add up differently however often she checked them.

“Mum, look.”

“In a minute, darling.”

The words still hurt.

But a few moments later, unnoticed in Mira’s memory, her younger self did look.

“That’s wonderful,” she said.

“It’s a harbor,” Lucy told her. “For people who get lost.”

The bell sounded from somewhere beyond the dunes.

Mira remained kneeling until the beach grew pale around her.

***

She emerged into the office crying without much noise.

Ellis handed her a box of tissues.

“People usually want the big days,” he said. “Weddings. Births. Departures. We don’t hold many of those.”

Mira pressed a tissue beneath her eyes.

“I thought I’d missed all of it.”

“You missed some.”

“She said it was a harbor.”

Ellis waited.

“I didn’t remember that.”

“No.”

When she could speak steadily, she asked how to pay.

He took her downstairs.

The room was plain: a chair, a table, a window, a glass of water. On the wall hung a small painting of a bowl containing three lemons.

“Is that all?”

“There’s a bathroom through there.”

“No books?”

“No.”

“My phone?”

“I’ll keep it upstairs.”

She handed it over reluctantly.

At the door, Ellis turned.

“You can leave whenever you wish. But an incomplete payment means the recovered afternoon will fade back to the condition in which it arrived.”

“How long?”

“Until evening.”

Then he left.

***

At first, Mira inspected the room.

The table had a scratch resembling a river on a map. One leg of the chair was slightly shorter than the others. The window overlooked a small courtyard containing a drain, six paving stones, and an ambitious weed.

She drank the water.

She counted the paving stones again.

She thought about dinner, then shopping, then whether she ought to have chosen a different afternoon.

One with her mother.

One before her father became ill.

Could she recover a day she had shared with her ex-husband without spending most of it angry?

She wanted her phone. She wanted a book, a task, something to sort into piles.

Instead she took the cardigan from her bag.

Then she remembered Ellis had kept it upstairs.

For a moment, she resented him more than seemed reasonable.

Outside, a small bird landed beside the drain.

It turned its head, found nothing useful, and left.

***

The afternoon continued.

Mira became sleepy, then embarrassed by her sleepiness, though no one was there to notice. She let her eyes close.

When she woke, the patch of sunlight had moved from the floor onto the table.

She watched it touch the scratch.

After a while, she began to remember Lucy’s face without trying. Not just the child on the beach, but Lucy at fourteen, furious over a haircut, and Lucy last Christmas, standing at the sink with her sleeves pushed up.

She had a sudden desire to telephone her daughter.

There was nothing important to say. She could ask whether the youngest had lost his tooth yet.

The thought pleased her.

Eventually footsteps sounded in the corridor.

Ellis opened the door.

“That’s settled.”

Mira stood. Her knees were stiff.

“Was that really an entire afternoon?”

“Yes.”

“It felt longer in the middle.”

“It often does.”

Upstairs, he returned her phone and cardigan.

“Would you like to book another?”

She looked at the thick folder on his desk.

“Not yet.”

***

At home, she called Lucy.

“Everything all right?” her daughter asked immediately.

“Yes. Why?”

“You don’t usually call on Fridays.”

“I can call back on Sunday.”

“No, no. I’m just making pasta.”

Mira heard a cupboard close and a child shouting from another room.

“Do you remember building a sandcastle with a harbor?”

“At the seaside?”

“Yes.”

“Vaguely. Why?”

“I was thinking about it.”

“I remember Dad losing the car keys.”

“That was the following year.”

“Was it?”

Mira smiled.

For several minutes, they discussed school shoes and a leaking pipe. Lucy described a disagreement at work. Usually Mira would have begun assembling advice before the account was finished.

This time she listened to the whole story.

“That sounds miserable,” she said.

“It was.”

In the background, water boiled over.

“Oh, damn. Mum, can I—”

“Go. We’ll talk later.”

Afterward, Mira found her sewing tin.

She replaced the loose button. The thread was dark blue because she had no green, and after a brief search she decided she did not mind.

***

She returned to the department twice that summer.

Once she chose an afternoon with her mother, expecting tenderness and finding an argument about whether the kitchen needed new curtains.

Her mother stood on a chair holding fabric against the window.

“Too much yellow?” she asked.

“You’ve already bought it,” younger Mira said.

“That isn’t what I asked.”

They irritated each other for nearly an hour.

Yet Mira saw her mother climb down from the chair, put the kettle on, and quietly move the last good biscuit onto her daughter’s saucer.

The second time, she recovered an afternoon alone in a rented room at nineteen.

Nothing happened. Rain tapped the window. She ate toast over the sink and waited for someone to invite her somewhere.

Mira had expected to feel sorry for the girl.

Instead, she found herself admiring the green shoes abandoned beside the bed, the postcards on the wall, the recklessness of owning only two saucepans and believing that would always be sufficient.

***

By September, she had stopped thinking of the folder as something she ought to finish.

She asked Ellis what happened to uncollected afternoons.

“We keep them.”

“Forever?”

“We haven’t reached forever yet.”

“And if I don’t come back?”

“You don’t have to.”

He was eating another pear. She wondered whether it was always pear season in the department.

“Do you lose afternoons?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“But you know how it works.”

Ellis folded the stem into a scrap of paper.

“That helps less than you might think.”

Outside, the bakery was being renovated. Someone had scraped the promise of hot cross buns from the window.

Mira stood for a while watching a painter balance a ladder against the shopfront. Then she walked home by the long route through the park.

She had meant to clean the kitchen.

It could wait.

***

The following Tuesday, rain began shortly after lunch.

Mira sat beside her window with a book open on her knee. Across the street, a delivery driver struggled with a parcel while trying to keep his hood from falling over his eyes.

She read a page, then the same page again.

The kitchen needed cleaning. There was a bill to pay. Somewhere in Bellwether Lane, more than two hundred afternoons remained under her name.

She considered visiting one.

Instead, she put the book down and watched the rain.

After a while she fetched the cardigan, though it was not especially cold. The blue thread showed clearly against the wool.

She ran her thumb over the button.

Then she got up to make some tea.

There was enough water in the kettle for two cups, and for no particular reason she took out the good one, the thin white cup with a tiny painted branch inside the rim.

She carried it carefully back to the window.

The rain was easing. Across the road, someone opened an upstairs window and shook a cloth into the damp air. Mira watched the crumbs fall, briefly visible against the dark brick, and reached for her book again.

samples.result:
# The Bench at the End of the Street

On the municipal inventory, it was listed as **Street Furniture, Miscellaneous, Item 441-B**.

It stood at the end of Bellwether Street, where the pavement widened into a triangle before meeting a retaining wall. Beyond the wall lay a railway cutting. No passenger trains used the line anymore, though twice a week a freight train passed through carrying sealed containers toward the coast.

The bench faced neither the railway nor the street. It faced a patch of gravel, a drain, and the blank side of an electrical substation.

Someone had painted it green a long time ago.

***

Clara encountered the bench first as a discrepancy.

She worked in the borough’s Department of Public Assets, where discrepancies arrived in pale blue folders and generally involved objects that were missing, duplicated, or owned by someone who had ceased to exist legally.

A drinking fountain belonged to a dissolved temperance society. Three streetlamps were maintained under an agreement with a factory demolished in 1988. A bronze fox outside the library had no accession number and therefore, administratively speaking, was wildlife.

The bench presented the opposite difficulty. It existed, unquestionably, but nobody could explain why.

***

Its repair estimate was four hundred and eighty pounds.

Its removal estimate was one hundred and sixty.

This difference had acquired significance because the borough was short of money, as it had been throughout Clara’s nineteen years of employment. This year, however, the shortage had a slogan: **Making Space for What Matters**.

Her supervisor, Dennis, placed the folder on her desk.

“Just establish whether it serves a current function.”

“It’s a bench.”

“Yes, but there are benches near things. This one isn’t near anything.”

“It’s near the substation.”

Dennis looked at her.

“I’ll go and see,” she said.

***

Clara went on a Tuesday at eleven, carrying a clipboard that made her look as though she had authority over more than she did.

The bench had five wooden slats, iron legs, and one armrest polished almost silver where hands had worn through the paint. Grass grew between the paving stones beneath it. A crisp packet moved weakly against the drain.

She sat.

The view was worse from sitting down.

The substation wall had a water stain shaped like a country that had lost a war. Somewhere behind it, machinery hummed.

She wrote: **No evident amenity value.**

***

After nine minutes, a man appeared carrying two shopping bags.

He was large, red-faced, and dressed in a suit too warm for the weather. He stopped when he saw Clara.

“Oh,” he said.

“Am I in your way?”

“No. No, of course not.”

He stood for a moment, then put the bags down and sat at the other end. One bag contained flowers. The other contained something rectangular wrapped in silver paper.

They remained silent until he asked whether she knew the time.

“Eleven fourteen.”

“Plenty,” he said, though she had not asked.

***

At eleven twenty, he picked up the bags.

“Interview?” Clara asked, surprising herself.

He glanced down at his suit.

“Meeting my daughter.”

“How nice.”

“Well,” he said.

The word stayed between them.

“She works round the corner. We’re having lunch.”

Clara nodded.

He adjusted the flowers so their heads stood clear of the bag. Then he walked back the way he had come, slowly at first, and then with a sudden determined speed.

Clara looked at her clipboard.

After **No evident amenity value**, she added a question mark.

***

Dennis approved three observation periods.

“Not a sociological study,” he said. “Just enough to determine usage.”

On Wednesday morning, Clara found a woman in a fluorescent jacket eating porridge from a plastic tub.

“Council?” the woman asked.

“Yes.”

“You fixing it?”

“Assessing it.”

“Ah.”

The woman scraped the bottom of the tub.

Clara explained that the bench might be removed.

“Then where will I have breakfast?”

“There’s a café on Mercer Road.”

The woman looked at her porridge, then at Clara.

“I’ve got breakfast,” she said.

***

Her name was Bev. She drove the number forty-three bus.

Her first shift ended at nine twelve. Her second began at nine thirty-eight. The depot break room had a television nobody could switch off because the manager liked the financial news.

“Is this your nearest bench?” Clara asked.

“No.”

“Why this one?”

Bev considered.

“Nobody’s watching you arrive. Nobody’s watching you leave.”

She put the lid on her tub.

“Park benches, you feel you ought to enjoy the park. Here you can just sit.”

Clara wrote that down, though it did not fit any heading on the form.

***

At lunchtime, there were two schoolboys sharing a packet of biscuits.

They became innocent as soon as Clara approached.

“What’s this about?” one asked.

“The bench.”

“We didn’t do anything.”

“I haven’t said you did.”

They watched her clipboard.

She asked whether they used the bench often.

“Sometimes.”

“What for?”

“Sitting.”

The other boy laughed, then stopped when she wrote it down.

There was a chessboard between them, balanced on a flattened cardboard box. Several pieces were missing. A bottle cap stood beside a white king.

“Which piece is that?” Clara asked.

“Bishop.”

***

On Friday, it rained.

Clara expected the bench to be empty, but an elderly woman sat beneath a large black umbrella, reading a paperback.

Water dripped from its edges onto her shoes.

“Would you mind answering a few questions?”

“Yes,” the woman said.

Clara waited.

The woman turned a page.

After a while, Clara said, “We’re considering removing the bench.”

That earned her a look.

“Why?”

“It needs repairs.”

“So do I.”

“The question is whether the expense can be justified.”

The woman closed her book around one finger.

“By whom?”

“The council.”

“That must be exhausting for them.”

***

Her name, Clara learned eventually, was Mrs. Venn.

She had lived on Bellwether Street for forty-six years. She did not come to the bench every day, or every week. She came when her husband’s hearing aid made a particular whistling noise.

“He won’t admit it’s happening.”

“Couldn’t you ask him to have it adjusted?”

“I have.”

“And?”

“He says I’m imagining it.”

They listened to the rain.

“Are you?”

“Certainly not.”

Mrs. Venn reopened her book.

Clara stood beside the bench under her small departmental umbrella and felt, briefly, that she was the unreasonable party.

***

Back at the office, she entered her findings.

**Observed uses: rest, refreshment, recreation, private reading, anticipatory waiting.**

Dennis read the last phrase aloud.

“Anticipatory waiting?”

“Before an appointment.”

“That’s just waiting.”

“Not at the appointment itself. Somewhere else first.”

Dennis rubbed his forehead.

“Clara, I need a recommendation.”

She looked at the photographs attached to the file. The cracked slat. The rusty bolt. The substation.

“Retain and repair.”

“On what grounds?”

“Demonstrated use.”

He sighed, not unkindly.

“If four people use something, that doesn’t necessarily make it viable.”

“Six,” Clara said.

“Two of them were sharing biscuits.”

***

The recommendation went to a committee whose members had never visited Bellwether Street.

This was ordinary and not especially sinister. Committees could not visit everything. That was why reports existed.

Unfortunately, the report contained a photograph.

“Good heavens,” said Councillor Pike. “What a miserable spot.”

Someone suggested moving the bench to the riverside.

Someone else pointed out that moving it would cost more than removing it.

There was discussion of asset rationalisation.

Clara sat against the wall, present to answer factual questions. Nobody asked any.

The committee approved removal, subject to a fourteen-day public notice.

***

The notice went up on a Monday.

It was attached to a temporary post with plastic ties and printed in language that made the bench sound dangerous.

**PROPOSED DECOMMISSIONING OF SEATING ASSET.**

Clara stood looking at it.

A small part of her hoped for outrage. A petition. A newspaper photograph of angry residents pointing.

Instead, a dog urinated on the post.

Bev read the notice on Wednesday and said, “Typical.”

The boys asked whether they could have the bench.

Mrs. Venn said nothing at all.

The man with the flowers did not return.

***

On the eighth day, Clara came after work without her clipboard.

She had begun doing this occasionally.

Her flat was quiet, but it was a managed quiet: the refrigerator clicking, the washing machine waiting to be emptied, unopened letters arranged beneath a ceramic bowl. Even the comfortable chair reminded her of a lamp she needed to replace.

At the bench, nothing belonged to her.

She sat with her handbag on her knees and watched a weed growing out of the substation gutter.

After a while, she realised she had been sitting for twenty minutes without inventing a task.

***

An old man arrived carrying a spirit level.

He wore a knitted waistcoat over a shirt with the sleeves rolled up.

“Are you the council woman?”

“Yes.”

“Thought so.”

He set the spirit level on the bench.

The bubble drifted toward one end.

“Always did that,” he said.

“Do you know when it was installed?”

“Seventy-three.”

Clara straightened.

“Were you involved?”

“I put it here.”

His name was Arthur Bell. He had worked for the borough before most departments had departments in their names.

“Why here?” Clara asked.

Arthur looked around, as if checking nothing important had moved.

***

“There used to be a gate.”

He pointed toward the retaining wall.

“Footbridge over the railway. Factory entrance on the other side.”

“So it was for the workers?”

“Mostly.”

“What happened to the bridge?”

“Taken down. Ninety-one, perhaps.”

“And the bench was overlooked?”

Arthur picked up the level.

“Depends what you mean.”

Clara waited.

“People kept sitting on it.”

He said this without emphasis, as though explaining why a tap had been left connected.

She asked whether there were records.

“Probably. Everything went on paper. Whether anyone kept the paper is another matter.”

***

In the archive, Clara found the installation order inside a folder labelled **Pedestrian Access: East District, Sundry**.

The bench had cost thirty-two pounds.

There was a sketch, a purchase receipt, and a handwritten note from a works supervisor.

**Site seating here rather than directly at gate. Men waiting for wives prefer distance from entrance. Also used by night shift before going home.**

Below that, in another hand:

**Agreed.**

Clara read the note several times.

It was not a beautiful sentence. It had no larger ambition than to explain where a bench should go.

She photocopied it anyway.

***

Dennis listened.

“So its original function is obsolete.”

“The factory is gone. The function isn’t.”

“Waiting for factory workers’ wives?”

“Having somewhere to stop before the next thing.”

He leaned back.

“Clara.”

She knew that tone. It meant he understood her and would have preferred not to.

“We’re cutting maintenance on playgrounds. We’ve got a handrail outside the clinic held together with tape.”

“I know.”

“Four hundred and eighty pounds matters.”

“Yes,” she said.

For the first time, she stopped thinking of him as an obstacle.

He looked tired. There was a sandwich on his desk, still wrapped at three.

***

She took the repair estimate to Arthur.

He studied it at his kitchen table while a radio discussed potatoes.

“They’re replacing everything.”

“That’s the specification.”

“Why?”

“To bring it up to standard.”

Arthur looked over his glasses.

“Most of it’s all right.”

The iron frame was sound. Four slats were sound. The fifth needed replacing. One anchor bolt had worked loose, which accounted for the slope.

“Can you write that down?”

“I can tell you.”

“I need someone qualified to write it down.”

“I was qualified when I put the thing there.”

“That was fifty years ago.”

“Yes,” Arthur said. “It’s stayed put.”

***

To her credit, the maintenance engineer agreed to inspect it.

His name was Samir. He was thirty, busy, and initially irritated by the request.

Then he crouched beside the bench, tested the frame, and said, “Oh.”

The original estimate had been based on photographs.

He revised it to ninety-six pounds, including labour.

“Provided we use a slat from stores.”

“Do we have one?”

“We’ve got seventeen.”

“Why?”

“Ordered for benches we removed.”

He returned to his van to fetch a spanner.

Clara stood beside Item 441-B and allowed herself one small, private smile.

***

The revised figure did not automatically reverse the decision.

A decision, once made, developed a protective shell of procedure.

There were emails. There was a question about whether repair constituted an unapproved variation. There was a reply beginning **For the avoidance of doubt**, which introduced several new doubts.

Finally, Dennis found a provision allowing officers to defer disposal where a lower-cost maintenance option became available.

He signed the authorisation.

“No ceremony,” he told Clara.

“I wasn’t planning one.”

“And no press release about saving a bench.”

“Certainly not.”

He handed her the paper.

“Good work.”

She took it before he changed his mind.

***

Samir repaired the bench on a Thursday morning.

Arthur supervised from a respectful distance, which became less respectful whenever Samir reached for a tool.

The new slat was brown, not green.

“We can paint it next cycle,” Samir said.

“When’s that?”

He gave Clara a look.

“All right,” she said.

By noon, the bench stood level. The notice had been removed. Apart from the brown slat, there was no visible sign that anything had happened.

Bev arrived with a sandwich, tested the seat with one hand, and sat down.

“Better,” she said.

That was the whole celebration.

***

A month later, Clara saw the man in the suit again.

This time he wore a blue jumper and carried no flowers. A young woman walked beside him, holding two takeaway coffees.

They stopped at the bench.

Clara was across the street, on her way to inspect a damaged bollard.

The young woman said something. The man laughed, then looked surprised by his own laughter.

Clara kept walking.

She did not know how lunch had gone, or what had preceded it, or whether things were now easy between them.

She was glad to have no reason to ask them anything.

***

At the end of the year, the inventory software was updated.

Every public asset now required a short description of its purpose. Most entries were straightforward: drainage, traffic control, pedestrian safety.

For Item 441-B, Clara typed **Public seating**.

She considered adding more, but the field was small, and public seating was accurate.

Outside, the afternoon was already darkening. Dennis was putting on his coat. Somewhere, a printer struggled with a final page.

Clara shut down her computer.

On her way home she took Bellwether Street. The bench was empty.

She sat for a little while before going on.

# A Bench With Somewhere to Be

The first time the bench moved, everyone blamed the students.

It had stood outside the municipal library for thirty-seven years, facing a sycamore tree and, beyond that, a bakery whose owners changed more frequently than its sign. On Monday morning, it was discovered two streets away, beside a bus stop that had no shelter. An elderly woman was sitting on it with a shopping bag between her shoes.

“Very thoughtful,” she told the man who came to retrieve it.

The man’s name was Leon. He worked for the Department of Streets and Public Furniture, a title that made his brother laugh every Christmas.

Leon examined the bench before loading it onto his truck. It was ordinary: five wooden slats, two cast-iron ends, a brass plaque dedicated to someone called Edith Bell. One armrest had been polished smooth by decades of hands. Underneath, among fossilized chewing gum and several ambitious declarations of love, someone had written THIS IS NOT THE END in green marker.

There were no wheels, no ropes, and no marks suggesting it had been dragged.

Leon called his supervisor.

“Students,” she said.

“That’s what I thought.”

“Then why are you calling?”

He returned the bench to the library.

***

On Thursday, it was outside the maternity clinic.

On Saturday, it appeared halfway up Bellwether Hill, where people regularly underestimated the slope. On Sunday morning, a jogger found it beside the river, facing the water rather than the path.

Each time, Leon brought it back.

He began doing this before his other assignments, partly because the truck was already empty and partly because he disliked imagining someone looking for a familiar place to sit and finding only four pale rectangles on the pavement.

The librarian, Mrs. Vale, watched him unload it for the fourth time.

“Perhaps Edith liked a change of scene,” she said.

“Did you know her?”

“No. But I’ve become acquainted with her bench.”

Leon checked the municipal records. Edith Bell had taught geography at the secondary school. The bench had been donated by former pupils after her retirement. She had lived another sixteen years and apparently spent much of that time traveling.

There was a photograph attached to the original application: Edith on a camel, wearing enormous sunglasses, looking unimpressed by whoever held the camera.

Leon printed the photograph and left it on his desk.

He did not believe in haunted furniture. He believed in loose bolts, misplaced paperwork, and people who said they had reported a broken streetlight when they had merely complained about it at dinner.

Nevertheless, he stopped calling the bench “it” quite so automatically.

***

After its sixth disappearance, his supervisor ordered him to bolt it down.

Her name was Anika Moss. She had inherited a department with three employees, two functioning vehicles, and responsibility for every public object nobody else wished to claim. She was not an unimaginative woman. She was a woman with a budget.

“People are posting photographs,” she said. “Someone has made it an account.”

“What kind of account?”

“An internet account, Leon. It has opinions about pedestrian access.”

He looked at her screen. The bench’s latest post read: SOME OF US ARE TRYING TO MAKE THIS CITY WALKABLE.

“That could be anyone,” he said.

“Precisely. Bolt it down.”

He took a drill, four heavy brackets, and a bag of anchor bolts to the library. The morning was bright. A child watched from the steps while Leon measured the distance between the bench’s feet.

“Does that hurt?” the child asked.

“The bench?”

The child nodded.

“No.”

“How do you know?”

Leon opened his mouth, then shut it.

The child’s father called from inside, and she disappeared before he had to settle the question.

He installed three brackets. At the fourth, he discovered a split in the wood beneath the seat, narrow but deep. It should have been repaired years ago. He sat back on his heels and pressed his thumb along the grain.

“Well,” he said. “That won’t do.”

Instead of bolting down the last foot, he loaded the bench onto his truck and took it to the workshop.

***

The workshop stood behind the recycling center, where the city’s ambitions arrived eventually as bent metal.

Leon liked it there. Things were allowed to be unfinished without anyone mistaking them for failures. A damaged sign lay beside a repaired gate. A drawer contained handles waiting for drawers. On the wall hung a clock that lost seven minutes every day, providing regular employment for the person assigned to correct it.

He removed the cracked slat, cut a replacement from seasoned oak, and sanded it until the edges were comfortable beneath his palm.

“You’ve been busy,” he told the bench.

The bench gave no sign of agreeing.

“My left knee isn’t what it was either.”

Outside, a loader tipped bottles into a container. The crash sounded briefly like applause.

He worked late, applying oil to the new wood and tightening the joints. When he finished, the bench looked unevenly young: four weathered slats and one golden replacement.

Leon considered staining the new piece to match. Then he decided against it. There was nothing wrong with a repair being visible.

He swept the floor, locked the workshop, and went home.

The next morning, the bench was gone.

The doors were still locked. The windows were intact.

On the floor, in a thin drift of sawdust, were four small impressions leading toward the wall.

Leon stood looking at them for a long time.

Then he called Anika.

“You should come down,” he said.

***

She arrived carrying coffee and the expression of someone determined not to have an interesting morning.

Leon showed her the empty space, the locked doors, and the tracks.

“Could be a prank.”

“Yes.”

“Could be someone with a key.”

“Yes.”

“Could be you.”

“It could.”

She looked at him.

“Is it?”

“No.”

They drank their coffee.

Eventually, Anika crouched beside the tracks. They were not footprints exactly. Each was the narrow, curved impression of an iron bench leg. They crossed the sawdust in an awkward alternating pattern, as though whatever made them was learning a difficult dance.

At the wall, they stopped.

Anika touched the plaster.

“I don’t have a procedure for this,” she said.

“That’s probably sensible.”

By noon, the bench had been found outside the employment office.

A man in a suit was eating a sandwich on it. Beside him, a woman was crying quietly into her phone.

Leon parked across the street. He watched the man offer her a paper napkin without interrupting his lunch.

For the first time, Leon did not immediately retrieve the bench.

He waited until both people had gone.

***

News traveled faster after that.

There were photographs, theories, and a short interview with a local historian who described the bench as “consistent with the district’s tradition of civic eccentricity,” which meant nothing but sounded reassuring.

Someone tied balloons to it.

Someone left flowers.

Someone attempted to sit on it for forty-eight hours, hoping to be transported somewhere meaningful. He lasted until shortly after midnight, when rain began falling and his girlfriend arrived in a taxi.

The bench remained stubbornly motionless whenever anyone watched.

It traveled only between observations, which made it difficult to film and impossible to insure.

Anika received emails from the mayor’s office, the legal department, and a company offering to sponsor the bench if its movements could be confined to commercially advantageous locations.

She deleted the last one with unusual force.

The trouble began when the bench appeared in a loading bay behind the central market.

It blocked a delivery van. The driver, already late, tried moving it alone and strained his back.

By afternoon, a complaint had become a report. By evening, the report had acquired the word liability.

The next morning, Anika showed Leon an instruction from above.

The bench was to be removed from public circulation pending assessment.

“What assessment?” he asked.

“That,” she said, “has not been assessed.”

***

They found it outside a shuttered cinema.

An old man was sitting beneath the faded posters, holding two takeaway coffees.

Leon recognized him vaguely. He had once sold newspapers from a kiosk near the station, before the kiosk became a machine selling phone chargers.

“Morning,” Leon said.

The man nodded.

“Mind if we take the bench when you’re finished?”

“Where to?”

“Storage.”

The man considered this.

“Everything goes there eventually.”

He lifted one coffee, then seemed to remember something and set it back down.

Leon looked away.

Across the road, Anika waited beside the truck. She had brought straps, wheel chocks, and a portable security camera purchased with money intended for replacement litter bins.

The old man stayed another twenty minutes.

When he left, he took both coffees.

They loaded the bench without speaking.

At the depot, they placed it inside an unused shipping container. Anika fastened a numbered seal across the doors.

“It’s temporary,” she said.

Leon nodded, although neither of them was looking at the other.

***

For three nights, nothing happened.

The security camera recorded rain, a fox, and Leon arriving earlier than necessary.

On the fourth morning, the bench was still inside the container, but its new slat had split.

Not badly. Just a fine crack along the grain.

Leon ran his finger over it.

Wood moved. He knew that. It expanded and contracted with humidity. Good timber could check in poor conditions, especially inside a steel box.

There was a perfectly reasonable explanation.

He brought in a thermometer, checked the ventilation, and moved the bench away from the wall.

The next day, another slat had cracked.

By Friday, the brass plaque had fallen off.

Leon picked it up from the floor. Edith Bell’s name sat cool and solid against his palm.

He thought of the photograph on his desk: the camel, the sunglasses, the expression of someone who had arrived somewhere and was already wondering what lay beyond it.

Then he did something unlike himself.

He went to the library and asked Mrs. Vale for help.

***

She listened without interrupting.

When he finished, she folded her hands on the desk.

“Do you want research,” she asked, “or accomplices?”

“Could we start with research?”

They spread a street map across a table.

Leon marked every place the bench had appeared. The bus stop. The clinic. Bellwether Hill. The river. The employment office. The market. The cinema.

Mrs. Vale added dates.

At first, the pattern seemed obvious: people needed somewhere to sit.

But there were already benches by the river. There were chairs inside the clinic. The market had a café.

“Perhaps it’s not just tiredness,” she said.

They looked again.

The bus stop had no shelter and a service that ran once an hour. The clinic’s waiting room closed before the final evening appointments. The market workers ate lunch on overturned crates behind the stalls.

The riverside bench nearest Edith’s chosen spot faced an advertising panel.

The cinema had closed nine months earlier.

They began making calls.

By dusk, the map was crowded with notes.

“It’s a list,” Leon said.

“Of what?”

“Places we’ve missed.”

***

Anika studied the map the next morning.

“You understand,” she said, “that I can’t submit a capital funding request on the grounds that a bench has conducted an accessibility audit.”

“Don’t mention the bench.”

“They will recognize the locations.”

“Say we conducted it.”

“That would require us to conduct it.”

Leon waited.

She sighed.

“Get your coat.”

They spent the next week walking.

They walked with an older residents’ group, with parents pushing buggies, with a woman who used crutches and knew more about the city’s gradients than its planning department.

They timed distances between seats. They noted which benches had backs, which had arms, which were surrounded by puddles, and which became too hot to touch in summer.

Leon learned that two hundred yards could be trivial or enormous.

Anika learned that a decorative stone cube outside the courthouse was not, despite its official classification, an adequate resting place.

They both learned how often people planned entire journeys around the availability of a seat.

On Friday, they submitted a report.

It contained no supernatural claims.

It did contain photographs, measurements, repair estimates, and a sentence Anika rewrote six times before allowing it to remain:

A public place is not fully public if some people cannot comfortably stay there.

***

The funding was modest.

Funding usually was.

Still, they repaired six benches, installed four more, and moved three that had apparently been positioned by someone with a grudge against shade.

Market traders paid for a sheltered seat behind the loading bays. The cinema’s owner agreed to leave space beneath the awning. A retired joiner volunteered two mornings a week at the workshop and spent most of that time criticizing Leon’s clamps.

Meanwhile, the container remained closed.

Leon visited every day.

He repaired the cracks, replaced two screws, and reattached Edith’s plaque. Sometimes he sat for a few minutes, listening to the metal walls tick in the sun.

When the work was finished, Anika came down to the depot with a folder.

“Temporary outdoor deployment,” she said. “Monitored. Subject to review.”

Leon read the form.

“Where?”

“The library.”

“And the bolts?”

Anika took the form back.

“There appears to be a clerical omission.”

They opened the doors.

***

The bench stayed outside the library for eleven days.

On the twelfth morning, it vanished.

Leon’s phone rang before breakfast.

For a moment, disappointment pressed against his ribs. He had wanted the repairs to mean something. He had wanted, perhaps unfairly, to be finished.

“Where?” he asked.

Mrs. Vale told him.

He drove to the edge of town, where a new housing estate ended abruptly beside an unfinished footpath.

The bench stood facing a field of waist-high grass.

A teenage boy was sitting on it, sketching the distant cranes. His bicycle lay nearby.

Leon got out of the truck.

“Good spot?” he asked.

The boy showed him the drawing. Above the roofs, an invented airship floated among the cranes.

Leon admired it, then sat at the other end and opened his notebook to a clean page. He drew the footpath, marked the bench’s position, and stayed until the boy finished shading the sky.

samples.result:
# The Department of Unfinished Things

On the morning the city decided to abolish the Department of Unfinished Things, a woman arrived carrying a staircase in a paper bag.

She set it on my desk between the stapler and the municipal seal. The bag was the ordinary brown kind used for bread, but I could hear footsteps inside it: someone climbing slowly, pausing every seventh step.

“It was supposed to go to a second floor,” she said.

“Was there a second floor?”

“There was going to be.”

I took out a blue intake form. Behind her, through the frosted glass of the office door, two men were measuring the corridor. They had the bright, impersonal expressions of people determining where a wall could be removed.

“Name?” I asked.

“Mine or the staircase’s?”

“Yours. Staircases generally don’t have names until they’re finished.”

She nodded as though this confirmed a private suspicion.

Our department occupied the least desirable corner of City Hall: fourth floor, north side, between Municipal Weights and an elevator that stopped there only when nobody pressed the button.

We accepted abandoned beginnings.

Not ordinary rubbish. Broken chairs belonged with Sanitation; lost umbrellas went to Transit. But a chair someone had begun making for a child who grew up before it was finished might find its way to us. So might an umbrella purchased for a journey never taken, if its owner had imagined the rain vividly enough.

People rarely knew our address beforehand.

They found themselves outside our door holding a recipe, a wedding invitation, a length of blue wool. Then they saw the sign and understood.

I had worked there for twenty-three years.

The woman’s staircase had been intended for a house overlooking the reservoir. Her husband laid the foundations. She drew the upstairs rooms in a school exercise book.

“Two bedrooms,” she said. “A bathroom with a window. Nothing grand.”

Then the reservoir expanded, the road moved, and the land became worth enough to settle debts they had stopped opening letters about.

“We sold.”

“And your husband?”

“Still alive. You needn’t lower your voice.”

I apologized.

“He says we were lucky. We were lucky. But every night I hear him going upstairs in his sleep.”

The bag shifted toward her.

“Do you want to recover the project,” I asked, “or release it?”

She looked at the ceiling.

“What’s the difference?”

“Recovery keeps it available. Release lets it become something else.”

“Such as?”

“We don’t determine that.”

For several seconds, she listened to the footsteps.

Then she checked the box marked RELEASE.

After she left, I carried the staircase into Storage Room C.

Inside, the air smelled of sawdust and weather that had not yet happened. Shelves held the usual stock: half-learned languages in cloudy bottles, unsent letters folded into birds, a violin concerto represented by a single sleepless wasp.

The staircase emerged from the bag as a narrow ribbon of oak. It unrolled to the floor, rose three inches, and waited.

I stamped the form.

The ribbon loosened into shavings. They turned in the draft from the door, then settled around my shoes. Somewhere in the building, a child laughed.

By tomorrow, the shavings would be gone.

No one had ever established where they went. Our quarterly reports called the process “authorized dispersal.”

My supervisor, Mr. Vale, was waiting beside my desk.

He had been my supervisor for sixteen years and had spent most of that time trying to get a window that opened.

“They’re closing us Friday,” he said.

“It’s Tuesday.”

“Yes. They feel they’ve provided notice.”

He handed me a memorandum headed SERVICE MODERNIZATION.

The department’s functions were to be distributed among several existing agencies. Records would be digitized. Physical holdings would be assessed for practical value. Materials without practical value would be destroyed.

I reread that sentence.

“Who’s assessing them?”

“Procurement.”

From the corridor came the whine of a drill.

Mr. Vale removed his glasses and held them up to the light, although I had never seen them clean.

“I’ve argued,” he said.

“I know.”

“I can argue once more.”

“Save it until we know what to ask for.”

That afternoon, I began with the oldest inventory.

There were things we had kept for eighty years: a gardener’s plan for a public orchard, seven chapters of a novel written on tram tickets, an apology from a mayor whose portrait hung downstairs.

Some remained lively. The orchard plan smelled of pears. The apology thumped against its box whenever a school group passed beneath the portrait.

Others had become quiet enough to touch without gloves.

Our instructions were to contact the owners before disposal, but many had died. For those, we were supposed to contact their descendants.

I imagined telephoning a stranger.

Good afternoon. Your great-grandmother intended to learn to swim. We have the first stroke here. Would you like it?

Near closing time, I found my father’s name.

It was written on a long, flat crate beneath the municipal allotments that had never been approved in 1948.

I knew his handwriting immediately. He made his capital E like a comb missing a tooth.

Inside was a boat.

Not a model. Not exactly a full-sized boat, either. It occupied the crate the way a view occupies a window: impossibly deep, complete in distance but unfinished at the edges.

The hull was painted green. The seats had not been fitted.

I could smell our old garage.

My father had begun building it when I was eleven.

We lived forty miles from any water large enough to require a boat.

This did not trouble him.

He bought plans by post and laid them on the kitchen table, pinning the corners with tins. All winter he steamed strips of wood over a kettle and came indoors with his glasses fogged.

In the spring, he asked me to help.

I held one end of a plank while he bent the other.

“Steady,” he said.

“I am steady.”

“Then a little steadier.”

At fourteen, I became embarrassed by the boat. At seventeen, I left home. At twenty-six, I paid someone to clear the garage after his funeral.

Until that afternoon, I had forgotten the green paint.

The intake form was dated three weeks before he died.

Under INTENDED USE, he had written: Going somewhere together.

I sat on the floor for a while.

Beyond the door, the cleaners moved their buckets along the corridor. One of them was singing under her breath. The song kept stopping while she shifted furniture, then starting again in the middle of a line.

My father had never mentioned bringing the boat here.

He must have found the office as everyone did. He would have been thinner by then, impatient with the stairs, carrying this crate under one arm.

Perhaps he had sat in the same chair as the woman with the staircase.

Perhaps I had been at lunch.

I looked for the receiving clerk’s signature.

It was mine.

I took the form to Mr. Vale.

He studied it without surprise.

“This happens,” he said.

“You knew?”

“I knew it could happen.”

“I would have remembered him.”

“You remember the visitors who can bear being remembered.”

I disliked this answer. It sounded like something printed beneath a mountain on an office calendar.

Mr. Vale seemed to hear that.

“He was protecting himself,” he said. “Possibly you, too. The department accommodated him.”

“Did I speak to him?”

“Yes.”

“What did I say?”

“We don’t record conversations.”

I wanted to accuse him of carelessness, or secrecy, or a failure to preserve the only record I now wanted.

Instead, I asked whether I could take the crate home.

“Of course,” he said. “It’s yours to decide about.”

At home, the boat would not fit through my kitchen door.

The crate did, but the boat objected. Its bow pushed against the doorframe from somewhere inside the wood, and a small wave washed over my shoes.

I left it in the sitting room.

All night I heard tools being set down.

At three, I got up and opened the crate.

My father was not there.

I mention this because I had expected him to be. I had spent years explaining our procedures to people, and still, confronted with something of my own, I wanted an exception.

There was only the unfinished boat and the smell of glue.

I put my hand on the gunwale.

The wood was cold.

On Wednesday, Procurement sent an assessor named Denise.

She wore red boots and carried a tablet with a cracked corner.

“I’m supposed to estimate resale,” she said.

“Of what?”

She consulted the screen.

“All assets.”

I showed her a drawer of proposed changes of career.

One rattled violently when she passed.

“What’s that?”

“A dentist who wanted to keep bees.”

“Can I see?”

I opened the drawer.

For a moment, the office filled with a summer field. Denise stood very still. A bee investigated the silver ring on her thumb.

Then the field folded back into its envelope.

She entered something on her tablet.

“Zero,” she said.

I folded my arms.

“Market value,” she added. “Not another kind.”

By lunchtime, Denise had assessed forty-seven items at zero and one unfinished puppet theatre at twelve pounds.

“Why that one?” I asked.

“Good hinges.”

She had begun putting small pencil marks beside certain entries.

I asked what they meant.

“Things that can go somewhere without being sold.”

“The department exists because most places won’t take them.”

“Most places haven’t been asked properly.”

She showed me her list.

The unapproved orchard could go to Parks. The half-learned languages might go to the evening college. A collection of dances nobody had dared attempt could go to the community centre, provided the caretaker agreed to move the tables.

“What about the rest?” I asked.

Denise looked around the room.

“How many owners are still alive?”

We worked until nine drafting a notice.

Mr. Vale rejected my first version for sounding like a tax demand. Denise rejected his for using the phrase “final opportunity,” which she said made people expect a sale on mattresses.

In the end, we printed:

**Have you left something with us?**

**We’re closing. Come and decide what happens next.**

We put notices in libraries, laundrettes, bus shelters, and the hospital café.

By Thursday morning, the queue reached the stairs.

An old man reclaimed a tap-dancing lesson. Two sisters released a restaurant. A woman collected the first page of a mathematics degree and tucked it into her coat without reading it.

Some visitors arrived empty-handed and left that way.

We counted them anyway.

Not everyone was grateful.

A man accused us of losing his youth.

“We don’t accept periods of life,” I told him.

“You accepted mine.”

His file contained a scheme for importing motorcycles.

He stared at it for a long time.

“That was going to make everything happen.”

“Would you like to keep it?”

He asked whether it would work now.

I said I didn’t know.

This angered him more than a refusal might have.

At last he took the envelope, then returned ten minutes later and placed it on my desk.

“I need another day.”

“We close tomorrow.”

“Then I’ll come tomorrow.”

And he did.

At noon, a girl of about sixteen arrived with her mother.

The mother did most of the talking.

“She gave up piano after seven years. We’ve still got the instrument. It’s taking up half the front room.”

The girl watched the floor.

“What have you brought?” I asked her.

Her mother produced a small glass box. Inside, two hands moved silently above invisible keys.

“It seems such a waste,” she said.

I asked the girl whether she wanted to recover or release it.

Her mother began to answer.

I waited.

At last the girl looked up.

“Can I keep the music and stop having lessons?”

“Yes,” I said. “But you’ll have to arrange that yourselves.”

On Friday afternoon, I brought my father’s crate back.

I had considered finishing the boat.

For several hours this had seemed the correct response. I looked up woodworking classes. I measured the sitting room. I calculated what a small trailer might cost.

Then I remembered holding the plank.

I had been bored that day. My arms hurt. My father kept correcting me, and when I finally let go, the wood sprang loose and struck his wrist.

We shouted at each other.

Later he brought me a sandwich cut into four triangles, although I had recently announced that triangles were for children.

We ate on the back step without apologizing.

I had remembered that sandwich all my life.

The boat contained more than our best intentions. Leaning over its green hull, I could feel the damp garage, the impatience, the love we kept expecting the other person to recognize without assistance.

I could finish it, perhaps. I might even enjoy learning how.

But I would not be finishing our afternoon.

I filled in the release form.

Then I crossed out my signature.

Mr. Vale, passing with an armful of files, stopped.

“Trouble?”

“Do we have to do it today?”

“No.”

“The department closes today.”

“Yes.”

I looked at the crate.

He shifted the files against his chest.

“You can decide something without an office witnessing it.”

The last visitor left at six.

The motorcycle man had taken his envelope home.

Denise found places for more than half the remaining holdings. The rest went into temporary storage under her personal inventory number, which she admitted might cause trouble.

“I’ll answer the email when it comes.”

Mr. Vale opened the office window. After sixteen years, it lifted easily.

We stood beside it, listening to traffic.

Then we switched off the lights.

At home, I moved the crate beneath the sitting-room window.

On Saturday, I bought sandpaper.

I did not buy plans, or a trailer, or enroll in a class. I sanded a rough place on the gunwale where a hand might rest.

It took twenty minutes.

Afterward, I made a sandwich and ate it outside.

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

My aunt left me a museum and seventeen pounds. The money was in an envelope marked FOR EMERGENCIES, which suggested either considerable optimism about the cost of emergencies or a private joke I would never understand. The museum stood between a locksmith and a shop that sold aquarium supplies. It had no windows, only a green door and a brass plate polished so often that its inscription had become a suggestion. I had walked past it throughout my childhood without once wondering what was inside. Children are good at accepting locked doors. It is adults who insist that everything must open.

At the time, I repaired ticket machines for the municipal railway. It was work that rewarded a modest view of human nature. People inserted coins covered in jam, tried to purchase journeys with foreign buttons, and struck the screens when told that a destination did not exist. I liked the machines because their disappointments were specific. A damaged spring could be replaced. A blocked coin chute could be cleared. If a machine said it could not help you, there was usually a diagram explaining why. My aunt’s solicitor gave me three keys and said there were no diagrams for the museum.

The first key opened the green door. The second opened a narrow office behind the entrance desk. The third was made of something warm and pale that I initially mistook for bone. Attached to it was a paper label in my aunt’s handwriting: YOU WILL KNOW. This annoyed me immediately. I had spent twelve years maintaining equipment whose manufacturers believed that adequate labeling was a form of moral weakness. Inside the office, beside an electric kettle furred with lime, I found a ledger, a cardigan, and a biscuit tin containing receipts for expenses that had apparently been incurred in dreams.

The museum itself was larger than the building containing it. I established this by walking the central corridor, counting my steps, and then going outside to examine the neighboring shops. The locksmith was eating a pear. When I asked whether he had noticed anything unusual about the dimensions of the premises next door, he said my aunt had been an excellent tenant. The aquarium shop owner was less evasive. “Don’t measure it,” she advised. “Your aunt tried that in 1986. We had an extra staircase for a month, and it frightened the fish.” She sold me a small, unnecessary thermometer.

There were seven galleries on my first visit, though the printed guide listed nine and the wall directory listed Tuesday. The nearest room contained abandoned hobbies. A violin rested in a glass case beside a half-knitted yellow sleeve. There were watercolors, telescopes, gardening gloves, a chessboard with only the opening moves completed. None of this seemed remarkable until I noticed a breeze stirring the yellow wool. The sleeve was trying, very slowly, to become a jumper. Its stitches advanced and retreated like the legs of a sleeping animal. A label read: BEGUN WITH GREAT CONFIDENCE. SET ASIDE DURING AN ORDINARY WEEK.

I found my aunt’s instructions under the ledger. “Nothing here is broken,” she had written. “Do not confuse unfinished with defective. Do not complete an exhibit on its owner’s behalf. Dust on Thursdays. Visitors may reclaim their property, but only what belongs to them. If someone asks to see a future, explain that we do not collect those. We collect the places where people stopped.” Below this, in smaller letters, she had added: “The kettle needs replacing.” I stood for some time holding the page. My aunt had died at eighty-three, apparently after postponing a kettle purchase for twenty years.

The first visitor arrived that afternoon, a woman carrying a motorcycle helmet and a supermarket bag. She asked for the gallery of letters. I admitted that I did not know where it was. “It moves,” she said kindly, as though excusing a nervous dog. We found it beyond a room full of unplanted orchards. Thousands of envelopes floated upright in long glass cabinets. Some were sealed. Others stood open, their pages trembling. The woman searched without hesitation and selected a blue envelope. She read the first line, laughed once, and sat down so abruptly that I fetched her a chair.

“It’s a complaint to my old landlord,” she said. “I thought it would be something important.” She showed me the page. There were three paragraphs about damp, followed by the beginning of a sentence: I have spent my whole life trying not to be difficult, but—. Nothing followed. “I wrote this when I was twenty-four.” She turned the page over. “Thirty years ago.” I asked whether she wanted to take it. She considered the letter, then folded it carefully into her bag. “The landlord’s dead,” she said. “Still, there might be someone else.” She left without visiting another room.

Over the next month I learned that the museum charged no admission, accepted no donations, and somehow paid its electricity bill. Visitors arrived irregularly. A man reclaimed a recipe he had stopped making after his divorce. Two sisters came to argue beside an unfinished sandcastle whose towers contained an entire August afternoon. A retired teacher spent six hours looking at a suitcase she had packed for Argentina in 1971. She did not take it. “I’m happy,” she told me before leaving, although I had not asked. Then she returned to the desk and added, “Mostly. That ought to count.”

There were rules the instructions had omitted. Exhibits could not be photographed: cameras recorded whatever the photographer had last forgotten. My phone produced twelve pictures of an overdue dentist appointment. Food was permitted, but crumbs attracted small, transparent birds from the gallery of unwritten poems. Never follow music unless you could name the instrument. Never tell a visitor that it was not too late, because sometimes it was, and the museum disliked careless reassurance. I learned this last rule after speaking to an elderly dancer. For three days afterward, every clock in the building showed a different, entirely correct time.

I kept my railway job and opened the museum in the evenings. The two occupations complemented each other badly. After a shift spent extracting chewing gum from card readers, I lacked patience for a corridor that refused to lead to the same place twice. One night I shouted at it. The corridor shortened itself by several yards and deposited me in a gallery I had not seen before. There were no cases here, only tables bearing ordinary objects: a chipped mug, a folded scarf, a child’s red shoe. At the far end stood my father’s workbench, exactly as I remembered it.

My father had been a carpenter with beautiful handwriting and an inability to apologize directly. When he was sorry, he repaired something. After missing my school play, he built shelves above my bed. After saying that my chosen career amounted to servicing expensive vending machines, he replaced the rotting frame around my kitchen window. His repairs were excellent. His timing made them difficult to enjoy. We had quarreled for the last time over something so small that I had spent years improving it in memory. In the more flattering versions, I defended a principle. In the true one, we were both tired.

On the workbench was a birdhouse without a roof. I recognized the penciled measurements, the square doorway, the tiny crescent scar where a chisel had slipped. He had been making it for my garden when he died. Beside it lay an object like a length of dark thread, curled inside a saucer. I bent closer and heard his voice, faintly, as if from another room: “What I meant was—” The thread moved. I put both hands on the bench to steady myself. For a ridiculous instant, I worried that I would leave fingerprints in the varnish. It had always mattered to him.

I went back every night. Sometimes I looked at the birdhouse. Mostly I listened to those four words. They were not necessarily an apology. What he meant might have been harsher than what he had said. He might have intended to explain a measurement or correct a date. Yet the beginning of the sentence had a softness I remembered from childhood, when he spoke to me while carrying me upstairs and assumed I was asleep. I searched the ledger for acquisition records. There were none. The museum catalogued origins only vaguely: A KITCHEN. LATE NOVEMBER. AFTER EVERYONE HAD BECOME TOO PROUD.

Eventually I tried to pick up the thread. It passed through my fingers and left them cold. I used tweezers, then the small magnetic probe from my railway toolkit. Nothing worked. The birdhouse, however, lifted easily. Underneath it was a label: FOR SOMEONE WHO DID NOT ASK. I knew at once that I could take the wood but not the words. They had belonged to my father. I considered ignoring this distinction. I considered that more seriously than I like to remember. Grief had made me feel entitled to things that ordinary love would never have claimed.

The next Thursday, while dusting a collection of half-forgiven offenses, I found another note from my aunt. It was tucked beneath a stone the size of a plum. “You’ll want the museum to prove that people loved you,” it said. “It can’t. Objects are not verdicts. Neither are intentions.” I read it several times, irritated by its accuracy. My aunt had always possessed the unfair advantage of knowing me before I learned to disguise myself. At the bottom she had drawn a kettle with steam rising from its spout. Even in death, she remained unwilling to let a practical matter go.

Winter brought more visitors. Perhaps the early dark made unfinished lives easier to notice. People arrived with wet shoulders and the expression of having taken a wrong turn on purpose. I became better at offering chairs and worse at offering advice. A boy came to retrieve a story he had abandoned because his classmates laughed at it. An old man returned a promise he had discovered he could not keep. This surprised me; I had thought everything entered the museum by accident. “Some things need somewhere to rest,” he said. I found a place for it beside an untended allotment.

One evening, the woman with the motorcycle helmet returned. She had written the complaint, she told me, although not to a landlord. She had written to her brother, who expected her to manage their mother’s appointments, bills, prescriptions, and every minor domestic crisis. “It went badly,” she said. I began to apologize, but she waved me quiet. “Badly isn’t the same as wrong.” She had brought a packet of biscuits for the desk. We ate them in the office while the kettle rattled. When it finally switched itself off, she looked at it and said, “You really should replace that.”

I bought a new kettle the following morning. It was red, efficient, and entirely without atmosphere. While clearing space for it, I discovered a drawer I had never managed to open. Inside was a map of the museum, drawn by my aunt. Most rooms had been crossed out and relabeled repeatedly. At the center was a small square marked RELEASES. Beside it she had written: NOT AN EXIT. I took out the pale third key. It had grown warmer. For the first time, I felt less annoyed than frightened by the possibility that I did, after all, know something.

The release room lay behind my father’s gallery. Its door was small enough that I had to bow to enter. Inside stood an empty table beneath a wide opening in the ceiling. Through it I could see a sky unlike the winter sky outside: pale, spacious, crossed by birds too distant to identify. There was no machinery, no furnace, no helpful instructional diagram. A card on the table said: NOT EVERYTHING MUST BE FINISHED. Underneath, someone had written in pencil, probably my aunt: THIS IS NOT PERMISSION TO BE CARELESS. I laughed then, with the sudden embarrassment of being understood.

I carried the birdhouse into the room. It looked smaller away from the workbench. The unfinished roofline was rough beneath my thumb. I had imagined completing it, hanging it in the garden, and receiving some modest revelation when the first bird moved in. Standing there, I saw how much work I had assigned to a bird. I set the house on the table. Nothing happened. Then I understood that setting something down was an action I might have to perform more than once. I picked it up again, took it home, and placed it on a shelf beside the window.

Spring came slowly. I reduced my railway hours. The museum acquired an unfinished opera that made the radiators sing, and I spent a week negotiating silence after ten. A visitor reclaimed an apology, then brought it back with additional pages. The retired teacher returned to look at her suitcase and finally took out a yellow dress, leaving the rest. I stopped trying to guess which visitors would feel better. Some left smiling and returned furious. Some cried at the entrance and emerged asking where they could get a decent lunch. I kept a list of nearby cafés behind the desk.

Sometimes I still listened to my father’s sentence. I never heard more than those four words, though once I thought I heard him draw breath afterward. I sat beside the workbench until closing, remembering an afternoon when we had built a gate together. He held the frame steady while I drove the screws. Rain began before we finished, and neither of us wanted to be the first to suggest stopping. We worked on with water dripping from our noses, making increasingly foolish claims about the quality of the weather. I had forgotten that afternoon while remembering the quarrel.

In May, a wren inspected the birdhouse through my open window. She landed on the sill, tilted her head, and delivered a sharp assessment of its shortcomings. I watched from the kitchen, scarcely breathing. She entered, emerged, and flew away. The next morning I bought a small piece of cedar. I cut a roof, sanded the edges, and fixed it in place with brass screws. The work took less than an hour. There was no revelation. I had to recut one panel because I measured it badly. My father would have noticed. I hung the finished house under the eaves.

The museum is open most evenings now. You can find it between the locksmith and the aquarium shop, though the door sometimes appears blue in rain. If you come, I will not ask what brought you. There are chairs in every gallery and a kettle that works. You may stay as long as you need, within reason; I do occasionally want to go home. Perhaps you will find something of yours. Perhaps you will decide to leave it where it is. At closing, I walk the rooms, turn out the lights, and check that nobody has mistaken a corridor for an answer.
