The first thing the city did after the old train station closed was remove the clocks. There were seven of them, each showing a slightly different time, and for forty years commuters had learned which one to trust. The clock above the bakery ran three minutes fast. The one beside platform four stopped whenever it rained. The great brass clock in the entrance hall was accurate only by accident, but people checked it anyway, perhaps because a clock that large seemed entitled to an opinion. By Monday morning, all seven were gone, leaving pale circles on the brick walls.

Only the bench remained. It stood beneath the empty place where the brass clock had been, made of dark wood polished by generations of waiting. There were scratches from suitcases, initials carved beneath the seat, and a small burn mark shaped like a country nobody could identify. The demolition crew had marked it with orange paint, but the driver of the removal truck forgot it. Then the project lost funding. Then winter arrived. By spring, the station was fenced off, the tracks were growing grass, and the bench sat in an abandoned room, waiting for absolutely nothing to happen.

A woman named Mara discovered it while looking for a place to eat an orange. She repaired elevators for a living and had spent the morning inside a building where everyone apologized for needing to go somewhere. The station door had been left open by a surveyor. Mara stepped inside, sat down, and began peeling the orange in one continuous spiral. The room smelled of dust and old rain. Somewhere high above her, a pigeon rearranged itself. For the first time that day, nobody pressed a button expecting her to arrive. She stayed until the light reached her muddy boots.

The next day, she came back with a sandwich. On Thursday, she brought a thermos. By the following week, she had developed a private attachment to the place, though she would have denied this if asked. She was not sentimental about buildings. Buildings contained cables installed by optimists and maintained by people with insufficient budgets. But she liked the station because it had stopped making demands. Even its neglect seemed restful. Nothing there required a password, a purchase, or an explanation. You could sit under the absent clock and finish your lunch without being gently encouraged to improve your experience.

In April, Mara found someone else on the bench. He was an elderly man wearing a coat too warm for the weather, with a paper bag between his shoes. She nearly turned around. Instead, he moved the bag and nodded toward the empty space. They sat without speaking. After a while, he took out a small radio, considered it, and put it away again. Mara offered him half her orange. He accepted with the solemn care of someone receiving an important document. When she left, he said, “The bakery clock was the best one. You had time for another coffee.”

His name was Elias, and he had once sold newspapers outside platform two. He knew which passengers were having affairs, which conductors wrote poetry, and which departures made people cry. He told these stories sparingly, never more than one in an afternoon. Mara appreciated this. Her brother told stories as though paid by the mile. Over the next month, other people appeared: a student with an unopened textbook, a courier between shifts, a father carrying a sleeping child. No one organized anything. The bench simply became a place people remembered when the rest of the city felt a too full.

By June, somebody had swept the floor. Somebody else had cleaned the windows within reach. A second chair appeared, then a third, neither matching anything. The student brought a plant that seemed unlikely to survive but did. Mara tightened the bench bolts with a wrench from her van. Elias objected to the orange demolition mark, so they sanded it away. They did not call themselves volunteers. There was no committee, no statement of purpose, and no photograph of them holding oversized scissors. When rain came through the roof, they moved the chairs and put a bucket underneath the steady drip.

The city noticed in August. A man with a clipboard arrived and explained that the building was unsafe. Mara asked which parts. He looked relieved to be asked a question with an answer. They walked around together, discussing loose masonry, damaged wiring, and the roof. The repairs were expensive, but less expensive than everyone had assumed. The man returned the next week without his clipboard and sat for twenty minutes. Then came inspections, applications, arguments, and several meetings that made Mara long for the straightforward hostility of a broken elevator. By November, the entrance hall was officially allowed to exist.

They could not reopen the platforms, and nobody wanted to. The tracks beyond the windows became a narrow meadow, full of stubborn yellow flowers. A local carpenter made another bench. The bakery, now three streets away, sent yesterday’s bread on Fridays. There were rules eventually, but only a few: leave room for others, clean up what you spill, and ask before turning on music. The student passed her exams. The father’s child learned to walk. Elias missed several afternoons in February, then returned with a cane and a furious account of the food served in hospital. Spring returned soon afterward.

Mara sometimes wondered why the place mattered so much to her. Nothing remarkable happened there. People lost gloves, disagreed about the weather, and left crumbs between the wooden slats. Some days she arrived tired and went home tired. Still, when her brother asked what they had built, she found herself unable to dismiss it. “A waiting room,” she said at last. “What are people waiting for?” She considered the question. Across the hall, Elias was teaching the courier how to mend a torn pocket. Outside, the train passed without stopping. “Nothing,” she said, surprised by how good the answer sounded.

The first thing Mara inherited from her uncle was a drawer full of keys that opened nothing she could find. The second was his shop, wedged between a bakery and a travel agency that still advertised countries under their former names. The third was a reputation for being able to fix anything, which was inconvenient because Mara could barely replace a bicycle chain. On the morning she unlocked the shop, a woman was waiting outside with a toaster in a shopping bag. “It burns one side,” she said. “So do I,” Mara replied, and immediately regretted trying to be funny.

The woman did not laugh. She set the toaster on the counter with the care people reserve for sleeping animals and disappointing relatives. A paper label dangled from its cord. In her uncle’s handwriting, it said: MRS VALE. DOES NOT LIKE SURPRISES. Beneath that, in smaller letters: HUSBAND DIED IN APRIL. Mara looked up, but the woman was studying the shelves. “Your uncle knew what was wrong,” she said. Mara turned the label over. There was no diagnosis, no price, only a penciled reminder to return the toaster before Friday. She promised to try, which was not quite a lie.

Behind the counter she found eighteen notebooks, each filled with diagrams, measurements, and observations that seemed only loosely connected to repair. A broken lamp belonged to someone who worked nights. A radio needed its tuning knob enlarged because its owner’s hands had begun to shake. Beside a drawing of a kettle, her uncle had written: Let him explain twice. He is practicing being understood. Mara sat on a stool and read until the bakery next door began selling yesterday’s bread at half price. She had thought she was inheriting a business. It appeared she had inherited instructions for paying attention.

She kept the shop open because closing it required decisions she could not yet make. On Tuesday, she learned to solder from a woman on the internet who spoke with magnificent impatience. On Wednesday, she discovered that unplugging an appliance was not the same as knowing it was safe to touch. On Thursday, she carried the toaster to an electrician across town and paid more to repair it than she could reasonably charge. Mrs Vale collected it on Friday. “What was wrong?” she asked. “A connection,” Mara said. This was technically true, and seemed sufficient for them both that morning.

By November, word had spread that the shop was open, although its new proprietor was slower and occasionally sent customers elsewhere. People brought clocks, fans, music boxes, and a mechanical singing fish that Mara privately hoped would remain silent. Some things she repaired. Some she learned to declare beyond repair. This was harder. People heard an accusation in it, as though they had loved an object incorrectly. She began explaining what had failed and showing them the piece. A cracked gear was easier to accept than a verdict. Often they asked to keep it, wrapped in a little paper bag.

One afternoon, a boy arrived carrying a globe with a dent in the Pacific Ocean. He placed it on the counter and spun it gently. Countries shivered past. “Can you fix this?” he asked. Mara examined the seam around the equator. The globe was cheap, its surface printed on paper stretched over cardboard. Opening it would probably destroy it. “What happened?” she asked. “I dropped it.” He paused. “My dad gave it to me before he moved.” Mara reached for a notebook, then stopped. Not everything a person said belonged in a record someone else might someday sit and read.

She told him she needed time to think. That evening, she walked home by the river, where the council had installed benches facing a wall of flood defenses. Above the concrete, a narrow strip of water caught the lights of passing buses. Her uncle would have known what to do, she thought, then distrusted the thought. Dead people became alarmingly competent when no longer available to make mistakes. In his notebooks were crossed out calculations, angry question marks, and one entire page devoted to a vacuum cleaner he had called a vindictive bucket. She went home and ate standing up.

The next day, Mara telephoned the boy’s mother and asked permission to try something that would not restore the globe exactly. Then she visited the stationery shop and bought a small sheet of blue paper, several brushes, and paint. She practiced on scraps until she could match the faded ocean. Over the dent she built a tiny island, with a crooked coastline and a mountain no larger than a grain of rice. She added a harbor, three roads, and a square of green. It was not invisible. It was plainly an intervention, and she worried he would hate the change.

The boy studied the island for a long time. “That’s not really there,” he said. “No,” Mara admitted. “I couldn’t make it how it was.” He turned the globe once, then brought the island back beneath his finger. “Is that a school?” “It could be.” “It needs a football field.” She handed him the smallest brush. He painted a green rectangle beside the harbor, concentrating so fiercely that his mouth fell open. Before leaving, he asked what he owed. Mara charged him for the paper. She had not yet learned how to charge for work she was proud of doing.

That winter, she finally sorted the drawer of keys. Most remained mysteries. One opened a cabinet containing spare hinges; another fitted the back door, which everyone had assumed was painted shut. The smallest unlocked a tin box holding photographs of her uncle as a young man, standing proudly beside appliances almost nobody owned anymore. On the back of one photograph, someone had written: Still learning. Mara put that photograph above the counter. Then she opened a fresh notebook and wrote down the things she needed to order: wire, screws, paper bags, blue paint. Outside, someone tried the door. It opened.

The town had a department for unfinished things.

It occupied two rooms above the public swimming pool, where the air smelled of chlorine and wet wool. There was no sign outside. People found it because someone told them, usually in a lowered voice, as though recommending a discreet dentist. Inside, a woman named Ada sat behind a desk with a green lamp. Behind her stood shelves full of objects that seemed ordinary until you looked closely: a sweater with one sleeve, a letter ending halfway through a sentence, a wooden bird that had never been given wings.

Ada did not finish these things. That was the first misunderstanding she had to correct. People arrived carrying their broken intentions and assumed she would repair them.

“I keep them,” she explained.

“For how long?”

“Until you know.”

Most people disliked this answer. They wanted a date, a fee, a form with numbered boxes. Ada had forms, but they asked unhelpful questions. *What did you believe this would become?* *Who were you when you began?* There was a space at the bottom for anything the applicant preferred not to explain. It was almost always filled.

One November morning, a man brought in a door.

He maneuvered it up the stairs sideways, apologizing whenever it struck the wall. He was perhaps seventy, with a broad, embarrassed face and sawdust caught in the seams of his coat. The door was small, painted yellow, with a round window near the top.

“For a treehouse,” he said.

Ada looked at the door, then at him.

“My daughter’s.”

He rubbed a thumb against a patch of paint. Downstairs, someone blew a whistle. The sound rose through the floorboards, sharp and official.

“She’s forty-three now,” he added.

Ada fetched the large-object form.

The man’s name was Daniel. He had built the platform, he explained, and two of the walls. Then his mother became ill. Then work became uncertain. Then winter came, and the following spring his daughter had discovered other children, other gardens, other ways of spending an afternoon. The platform remained in the tree for years. Eventually the tree grew around one of the bolts.

“I kept meaning to take it down.”

“The platform?”

“The idea.”

Ada nodded. She had a shelf of university applications from people approaching retirement. She understood that structures could remain standing after their practical use had ended.

Daniel left the door and returned the following Thursday.

He said he had been nearby, though Ada knew he lived across town. He looked at the shelves. There were three incomplete jigsaw puzzles, a proposal for a neighborhood orchestra, and a jar containing the first seventeen folded cranes of someone’s intended thousand.

“Do they ever come back for them?” he asked.

“Sometimes.”

“And finish?”

“Sometimes.”

This irritated him.

“You don’t say much.”

“I used to explain more,” Ada said. “People generally remembered the part they needed anyway.”

Daniel considered this, then asked whether she wanted tea.

After that, he came every Thursday. He brought tea in a flask because the department’s kettle tasted faintly of pennies. Ada provided biscuits from a tin whose lid showed a castle neither of them could identify. They rarely discussed the door. Instead they talked about the swimming lessons below, the difficulty of buying good pears, and the strange conviction among younger people that every surface needed a password. Daniel sometimes repaired small things around the office. He tightened a chair leg and unstuck a drawer. Ada allowed this, provided he asked first and did not touch anything on the shelves.

In January, Ada was absent.

A note on the desk said she would return Monday. Daniel stood in the doorway holding the flask. Without her, the room looked less mysterious. The carpet was worn through beside the filing cabinet. A damp patch had spread across the ceiling. He noticed, beneath her desk, a cardboard box he had never seen before.

It held a pair of walking boots, a map, and a photograph of a woman standing beside a mountain.

When Ada returned, he asked about it.

“My sister,” she said.

“Were you going somewhere?”

“We were.”

He waited.

“We postponed.”

That was all she offered, and he did not ask again. But something altered afterward. He had imagined Ada as the keeper of a condition from which she was somehow exempt, like a lifeguard who never entered the water. Now he noticed how carefully she lowered herself into her chair, and how she sometimes paused over the forms before filing them. He began carrying the tea upstairs in two smaller flasks. Neither mentioned it. One Thursday, while Ada searched for a receipt, he looked at the yellow door and realized he could no longer remember his daughter’s childhood height.

In March, he telephoned his daughter.

He asked if she remembered the treehouse. She laughed.

“The squirrel palace?”

“Is that what we called it?”

“That’s what I called it. You were very serious about keeping the squirrels out.”

He had remembered her waiting at the window, disappointed. She remembered stealing screws from his toolbox to use as money in elaborate games. When he apologized, she went quiet.

“Dad,” she said eventually, “I wanted you to come up there with me.”

The following Thursday, Daniel collected the door. Ada helped him down the stairs. Neither of them discussed the form.

He made it into a little cupboard for his granddaughter. The round window showed shelves of crayons, stones, and plastic animals. Its yellow paint clashed magnificently with the kitchen.

In April, Ada took a week off. She did not climb the mountain. She caught a train to the town below it and walked as far as a lake, where she ate a cheese sandwich in the wind.

When she returned, Daniel asked how it had been.

“Cold,” she said.

He poured the tea.

After a while, she took a photograph from her bag and slid it across the desk.

The Museum of Unfinished Things stood between a bakery and a shop that repaired watches. Most people walked past it. Its sign was modest, its windows dusty, and its opening hours were written in pencil. Sometimes it opened at nine. Sometimes the curator needed a little longer. Nobody complained, because nobody who entered the museum was in much of a hurry afterward.

Admission cost nothing, although visitors were asked to leave something at the desk: a worry, a mistaken certainty, a receipt they had been carrying for no reason. The curator accepted everything with equal seriousness and stored it underneath the counter.

The first room contained ordinary objects. A blue sweater with only one sleeve. A crossword abandoned on a Sunday afternoon. Three pages of a novel about a woman who discovers that her neighbor is secretly the moon. Beside each exhibit was a small card explaining where its maker had stopped.

The sweater’s card read: *She moved somewhere warmer.*

The crossword’s read: *He remembered he could call his brother.*

The novel’s read: *The author could not decide whether the moon should pay rent.*

People laughed at that one. Some returned later, alone, and stood before it for a surprisingly long time.

Beyond this room was the Gallery of Interrupted Meals. Here, under glass, sat a birthday cake missing its candles, a bowl of soup, and a peach with one bite taken from it. Nothing decayed. This was not the museum’s most remarkable property, but it was the one health inspectors found hardest to accept.

The curator explained that preservation was different from freshness.

“Freshness belongs to the present,” she said. “These things belong to the moment just before something else happened.”

“What happened?” visitors asked.

“Usually something ordinary. A telephone rang. A child woke up. Somebody knocked.”

“And sometimes?”

The curator nodded.

There was a room devoted to arguments that had never reached their conclusions. It was almost empty. Two chairs faced each other beneath a soft yellow light. Visitors occasionally heard fragments of conversation, though never enough to choose a side.

“That isn’t what I meant.”

“You always say that afterward.”

“I was trying to—”

The curator kept this room warmer than the others. She had discovered that people listened differently when they were cold.

Some visitors found the room unbearable. Others sat for hours, waiting for an apology that the museum could not supply. At closing time, she would gently open the door.

Children preferred the staircase. It climbed seventeen steps and then stopped in midair. There was no barrier at the top, but nobody had ever fallen. The unfinished staircase seemed to understand its responsibilities.

“Where was it going?” children asked.

“The second floor.”

“Why isn’t there a second floor?”

“There were difficulties.”

“What difficulties?”

“Money, mostly.”

This disappointed them. They wanted dragons, curses, architectural betrayal. So the curator sometimes added, “And a very stubborn dragon.”

Adults disapproved of this embellishment until they learned that the dragon had insisted on being paid fairly, at which point several admitted it sounded plausible enough.

At the back of the building stood a locked door. Behind it was the Collection of Unsaid Things.

The curator rarely opened it.

The contents were not uniformly sad. There were declarations of love, certainly, and apologies postponed until postponement became permanent. But there were also jokes wisely withheld, cruelties swallowed, secrets protected, and the wonderfully unnecessary advice that someone, through a heroic exercise of restraint, had decided not to offer.

People assumed silence was an absence. The room suggested otherwise. Silence could be crowded, deliberate, generous. It could also be cowardly. The labels were careful not to confuse these.

One rainy Thursday, a man arrived carrying a wooden boat. It was small enough to fit in his palms, with a painted hull and no mast.

“My father started it,” he told the curator.

She cleared a space on the desk.

“He died?”

“No. He lost interest.”

The curator waited.

“I keep thinking I should finish it.”

“Do you want to?”

“I want to be the sort of person who would.”

Outside, a bus sighed at the curb. The man turned the boat over. Its underside was rough, marked by tools that had stopped working forty years earlier that spring.

The curator did not tell him to finish the boat. She did not tell him to let it go. Museums, she believed, became dangerous when they started issuing instructions.

Instead, she asked what he remembered.

He remembered sitting beside his father in a shed. He remembered the smell of sawdust and the alarming seriousness with which adults handled small bottles of glue. He remembered being allowed to paint a stripe crookedly, and his father leaving it crooked.

For a while neither spoke.

Then the man put the boat back in his bag.

“I think I’d like to keep it,” he said.

People sometimes accused the museum of encouraging failure. They said the world had enough abandoned projects, enough weak resolve, enough drawers full of expensive supplies purchased during brief episodes of optimism.

The curator understood the objection. She herself owned a violin.

But a thing could stop for many reasons. A person might discover the work was wrong, or that someone else needed them, or that they had mistaken admiration for desire. Someone who loved music might not enjoy practicing scales. She had rented her violin before buying it and practiced faithfully for six months. She still liked to open its case occasionally.

At closing, the curator walked from room to room, straightening cards and checking windows. She paused beside the unfinished novel, as she always did.

Then she went upstairs.

There was, of course, a second floor. The staircase in the gallery was merely one way of failing to reach it.

In her office, she opened a notebook and wrote a sentence. She crossed out half, restored a word, and considered what should come next. Downstairs, the watches ticked through the wall, and the baker began preparing tomorrow’s dough.

She left the notebook open on her desk and went home for supper.

The museum opened on a Tuesday because nobody had strong feelings about Tuesdays. Its founder, a retired locksmith named Ada Bell, rented the ground floor of an old bakery and painted the walls the color of unbuttered bread. In the window she placed a handwritten sign: MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS. Beneath it, in smaller letters: Admission free. Explanations optional. For the first three days, nobody entered. People paused outside, examined the sign, and continued toward destinations where things could be purchased, repaired, or conclusively decided. Ada sat behind her desk, drinking tea and enjoying the unfamiliar luxury of being misunderstood.

The first donation was a blue sweater with one sleeve. A woman brought it in a grocery bag, along with the knitting needles still attached. “My mother was making this for my father,” she said. Ada waited. The woman looked around at the empty shelves. “He didn’t die, if that’s what you’re thinking. They divorced. She learned the accordion.” On the donation form, under Reason for abandonment, Ada wrote: A change in the weather. The woman laughed so suddenly that she had to sit down. Before leaving, she touched the unfinished sleeve with the cautious affection usually reserved for animals.

After that came a chess game preserved on a board, a dissertation about medieval drainage, and seventeen pages of a detective novel in which everyone seemed guilty except the murderer. A boy contributed a model ship whose rigging had defeated him. A man arrived with a sealed envelope addressed to his brother, then stood for twenty minutes without handing it over. Ada offered him tea. He declined, accepted, and finally took the letter home again. She considered this a successful visit. The museum had no acquisition targets. Its only policy was that nothing should be surrendered merely to satisfy paperwork.

By winter, the rooms were full. Visitors moved quietly between the exhibits, although Ada had never asked for silence. There was something about an abandoned effort that made people lower their voices. Finished things could defend themselves: a chair was a chair, a painting had its frame. Unfinished things remained exposed. You could see where confidence had thinned, where money had run out, where somebody had discovered that wanting a thing and wanting to make it were different desires. Beside each object, Ada placed a card containing whatever its donor wished to say. Some cards were blank. These attracted attention.

A local newspaper sent a reporter who asked whether the museum celebrated failure. Ada was fitting a broken drawer into a cabinet that had itself been donated unfinished. “Does a bus stop celebrate not being home?” she asked. The reporter smiled politely and wrote down nothing. He wanted a message, preferably one that could fit above a photograph. Ada understood. She had spent forty years opening locks for people who wanted to get somewhere else. Still, she could not supply him with a slogan. Sometimes a stopped thing was a failure. Sometimes it was an escape. Often nobody knew yet.

In January, a girl named Mina began visiting after school. She was twelve and wore a yellow coat with pockets that appeared to contain geological samples from several continents. Her favorite exhibit was an unfinished map of an imaginary country. The western coast was detailed: harbors, salt marshes, a lighthouse called Last Argument. Inland, the roads dissolved into pencil marks. Beyond a mountain range, the paper was untouched. “Why didn’t they finish?” Mina asked. “They didn’t say.” “Maybe they hadn’t been there.” Ada considered the blank country. “That seems possible.” Mina returned the next afternoon with a magnifying glass and questions.

For several weeks, Mina studied the map without touching it. Then she asked permission to draw a town beyond the mountains. Ada said no. Mina looked wounded. “But it isn’t finished.” “That doesn’t mean it belongs to us.” The girl was silent for a while. Outside, sleet clicked against the window like handfuls of dry rice. Finally Ada fetched a sheet of tracing paper. Together they laid it over the map. Mina drew a road through a mountain pass and, at its end, a town built around an enormous pear tree. She named the town Nevertheless. Ada made another cup.

Word spread that the museum allowed additions on tracing paper. Soon visitors were composing possible endings to stories, sketching second sleeves, and proposing conclusions to the drainage dissertation with varying degrees of scholarly responsibility. Ada kept these contributions in drawers beneath the exhibits. The originals remained untouched. People disagreed about whether a detective should confess, whether the ship required historically accurate ropes, and whether Nevertheless needed a railway station. Nobody could enforce an answer. This proved frustrating to certain visitors and deeply restful to others. One afternoon, two strangers spent an hour discussing the imaginary town’s flood defenses, then exchanged addresses.

In spring, Ada received a parcel containing a brass key and a note from her former apprentice. The key was one she had begun cutting years earlier, before a customer canceled the job. Her apprentice had found it behind a workbench. One edge was toothed; the other remained smooth. Ada held it in her palm and remembered the workshop: oil, metal dust, the radio that worked only when it rained. She had liked that life. Leaving it had still been right. For the display card she wrote: Intended for a door that no longer required opening. Then she crossed out Intended.

On the museum’s first anniversary, Mina brought a cake that sagged dramatically in the middle. They ate it with the knitting woman and three visitors caught in a downpour. Someone asked Ada how she would know when the museum was complete. Before she could answer, a leak began dripping into the imaginary country, just offshore from Last Argument. Everyone moved at once. They lifted the map, found a bucket, fetched towels. Mina carried the drawers to safety. Later, while Ada telephoned the landlord, the others stood around the rescued coast, examining a small, new island made entirely out of rain.

The shop appeared between a bakery and a locksmith’s on a Tuesday, which was the first suspicious thing. Nothing interesting had ever happened on that street before Thursday.

Its window displayed a brass bell, a blue mitten, and a glass of water. Above the door, gold letters announced:

**REPAIRS TO THINGS THAT ARE NOT BROKEN**

Below this, in smaller letters:

**Please do not bring printers.**

Mara noticed the shop while carrying home a lamp she had bought because her apartment needed something, though she doubted it needed a lamp. She stopped to look through the window. Behind a wooden counter, a man was carefully ironing a map.

The man looked up and beckoned.

Mara pointed at herself.

He nodded.

She entered with the reluctance of someone who has accidentally made eye contact with a person holding a clipboard.

“Excellent,” he said. “You’ve brought your lamp.”

“It works.”

“I should hope so. There’s a repair shop for broken ones near the station.”

He wore a gray cardigan with mismatched buttons. On the counter stood a jar labeled QUESTIONS THAT CAN WAIT. It was empty except for a folded scrap of blue paper.

“What do you repair?” Mara asked.

He set down the iron.

“Things that work perfectly well but have stopped doing what they’re for.”

“Such as?”

“Dining tables where nobody eats. Windows nobody looks through. A very expensive telescope owned by a gentleman who uses it to watch parking spaces.”

“That sounds less like a problem with the telescope.”

“Most problems are less like problems with telescopes than people initially suppose.”

Mara almost smiled. She placed her lamp on the counter.

The man plugged it in. A warm yellow circle appeared on the wood.

“Yes,” he said. “I see.”

“What?”

“Too early to say. Where were you planning to put it?”

“In the living room.”

“Beside what?”

“The sofa.”

“And what happens on the sofa?”

“I sit there.”

He waited.

“I watch things. Sometimes I eat.”

“Do you like the things you watch?”

“I don’t always remember them.”

He unplugged the lamp.

“This may take until Friday.”

Mara should have left with her purchase. Instead she asked how much it would cost.

“Bring something you’ve been saving for a special occasion.”

At home, the empty place beside the sofa seemed more noticeable than it had before she bought the lamp. Mara ate noodles standing in the kitchen. She opened a video on her phone, then another, and eventually put the phone facedown.

The apartment was quiet.

Her father had been dead for eleven months. This fact occurred to her at unpredictable times, but especially when something happened that would once have become a phone call. She had recently seen a dog carrying an enormous stick through a very narrow gate. Getting that dog through the gate would have occupied her father happily for twenty minutes.

She had watched alone.

On Wednesday she passed the shop without stopping. A woman was leaving with a kitchen chair held tenderly against her chest.

On Thursday the window contained a shoe, an hourglass, and a photograph facing inward.

On Friday Mara brought a tin of tea.

Her father had given it to her two birthdays ago. It was good tea, he had said, from a place where they knew what they were doing. She had kept it for company, then for better company, then for some future afternoon sufficiently important to justify opening it.

The shopkeeper accepted the tin without comment.

Her lamp stood on the counter. It looked unchanged.

“What did you do?”

“Adjusted its expectations.”

“Does that mean anything?”

“Not to the lamp.”

He handed her a small paper envelope.

“Put it wherever you like. Open this after you turn it on.”

“Is this some kind of therapy?”

“No. I haven’t the qualifications. Would you like a receipt?”

She took one. It read:

*One lamp. Returned to service.*

At home, Mara put the lamp beside the sofa and switched it on.

Inside the envelope was a photograph.

For a moment she thought it showed her father. Then she saw that it was an ordinary picture of a kitchen: wooden chairs, an open cupboard, sunlight on a table. A stranger’s kitchen. On the back, someone had written, *Before we painted it green.*

She examined it beneath the light.

There was a chipped bowl on the table. A jacket hung from a chair. Whoever had taken the photograph had caught the edge of a finger in the corner.

Mara turned it over again.

Then she went to the cupboard and took down her own box of photographs.

She had meant to organize them for years. There were envelopes from holidays, duplicate school pictures, three blurred images of a cat. She carried the box to the sofa and began making piles.

At ten she found her father standing beside a barbecue in the rain, holding a newspaper over his head. At eleven she called her sister.

“Do you remember that holiday where Dad insisted the weather was clearing?”

“The whole holiday?”

They laughed. Her sister remembered the photograph but not who had taken it. They argued about this for a while, then talked about other things.

When Mara finally went to bed, photographs covered the sofa. She left them there.

The next morning she returned to the shop.

The man was sewing a button onto a wedding dress.

“That wasn’t my photograph,” she said.

“No. Yours were at home.”

She put it on the counter.

“Did the tea count as payment?”

“Certainly.”

“Have you opened it?”

“Not yet.”

“Go on, then,” Mara said.

He fetched two cups from beneath the counter. While the kettle boiled, she watched people pass the window: a courier, a child, a woman holding flowers upside down.

“Good light in here,” she said.

“Yes,” he replied, looking up. “Especially in the morning.”

samples.result:
The shop appeared on a Tuesday between the bakery and the place that repaired phones. There had always been a narrow passage there, just wide enough for a person carrying bad news. Now there was a green door, a brass handle, and a window displaying a single handwritten card:

**SMALL REPAIRS TO THE WORLD.  
NO APPOINTMENT NECESSARY.**

Mara noticed it because she had broken an umbrella that morning and was, in a less visible way, having trouble with everything else.

Inside, the shop smelled of pencil shavings and rain on warm pavement. Shelves held jars with labels: *Courage, mild.* *The last five minutes before guests arrive.* *October light, western exposure.* Behind the counter sat an elderly man untangling a necklace with two needles.

“Do you fix umbrellas?” Mara asked.

“No,” he said. “But the hardware shop does. Ask for Leena.”

“What do you fix?”

He raised the necklace. “This, presently.”

She almost left. Instead, she pointed to the jar of October light.

“Is that actually what it says?”

“Open it.”

The lid resisted, then gave. For a moment, the room became the kitchen of her childhood home. Not in appearance: the shelves remained shelves, the man remained a man. But everything acquired the exact warmth of a late afternoon when her mother was peeling apples and there was still an hour before anyone expected anything of her.

Mara shut the jar.

“How much?”

“That one isn’t for sale. It’s a reference sample.”

She looked at him.

“For matching,” he explained.

Mara returned the following day with a problem she considered small enough to mention.

“The tree outside my flat was cut down last month. I keep looking for it when I come around the corner.”

The man introduced himself as Ivo and took a ledger from beneath the counter.

“Did it need cutting down?”

“The roots were damaging a pipe.”

“Were they?”

“I don’t know.”

He wrote something.

“I can’t restore the tree,” he said. “Living things aren’t repairs.”

“Then what can you do?”

“We could repair the looking.”

She disliked the suggestion immediately. The repeated disappointment seemed, somehow, like something she owed the tree.

Ivo nodded when she explained this.

“People often prefer to keep that.”

For a week, she visited at lunchtime. Sometimes someone was already there: a courier whose luck had become unreliable at traffic lights, a woman carrying the silence that followed an argument, a boy who had forgotten the sound of his grandfather’s laugh.

Ivo could not help everyone.

The courier needed lunch and better brakes. The woman left with instructions to make a telephone call she had been avoiding. For the boy, Ivo opened a drawer containing hundreds of small paper envelopes.

They listened to seven before finding the right laugh.

It was surprisingly rude.

The boy grinned.

“What would happen,” Mara asked one afternoon, “if you fixed something enormous?”

Ivo was repairing the particular heaviness of a public library door.

“Such as?”

“Hunger. War. All of it.”

He put down his tools.

“Would you trust a man in a shop to decide how?”

“If he could actually do it.”

“So would I,” he said.

He let her examine the door’s heaviness. It looked like a dull iron washer, heavier than its size suggested.

“I used to spend weeks searching the drawers for something large enough,” he told her. “I still look when new stock arrives.”

On Friday, Mara brought him a blue ceramic bowl, cracked from rim to base.

“My father made this.”

“Is he alive?”

“Yes.”

“Does he still make pottery?”

“No. His hands hurt.”

Ivo examined the bowl under a lamp.

“I can mend it.”

“So can glue.”

“Quite right.”

She waited, embarrassed by how much she wanted him to understand without requiring her to say it.

Finally, she said, “He doesn’t call.”

“Do you?”

“Sometimes.”

“Do you tell him you want him to?”

“No.”

Ivo placed the bowl between them.

“I’m afraid this really is a job for glue.”

She did not visit for several days.

During that time she bought glue, repaired the bowl badly, and called her father. They discussed the weather in two places, the cost of replacing a boiler, and a neighbour neither of them liked. Then there was a silence.

“I wish you’d call me sometimes,” she said.

Her father cleared his throat.

“I never know when you’re busy.”

“You can call and find out.”

“Oh,” he said.

Nothing transformed. But on Sunday her phone rang while she was washing rice, and she answered with wet hands.

When she returned, Ivo was packing.

The shelves were mostly empty. Without their jars, they looked cheap and a little crooked.

“Are you closing?”

“Moving.”

“Where?”

“I’ll find out when I get there.”

Mara felt a disproportionate panic. She had imagined the shop remaining indefinitely, an emergency exit from the ordinary rules.

“What if I need something repaired?”

“The hardware shop is excellent.”

“You know what I mean.”

He softened.

“Yes.”

He handed her a small envelope. Inside was a key, plainly cut, without ornament.

“What does it open?”

“This door. From either side.”

“But you’re taking the shop.”

“Someone has to run it.”

She laughed once, uncertainly.

“I don’t know how.”

“Neither did I.”

That evening, she sat behind the counter. Ivo had left the ledger, the needles, three jars, and a forwarding address that was either incomplete or a joke.

For an hour, nobody came.

She considered locking up. Instead, she wrote Leena’s name and the hardware shop’s opening hours on a card beside the till.

Just before six, a woman entered carrying a winter coat.

“The lining’s torn,” she said.

Mara nearly explained that this was not that kind of repair shop. Then she remembered she could sew.

“Let me have a look.”

The woman laid the coat across the counter. There was a rip beneath one sleeve, and someone had tried to close it with a safety pin.

“It catches my watch every morning,” she said.

Mara found thread in the drawer beneath the envelopes.

Outside, the bakery switched off its sign. She pulled her chair closer to the lamp and began.

samples.result:
The first thing the town lost was the sound of its clock.

For ninety-three years, the clock above the railway station had struck every hour with a note so deep that people claimed they could feel it through the soles of their shoes. Then, one Tuesday in October, the mechanism stopped. Nobody saw it happen. At eleven, the bell had sounded. At noon, there was only traffic, rainwater slipping through gutters, and a dog barking at a delivery van. Most people assumed they had been distracted. By evening, everyone knew. The hands remained fixed at seventeen minutes past eleven.

The council put up a notice explaining that repairs would begin as soon as a specialist could be found. Specialists, it turned out, were scarce. The company that had built the mechanism no longer existed, and its last apprentice had retired to an island where he repaired boats and refused to answer emails. A newer clock could be installed, someone suggested. This proposal generated forty-seven letters, two public meetings, and an argument outside the bakery that nearly ended a friendship of thirty years. Meanwhile, the old clock continued displaying its one unchanging opinion about the time.

At the station café, a woman named Mara began noticing small disturbances.

Customers stayed longer because they no longer heard the bell reminding them to leave. Others arrived early, suspicious of their watches. A retired geography teacher missed his usual train, though he wore two watches and carried a phone. “It’s not the information,” he told Mara, stirring a coffee that needed no stirring. “I have the information. It’s the permission.”

“Permission for what?”

“To stop doing one thing and start doing another.”

After that, Mara listened differently to the silences between cups touching saucers.

She had inherited the café from her father, along with three good knives, a temperamental refrigerator, and his conviction that every customer should be greeted before being asked what they wanted. For years, the clock had divided her working day into manageable pieces. Seven meant the first rush. Ten meant a quiet breakfast standing behind the counter. Three meant schoolchildren buying buns with coins warm from their pockets. Six meant wiping tables while her father, and later nobody, counted the till. Without the bell, afternoons spread unevenly. Some lasted minutes. Others seemed to contain entire unsuccessful versions of her life.

One Thursday, an elderly man entered carrying a wooden box tied with blue cord. He ordered tea and asked whether anyone had been up to look at the clock.

“Several people,” Mara said. “They all came down looking expensive.”

He smiled but did not explain himself.

When his tea arrived, he opened the box. Inside lay tiny drawers, screwdrivers, a folded cloth, and instruments whose purposes Mara could not guess. He took out a watch, listened to it, and wound it twice.

“Are you the specialist?” she asked.

“No,” he said. “I used to be his brother.”

Mara waited. Years of serving strangers had taught her that questions sometimes closed a conversation more firmly than silence.

“He died in February,” the man said. “On the island. I found the council’s letters when I went through his things.”

Outside, a train arrived with the tired metallic complaint of brakes.

“Can you repair it?”

“I don’t know. He understood large things. I worked on watches.”

“But you came.”

“Yes.”

He drank his tea carefully, holding the cup with both hands. Mara wrapped two sandwiches in paper and gave him the key to the tower.

For three days, nothing happened that anyone could see. The man climbed the tower each morning and returned in the late afternoon, bringing down dust on his shoulders. His name was Elias. He liked mustard, disliked the café’s radio, and sometimes spoke about his brother as though they had quarreled that morning. They had, in fact, quarreled twenty-two years earlier. Neither could remember what had started it, but both had maintained the disagreement with admirable consistency. Once, while Mara washed cups, Elias said, “You can become very skilled at keeping something broken.” She let the water run a moment longer.

On Sunday, he asked Mara to come upstairs.

The tower smelled of iron, cold wood, and old bird nests. Inside the clock, wheels stood taller than dinner plates. Cables descended into darkness. The machinery looked less like an instrument than a small, sleeping factory.

Elias pointed to a worn part resting on his cloth.

“I can replace this,” he said. “But there’s damage elsewhere. It won’t keep perfect time.”

“How imperfect?”

“A minute, perhaps two, over a week.”

Mara looked through the narrow window. Below, a woman was helping a child fasten a coat.

“Neither does anyone,” she said.

The bell sounded at four that afternoon.

It startled a cyclist, interrupted a wedding photograph, and caused the geography teacher to spill soup on his newspaper. In the café, six people looked up simultaneously. Mara, carrying a tray, stopped so abruptly that coffee slid into two saucers.

The sound was not quite as she remembered it. There was a roughness at its edge, a slight unevenness that might always have been there. She had expected to feel her father’s presence when it returned. Instead, she noticed that table four needed clearing and that someone at the counter was smiling.

Elias left the next morning. Mara put sandwiches beside his tea, and this time he paid for them before she could object. She watched him cross the platform carrying his wooden box. The clock said eight; her phone said two minutes after. She decided not to reset it yet. When the train had gone, she returned to the café and found the geography teacher waiting outside. He had forgotten his book and wanted another coffee. Mara unlocked the door, turned on the lights, and asked whether he had caught his train yesterday. “Eventually,” he said, taking off his coat.

samples.result:
Nobody noticed the extra minute until the clocks began apologizing. At noon on Tuesday, every clock in Bellwether paused, clicked twice, and displayed a small blue word where the time should have been: SORRY. Wristwatches whispered it. The station clock announced it through a speaker that had been broken since spring. Even the sundial in the mayor’s garden somehow arranged its shadow into an expression of regret. Then everything resumed. Buses arrived late, bread burned, and a child named Ada discovered that her ice cream had melted upward, leaving a small vanilla cloud tethered to the cone by a sticky thread.

By evening, the town had divided into those who blamed the government and those who blamed the weather. Ada blamed neither. She had watched the minute closely and seen something everyone else had missed: a man in a gray coat hurrying between the seconds, carrying a bucket. He looked exhausted. His shoes were wet, and whatever sloshed inside the bucket shone like sunlight seen through closed eyelids. When the clocks started again, he vanished behind the bakery. Ada finished her cone, folded the empty napkin into a square, and decided that tomorrow she would ask him what he was doing.

She found him just before noon behind the bakery, sitting on an overturned crate. His bucket stood between his feet. Up close, he looked less like a mysterious stranger than a plumber who had received bad news. “You can see me,” he said. “You’re not especially hidden,” Ada replied. He considered this, then nodded with the solemn gratitude of someone encountering useful criticism. His name was Mr. Vale, and he maintained the town’s unused time. Usually, he explained, there wasn’t much. A forgotten appointment. A kettle watched too carefully. The moment after someone says goodbye but before they actually leave.

“Lately, though,” he said, lifting the bucket, “there’s been a terrible surplus.” Ada peered inside. She saw a summer afternoon, a woman standing outside a hospital room, and three boys pretending not to wait for an invitation. She saw her father in his parked car, hands resting on the steering wheel long after the engine stopped. “That’s not unused,” she said. Mr. Vale sighed. “I know. The forms are very old.” He produced a damp sheet labeled UNPRODUCTIVE INTERVALS. Beneath it were boxes for hesitation, grief, wonder, and miscellaneous. Someone had crossed out wonder and written inefficiency in red pencil.

Ada attended a school where every minute belonged to something before it even happened. Reading minutes. Running minutes. Quiet minutes, during which silence was measured by a machine shaped like a cheerful ear. She understood the appeal of a box. Boxes kept things from spilling. But looking into Mr. Vale’s bucket, she wondered whether some things were supposed to spill. “Where does it go?” she asked. He pointed down. Beneath Bellwether, beneath the pipes and roots and sleeping beetles, stood an enormous reservoir. For years it had held everything the town considered wasted. Now its ancient walls were giving way.

They entered through a door inside the bakery’s flour cupboard. The baker waved without looking up. “Everybody knows?” Ada whispered. “Everybody knows something,” said Mr. Vale. A staircase descended farther than seemed reasonable. At the bottom lay a lake without a shore, luminous beneath a ceiling of tangled clockwork. Waves broke against the stairs, each carrying a sound: unfinished laughter, rain on a tent, somebody practicing an apology. Across the water, a crack ran through the darkness. Light leaked from it in bright, irregular pulses. Mr. Vale set down his bucket. Against that immense lake, it looked almost unbearably small.

“There’s a procedure,” he said. “We drain the excess into next winter. People feel a little older. Nothing dramatic.” Ada watched a wave unfold the afternoon her mother had taught her to whistle. Neither of them had succeeded. They had laughed until dinner went cold. She had forgotten that afternoon, which seemed different from having wasted it. “What if we give it back?” Mr. Vale removed his hat. Underneath, his hair stood up like grass after a storm. “People might not want it.” “They wanted it once.” He looked at the crack, then at the bucket. “There is another procedure.”

At noon the following day, every clock in Bellwether stopped. This time, none apologized. The baker sat beside his oven and remembered why he liked making bread. A bus driver opened both doors and listened to the trees. In the mayor’s garden, two strangers shared a bench without discussing the weather. Ada’s father came home early, although later he could not explain what early meant. He found her on the step. “Would you like to go somewhere?” he asked. She shook her head. They stayed there, watching ants carry something much larger than themselves through a crack in the pavement.

The extra minute lasted long enough for several things that could not be hurried. An apology reached its difficult middle. A child finished describing a dream. Someone standing outside a hospital room finally opened the door. Not everything improved. Some people were bored. One man spent the entire interval complaining that his watch was broken. But below the town, the lake fell, and the crack began to close. Mr. Vale stood on the stairs with his empty bucket, hearing the machinery settle into a gentler rhythm. For the first time in years, he did not check how long it took.

Afterward, Bellwether changed in ways too small for official records. The school’s cheerful ear disappeared. The mayor occasionally missed appointments because the garden was particularly beautiful. Ada’s father still sat in his car sometimes, but now she joined him. They said nothing together. Behind the bakery, Mr. Vale replaced his bucket with a watering can. He had discovered that certain minutes, properly tended, grew into something else. Nobody could agree on what to call it. Happiness was too simple. Rest was too small. Ada, who visited often, never bothered with a name. She simply stayed until she felt like leaving.

samples.result:
The first thing Ada repaired was a toaster that had forgotten what bread was.

It sat on her workbench with an air of injured dignity, rejecting every slice she offered. The heating elements worked. The lever worked. Even the little dial, which promised a spectrum from pale gold to archaeological charcoal, turned smoothly. But the bread sprang back out as if the machine objected on principle.

“Fair enough,” Ada told it. “We all lose track.”

She cleaned its contacts, replaced a tired spring, and discovered a marble wedged beneath the carriage.

After that, it remembered.

***

Her repair shop occupied the narrowest building on Bellwether Street. Between a pharmacy and a bakery, it looked less like a business than a gap someone had reluctantly roofed over. The sign above the window said ADA VALE: REPAIRS, and below that, in smaller letters, MOST THINGS.

People occasionally asked what the exception was.

“Depends on the week,” she said.

She repaired lamps, radios, kitchen chairs, music boxes, and the peculiar mechanical birds that had been fashionable thirty years earlier. Once, she repaired a velvet curtain by introducing its owner to a woman named June.

She considered that a successful repair.

***

One wet Thursday, a boy arrived carrying a cardboard box.

He was perhaps ten, with rain flattened into his hair and the stern expression children wear when they have decided not to cry.

“My grandfather said you fix things.”

“Sometimes.”

The boy placed the box on her counter. Inside lay a pocket watch, a grocery receipt, and a photograph of a man standing beside an enormous pumpkin.

“The watch?” Ada asked.

“The afternoon.”

She waited.

“The last afternoon I saw him. I spent it playing a game on my mother’s phone.”

Outside, a bus exhaled at the curb.

“I want it back.”

***

Ada had learned that impossible requests deserved a chair.

She pulled one over and put the kettle on.

“What’s your name?”

“Eli.”

“And your grandfather?”

“Granddad.”

“A good name.”

He gave her a suspicious look, checking for mockery. Finding none, he sat.

Ada examined the watch. Its case was scratched, its glass intact. The hands pointed to twenty past four.

“When did it stop?”

“I don’t know.”

She wound it gently. Nothing happened.

Eli watched her fingers.

“You can fix it?”

“The watch, probably.”

“And the afternoon?”

The kettle began its small, rising argument with the silence.

“Tell me about it,” she said.

***

At first, Eli remembered only the phone.

There had been a game involving towers and bright, furious creatures. He had nearly reached a difficult level. His grandfather had been talking, and Eli had said “Uh-huh” several times without listening.

“What was he wearing?” Ada asked.

“The brown cardigan.”

“Was it cold?”

“No. He always wore it.”

“What could you smell?”

Eli frowned.

“Tomatoes.”

Ada set two mugs on the counter. His contained mostly milk.

“He was making lunch?”

“No. We were in the greenhouse.”

A little space opened in his expression.

“There was a cracked pane. He’d taped it.”

***

The afternoon returned reluctantly, in pieces too ordinary to have seemed worth keeping.

His grandfather had watered the seedlings with a red jug. A bee had battered itself against the glass, ignoring the open door. Somewhere beyond the garden wall, someone was cutting timber.

“He said the bee was like Uncle Martin,” Eli remembered.

“Why?”

“I don’t know. He laughed.”

“What happened next?”

Eli looked down at the photograph.

“He gave me a tomato.”

“Was it good?”

“It was warm.”

He said this with surprise, as though warmth were information he had just received.

“I dropped some on my shirt.”

***

Ada opened the watch.

Inside, a small brass wheel had come loose. She found the escaped screw caught in a fold of the mechanism and set it carefully in a tray.

Eli leaned forward.

“Is that all?”

“That’s enough.”

While she worked, he remembered his grandfather finding a cloth to wipe the tomato juice. He remembered being irritated by the fuss.

“Was that before the game?” Ada asked.

“During. I had to pause it.”

The boy rubbed a mark on his sleeve.

“He asked if I wanted another one.”

“Did you?”

“Yes.”

Ada fitted the wheel back into place and checked it under her magnifying lamp.

***

“Did you ever do something like that?” Eli asked.

“Pay attention to the wrong thing?”

He nodded.

“My mother called while I was assembling a wardrobe. I let it ring because I was holding the door straight.”

“Did she die?”

“Not that day. Four years later.”

“Oh.”

“I called her back after supper. She wanted to know whether I needed curtains.”

“Did you?”

“Yes. But I said no.”

Eli considered this.

“Why?”

“I wanted to choose them myself.”

“Did you get ugly ones?”

“Terrible ones.”

He smiled into his mug, and Ada tightened the screw.

***

When the watch began ticking, Eli flinched.

The sound was surprisingly loud.

Ada closed the case and passed it across the counter.

“You haven’t fixed the afternoon,” he said.

“No.”

He held the watch against his ear.

“I still wish I’d listened.”

“I know.”

“Maybe he said something important.”

“Maybe. Did he often?”

“Sometimes he just complained about slugs.”

Ada nodded.

“He hated those,” Eli said.

He finished his milk while she wrote out the receipt. She charged him for the screw, although she had used the old one.

He paid with coins from a purse shaped like a football.

***

The following Thursday, Eli returned with his mother’s desk fan.

“It rattles,” he announced.

Ada plugged it in. The fan made a noise like cutlery falling downstairs.

“An accurate diagnosis.”

He watched her remove the guard. Then he took a folded sheet of paper from his pocket.

“I wrote down the greenhouse,” he said. “Mum helped. She knew why he laughed about Uncle Martin.”

He left the paper beside the fan while he went to the bakery.

Ada didn’t unfold it. She moved it clear of the screws, where he would see it when he came back.

samples.result:
The Museum of Almost occupied a former railway station at the edge of a city that had stopped appearing on most maps. This was not a catastrophe. The roads still reached it, and the baker still complained about flour. But mapmakers had gradually decided that other places were more important, and the city, tired of arguing, had allowed itself to become a little difficult to find. Visitors generally arrived while looking for somewhere else. They came through the station doors carrying suitcases, apologies, or the particular expression of people whose phones had just run out of battery.

Inside, there were no dinosaur bones, royal jewels, or paintings of men pointing at conquered hills. The museum collected unfinished things.

Its oldest object was a clay bowl abandoned four thousand years earlier when the potter heard someone calling from outside. One side rose smoothly toward the rim. The other remained thick and low, bearing the marks of three fingers. Nobody knew why the potter had left or whether they had intended to return. The label said only: *Bowl, interrupted.* Children liked it better than the complete bowls in other museums. It looked, they said, as though somebody had made it.

The curator was a woman named Ada, who wore practical shoes and had a habit of listening after people finished speaking. She had inherited the museum from her uncle, along with a leaking roof and seventeen keys whose locks could not be located. Her uncle believed every unfinished thing contained a small reserve of possibility. Ada was less certain. Some objects in the collection seemed merely abandoned, and a few were poorly made. She kept them anyway. Her task, as she understood it, was not to settle their worth but to prevent their disposal.

In the east gallery stood a wooden boat that had never touched water. A retired carpenter had built it for his daughter, who wanted to sail around the world. Before he finished, she discovered she preferred mountains. He continued working until she brought him photographs from her first expedition. Then he put down his plane and asked her to explain the ropes. The boat arrived at the museum years later, still smelling faintly of cedar. In its hollow belly, Ada placed a bench. People sat there to rest, which was not the use the carpenter had planned, but suited its shape.

There was a room of letters, naturally. Museums of this sort cannot avoid letters. Some ended after “Dear.” Others approached a confession through six pages of weather. One consisted of a single sentence: *I was wrong about the apricots.* Ada spent years wondering about that one. She imagined an orchard boundary, a stolen basket, an argument over jam. Occasionally she invented an entire family and followed its quarrels through three generations. Then she would close the drawer. Whatever had happened, someone had sat down with paper and tried to correct a very particular mistake.

The most controversial exhibit was an empty glass case labeled *An apology, prepared but not delivered.* Visitors complained that there was nothing in it. Ada agreed. Several accused her of pretending an ordinary empty case was an important artifact. She said they were welcome to that interpretation. One afternoon, a man stood before it for nearly an hour, then borrowed the telephone at the front desk. Ada went into the storeroom to give him privacy. When she returned, he was gone. Beside the telephone he had left enough money to cover the call, though local calls were free.

Not everything was melancholy. There were half knitted scarves in improbable colors, inventions defeated by basic physics, and a cookbook whose author had completed only the desserts. A symphony stopped halfway through a phrase that made musicians twitch. Schoolchildren were allowed to suggest endings. Their versions involved thunder sheets, animal noises, and, once, forty seconds of deliberate silence followed by someone dropping a spoon. Ada recorded each performance. By the following spring, the recording cabinet was full, and she had to move the unfinished symphony into a larger room to accommodate everything it had started.

Every Thursday, a man named Emil visited a painting in the northern corridor. It showed a kitchen table, a blue cup, and the outline of a woman near a window. His wife had begun it before her hands became too unsteady to hold a brush. After her death, friends suggested hiring someone to finish it. Emil refused, though he could not explain why until he saw it hanging in the museum. “That is where she stopped,” he told Ada. He seemed relieved that the outline could remain an outline. On later visits, he sometimes brought flowers from their garden.

Ada herself kept an unfinished thing in her office: an application to study astronomy, dated twenty three years earlier. She had filled out her name, address, and previous education. The section asking why she wanted to join the program remained blank. At nineteen, she had wanted the stars so badly that explaining herself to a committee felt impossible. Later, she blamed work, money, her uncle’s illness. These were genuine obstacles, but the blank space embarrassed her more. Sometimes she unfolded the application and tried a sentence on scrap paper. She had accumulated quite a stack without finding one she liked.

One winter evening, after a school visit, Ada found a paper star beneath the unfinished boat. A child had written a name on one side and crossed it out. She carried it upstairs, then sat beside her office window. Across the street, someone was washing dishes. Above the roofs, one bright point appeared in the thinning cloud. Ada could not identify it. She searched for the local observatory and found a public evening scheduled for Friday. The booking form asked only how many people would attend. She entered one, paid, and wrote the time on the back of the star.

The first thing my father repaired after he died was the kitchen clock.

This was inconvenient, because I had already told everyone I did not believe in ghosts. I had said it at the hospital, then at the funeral, and again when my aunt suggested that the robin on my windowsill might be carrying a message.

“It’s carrying a beetle,” I told her.

But on Tuesday morning, the clock began to tick.

It had been broken for eleven years. My father had promised to fix it for ten of them, which was the sort of arithmetic our family understood. For the final year, nobody mentioned it. There were other mechanisms to worry about.

I stood beneath it with my coffee cooling between my hands.

“Very funny,” I said.

The clock continued. It had always been a cheap clock, with a painted lemon on its face. Death had apparently done nothing to improve my father’s taste.

On Wednesday, the cupboard stopped squeaking.

On Thursday, the back door closed without requiring a shove from the hip.

By Friday, I had begun leaving things out.

A toaster with a treacherous lever. A lamp that worked only when its cord lay in a particular, humiliating curve. The little wooden horse I had broken when I was seven and kept in a drawer because throwing it away seemed worse than keeping it broken.

Every morning, something worked again.

There were rules, though I learned them slowly.

He could manage wood, metal, wire, and glue. Fabric defeated him, just as it had in life. I left a torn shirt on the table and found it unchanged beside a repaired stapler I had not realized was broken.

He would not touch anything that still worked, however badly. My laptop remained slow. The refrigerator continued its low, prophetic groaning.

And he never appeared.

I tried staying awake. I sat at the kitchen table with a book open and the lamp burning. Nothing happened until I went upstairs to use the bathroom. When I returned, the wobble had gone from my chair.

“Coward,” I said, but fondly.

Soon the house became intolerably functional.

Drawers slid. Windows opened. The bathroom tap stopped dripping, taking with it a sound I had once hated and now discovered had been keeping me company.

Without the drip, I heard the refrigerator. Without the cupboard squeak, I heard my own breathing. I began to understand how much noise a house could lose before it felt empty.

I missed the noises. I missed him more.

One evening, I put his old wristwatch on the table.

It was not broken. I knew this. I had wound it every Sunday since the funeral. But I wanted him to hold something he had held before. I wanted, absurdly, to give him a familiar job.

In the morning, the watch sat exactly where I had left it.

Beside it was a small screwdriver.

I knew the screwdriver. Its yellow handle had a burn mark from the time he had used it to poke a barbecue coal, insisting afterward that tools should be versatile.

I picked it up.

It was cold.

This disappointed me so sharply that I sat down.

For several days, I left nothing out. The house behaved itself. I went to work, bought groceries, answered messages, and did the ordinary things grief permits once it has stopped demanding every hour.

Then my neighbor knocked.

She carried a radio wrapped in a dish towel.

“I heard you fix things,” she said.

I almost corrected her.

Instead, I asked who had told her.

“Your aunt.”

Naturally.

The radio had belonged to her husband, who was alive but no longer knew what radios were. She wanted to play the cricket commentary in his room. Sometimes, she said, he still turned his head at the sound of applause.

I took it.

That night, I placed the radio on the kitchen table.

“Please,” I said.

In the morning, nothing had changed.

I checked the plug, the switch, the tuning dial. Silence.

For the first time, I was angry.

“You can mend a stapler,” I said to the empty kitchen.

The clock ticked with appalling neutrality.

I went to work. I came home. The radio waited.

Eventually, I fetched the screwdriver.

My father had taught me some things, though at the time I had considered them obstacles between myself and whatever I preferred to be doing. Unplug it first. Keep the screws in a saucer. Never force a part until you understand what is holding it.

Inside the radio, dust lay over everything like felt.

I cleaned it carefully. I found a loose wire near the speaker. I watched three videos, borrowed a soldering iron, and burned my thumb.

At midnight, the radio crackled.

A man was explaining the weather in a place I had never been.

I laughed so loudly that someone knocked on the wall.

The next morning, my father’s screwdriver was gone.

I searched the table, the floor, the drawer where I kept batteries. Nothing.

The clock had stopped, too.

For a moment, I stood very still.

Then I took it down.

Inside was a battery so old that its label had begun to peel. I replaced it with one from the drawer, and the second hand lurched forward.

That afternoon, I returned the radio.

My neighbor turned it on before I had finished explaining about the loose wire. Music filled her hallway, thin and bright.

“What do I owe you?”

“Nothing.”

She frowned.

“Tea, then.”

I stayed an hour.

When I got home, the kitchen was quiet except for the clock. I put the borrowed soldering iron by the door, ready to return, and washed the saucer that had held the screws.

Under it, I found one left over.

The first thing the Museum of Ordinary Things acquired was a blue plastic chair.

It arrived on a Tuesday, carried by a woman who said she was moving somewhere smaller. One leg was shorter than the others. There was a pale rectangle on the back where a sticker had been peeled away.

“Was it owned by anyone famous?” asked the museum’s director.

“No.”

“Did anything important happen in it?”

The woman considered this.

“My father used to sit there while he waited for the kettle.”

The director accepted the chair.

At the time, the museum occupied two rooms above a locksmith’s shop. Its funding came from a clerical error that nobody in the municipal government had yet discovered. Its director, whose name was Mara, had previously catalogued agricultural equipment. She knew how to distinguish seven kinds of obsolete seed drill, but not how to persuade people through a door.

For three weeks, nobody visited.

Then a boy came upstairs looking for the toilet.

Mara showed him where it was. Afterward, he stood in front of the chair.

“Can you sit on it?”

“Yes.”

He sat.

“It wobbles.”

“Yes.”

He stayed until closing time.

The next acquisition was a shopping list found inside a library book. It read: onions, batteries, rice, something nice.

Mara mounted it beneath glass.

She spent an entire afternoon writing the label, rejecting phrases like “domestic aspiration” and “the poetry of necessity.” Finally she wrote: Found on page 143. The book was returned six days late.

A retired bus driver brought a key that no longer opened anything he owned. A nurse donated a cardigan with one cuff stretched wider than the other. Someone left a jar of buttons outside the door, along with a note that said, Please don’t sort these. They have been together a long time.

Mara did not sort them.

By winter, the museum had acquired eleven regular visitors and a leak.

The leak appeared above the display of expired coupons. Mara placed a saucepan beneath it and moved the coupons somewhere dry. The sound of dripping accompanied the exhibits with irregular, metallic notes.

One visitor asked whether the saucepan was part of the collection.

“Not yet,” Mara said.

He nodded, apparently satisfied.

There were people who disliked the museum on principle. A columnist called it an attic with opening hours. A councillor asked what measurable benefit it provided. Mara invited him to visit, but he sent a questionnaire instead. She answered the questions she could and left the box marked “Projected Annual Growth” empty.

Her own doubts were less easily filed away.

Some afternoons she looked at the cardigan and saw only a cardigan. The heating failed. Dust settled on the jar. She wondered whether she had mistaken reluctance to throw things away for a worthwhile occupation.

Then the woman who had donated the chair returned.

She stood beside it without sitting down.

“I got this wrong,” she said.

Mara felt her stomach tighten. There were forms for returning donations, but she had never needed one.

“He didn’t wait for the kettle. He waited for my mother to finish getting ready. Every morning, even after he retired. She was always looking for something.”

“Would you like me to change the label?”

The woman shook her head.

“There isn’t a label.”

“No,” Mara said. “You didn’t want one.”

“Oh. Right.”

They stood there for a while.

Eventually the woman laughed.

“He complained every single morning.”

Mara brought another chair from her office. They sat together until the locksmith downstairs began pulling down his shutter.

After that, Mara kept a notebook of corrections.

Not corrections to facts, exactly. Corrections to what people first felt able to say.

The bus driver returned to explain that the useless key had belonged to his brother’s flat. The cardigan’s stretched cuff came from a child holding it while falling asleep. The shopping list remained anonymous, although three visitors claimed to recognise the handwriting and none agreed about whose it was.

The notebook stayed in Mara’s desk. Visitors who wanted a story sometimes seemed disappointed when she could offer only the object. She understood. She liked stories herself. But the nurse had asked her not to tell anyone about the cuff, and keeping that promise was easy.

In spring, the council discovered the funding error.

An email arrived with three attachments and an apology generated by software.

The museum would close at the end of the month.

Mara told the regular visitors. She ordered cardboard boxes and began contacting donors. Several telephone numbers no longer worked. The woman who had moved somewhere smaller had moved again.

On the last Tuesday, the boy returned.

He was taller now. He had originally come looking for the toilet almost two years earlier, and afterward had visited whenever his parents were arguing at home.

“What happens to the chair?” he asked.

“I haven’t decided.”

“Could it go downstairs?”

They asked the locksmith, who examined its uneven legs and agreed.

He folded a square of cardboard and tucked it beneath the shortest one. The boy tested the seat while Mara watched from the doorway.

“Better,” he said.

On closing day, Mara packed the shopping list, the buttons, the cardigan, and the key. She washed the saucepan. Without its contents, the museum looked much as it had before she rented it, except for clean rectangles on the walls.

Downstairs, an elderly man was sitting in the blue chair while the locksmith cut him a spare key.

Mara paused beside him.

“Comfortable?”

“Enough.”

Outside, rain had started. She stood under the awning with the last box balanced against her hip, searching her pockets for her umbrella.

Behind her, the locksmith asked the man whether he was in a hurry.

“Not especially,” he said.

Mara found the umbrella hooked over her arm. She put the box down to open it, then picked it up again and headed toward the bus stop. Before she reached the corner, the rain had soaked through one cardboard edge. She shifted the box beneath her coat and kept walking, slowly now, taking care not to spill anything.
