The town’s clock stopped at 3:17, and for a while everyone enjoyed having an opinion about it.

“Electrical,” said the baker, though the clock was mechanical.

“Mechanical,” said the electrician, pleased to be free of the matter.

The mayor promised a committee. Children discovered that if they ran home at the right moment, they could truthfully say the clock showed they weren’t late.

Only the woman who repaired watches seemed uninterested.

Her shop stood beneath the tower. Every morning she unlocked it at nine, set a little brass bell on the counter, and worked until the light withdrew from her window. People brought her wristwatches, carriage clocks, kitchen timers shaped like eggs. Once, a fisherman brought her a compass.

“It doesn’t point north,” he said.

She turned it over in her hand. “Neither do you, most days.”

He left it with her anyway.

Eventually the mayor came down.

“We were hoping you might look at the clock.”

“I’ve been looking at it for twenty-three years.”

“I mean professionally.”

“That will cost more.”

Up inside the tower, the air smelled of dust and old rain. The mayor followed her through a narrow hatch and watched as she examined the mechanism. He had prepared himself for something grand: a broken wheel, a snapped shaft, the expensive failure of an important part.

She found a bird’s nest.

It had been built carefully in the shelter of the gears, from twigs, blue thread, and a long strip of somebody’s grocery list. Three eggs lay inside.

“Well,” said the mayor.

“Yes,” she said.

“How soon can you fix it?”

She leaned closer to the nest, then stepped back.

“A few weeks.”

At the next council meeting, the mayor reported that the clock required a delicate intervention. This satisfied everyone. Delicate interventions sounded expensive, but also suggested the situation was under control.

Summer advanced. The bakery opened. Trains departed. Lovers arrived early and pretended they hadn’t.

And above the square, in the great suspended afternoon of 3:17, three small birds took their time.

The town hired a man to wind the clock in the railway station, even though no trains had stopped there for twenty-three years.

Every Monday, he unlocked the narrow door beside the ticket window and climbed eighty-one stairs. He carried a sandwich, a flask of tea, and a brass key the length of his forearm.

The clock lost four minutes a week. He had mentioned this to the council.

“Can you fix it?” they asked.

“Probably.”

“Then we’ll have to discuss whether that’s desirable.”

They never did.

His name was Emil. He had once repaired watches, but people stopped bringing them. A watch that broke was now an excuse to buy another watch, or to discover that a telephone knew the time. He still kept the tiny screwdrivers in their velvet case.

One Monday, he found a girl sitting on the stairs.

“You’re not supposed to be here,” he said.

“Neither are trains.”

He considered this, then stepped around her.

She followed him up.

Inside the clock room, the machinery occupied nearly all the space. Wheels turned with a deliberateness that made people lower their voices. Through the glass face, the town appeared divided by enormous black numerals.

The girl looked through the six.

“My mother says they’re closing this.”

“Your mother on the council?”

“She cuts their hair.”

“Better informed, then.”

He fitted the key and began to wind.

“What happens if you stop?”

“The clock stops.”

“And then?”

He rested one hand on the key.

“Then people look up and see the wrong time.”

“They do that now.”

“Yes,” he said. “But only a little.”

She stayed while he ate his sandwich. Before leaving, she asked whether she could come back next Monday.

“If you bring your own lunch.”

The following week, she brought a sandwich and a watch with a cracked strap.

“It was my grandfather’s. My mother said I could ask.”

Emil held it close to his ear, then turned the crown gently between two fingers.

“Well?” she asked.

“I’ll need my tools.”

“Are they here?”

“No. At home.”

“Can we go and get them?”

He looked at the station clock. There was no particular reason to hurry, but he wrapped the rest of his sandwich anyway.

The town’s clockmaker retired on a Tuesday and left a note in his window:

**IT IS PROBABLY THE BATTERY.**

For three days, people admired the practicality of this. On Friday, someone knocked anyway.

It was a girl holding a kitchen timer shaped like a tomato.

“It doesn’t have a battery,” she said when he opened the door.

The clockmaker considered this.

“An oversight in my announcement.”

He let her in.

His shop had become stranger now that it was no longer a shop. Without customers, the clocks seemed less like merchandise and more like an audience. They ticked with the faint, collective impatience of people waiting for a speaker to find his notes.

The girl set the tomato on his bench.

“It stops at four minutes.”

“What do you need five minutes for?”

“Nothing. But it ought to get there.”

He fetched a screwdriver.

Inside the timer was a spring, a little train of gears, and a grain of something that might once have been sugar. He touched it with the tip of a brush.

“There.”

“That’s all?”

“Usually, something small is in the way.”

She watched him put the casing back together.

“Is that why you retired?”

He looked up.

Outside, a delivery van was attempting to reverse into a space that had never been large enough for it. The driver had been trying for years, under different employers.

“No,” he said. “I retired because I’m tired.”

The girl nodded as if this were a satisfactory mechanical explanation.

He wound the tomato to five minutes. They waited.

At four minutes, he caught himself leaning closer. The girl stood with her chin just above the workbench, following the slow movement of the dial. Somewhere behind them, a clock struck eleven. Another, less dependable clock struck three.

The tomato rang.

The girl picked it up with both hands.

“What do I owe you?”

“Don’t keep it next to the sugar.”

After she left, he took down the note. He returned to the bench, found his pen beneath the brush, and added a line.

**IT IS PROBABLY THE BATTERY.**

**IF IT ISN’T, KNOCK QUIETLY.**

The repair shop at the end of the street fixed things that weren’t supposed to break.

Not clocks or kettles. There were other shops for those.

This one repaired the feeling of arriving home, the ability to enjoy a song after someone unkind had loved it, and the small but essential mechanism that lets a person say, “I don’t know,” without feeling diminished.

The proprietor was a woman named Ada. She wore a blue apron and kept a jar of mismatched buttons beside the till. These were not magical. She just liked buttons.

One wet Thursday, a man brought in his sense of wonder.

“It’s probably not worth fixing,” he said.

Ada laid it on a square of felt beneath the desk lamp. It looked like a little brass telescope, dented along one side.

“How long has it been like this?”

“Hard to say. I’ve been busy.”

She peered through it.

“Ah.”

“Bad?”

“Mostly clogged.”

“With what?”

Ada tipped the telescope over. A fine gray powder drifted onto the felt.

“Things you’ve already decided about.”

The man looked offended, then tired.

“Can you clean it?”

“Yes. But there’s a part you’ll need to replace yourself.”

She showed him a tiny empty slot near the eyepiece.

“What goes there?”

“A question you don’t already have an answer to.”

He considered this.

“Why is the world such a mess?”

Ada tried the question in the slot. It wouldn’t fit.

“That one appears to contain an answer.”

He stood by the window. Rain gathered on the awning and fell in irregular, heavy drops. Across the street, a pigeon was bathing in a puddle beside a perfectly adequate fountain.

“Why that puddle?” he asked.

There was a quiet click.

Ada looked through the telescope again, adjusted something with her thumbnail, and handed it back.

“What do I owe you?”

“Nothing today. The hinge is still loose. Bring it back next week.”

He put it carefully in his coat pocket.

Outside, he paused beside the fountain. The pigeon stopped bathing and watched him.

After a while, he crouched to look at the puddle.

From the shop, Ada saw him shift a few inches to the left, then to the right. She couldn’t tell what he’d found. She was tempted to go and see, but another customer had come in carrying a laugh that hadn’t sounded right for years.

The city employed one person to remove the names from things that no longer existed.

Her office was above a bakery. Each morning, while the first trays of bread cooled downstairs, she reviewed the notices: a demolished cinema, a drained pond, a footbridge carried away by the spring floods.

She updated maps. She retired signs. She wrote polite letters to people who continued to use obsolete addresses.

*There is no longer a Willow Street,* she would explain. *Your sister’s house now stands on Mercator Avenue.*

People rarely thanked her.

One Thursday, she received a notice concerning a bench.

**LOCATION:** Western edge of Bellwether Park  
**STATUS:** Removed  
**REASON:** Rot

There was no official name to retire, so she nearly filed it without further action. But someone had attached a page covered in different handwriting.

*The bench where Dad fed the birds.*

*Our lunch spot, 1998–2006.*

*Where I waited after the appointment.*

*The place with the good shade.*

She took her coat.

At the park, four pale squares marked where the legs had stood. A woman was standing nearby with a paper bag of crumbs.

“Are you here about the bench?” the woman asked.

“Yes.”

“Will they replace it?”

“I don’t know.”

The woman nodded, looking at the patch of bare earth. After a while, she scattered the crumbs and left.

Back at the office, the clerk searched for a form to request a replacement. There were forms for damaged property, missing property, hazardous property, and property installed without permission. She chose damaged property, though that was no longer quite accurate.

Under **DESCRIPTION**, she wrote: *One wooden bench.*

Under **RECOMMENDED ACTION**, she wrote: *Replace in the same location.*

Six weeks later, a metal bench appeared in Bellwether Park, bolted to a new concrete slab.

The clerk went to inspect it during lunch. The woman with the crumbs was there.

“It’s too hot,” the woman said, touching the seat.

They stood beside it in the good shade.

The city hired a man to remove weeds from the cracks in its public staircases.

There were forty-three staircases, climbing between streets too steep for roads. He was given a scraper, a stiff brush, a canvas sack, and a map on which each staircase had been marked in red.

For eleven years, he did the work.

He learned which steps stayed icy after the thaw. He knew where students sat to smoke and which landings offered shelter when rain came sideways. On the staircase behind the courthouse, someone regularly left an orange peel in one long, unbroken spiral.

In April of his twelfth year, he found a tomato plant growing beside the seventy-sixth step of the Bell Street stairs.

He recognized it because his father had grown tomatoes in buckets.

The plant had two true leaves and a stem no thicker than a thread. He worked around it with the scraper.

The following week, it had four leaves.

He put a little water on it from his flask.

By June, somebody had tied it to a pencil. By July, the pencil had been replaced by a bamboo cane. The man began carrying a second bottle of water, which he told himself was sensible in the heat.

His supervisor came for an inspection.

“You missed one,” she said.

“Yes.”

She looked at the plant. There were three green tomatoes on it.

“That’s going to obstruct the stairs.”

“I’ll keep it against the railing.”

She made a note on her clipboard. He never learned what the note said.

In August, the lowest tomato turned red.

For two days, nobody picked it. People who had never noticed each other began exchanging reports.

“Nearly ready.”

“Another day, I’d say.”

“Someone ought to take it before it splits.”

On Thursday morning, it was gone.

Beside the plant stood a small plastic tub, washed clean, containing six slices of tomato. There was salt folded into a scrap of paper and a note:

*Please have some. I took the biggest slice.*

The man ate one sitting on the step below. It was warm already, though the sun had only just reached the railing.

That winter, the plant died. He pulled out the dry stem, shook the soil from its roots, and put it in his sack. He kept the bamboo cane.

In his kitchen, the cane was too long for any drawer. He stood it beside the refrigerator, where it fell down whenever he swept.

He picked it up each time.

In March, he began checking the seventy-sixth step.

The Department of Lost Afternoons occupied the third floor of a building that, from the street, appeared to have only two.

Mara found it while looking for a dentist.

At the reception desk, a man in a green cardigan was repairing a paper umbrella.

“Appointment?” he asked.

“Possibly a root canal.”

“Second floor. But since you’re here, have you misplaced any time?”

“About thirty-seven years.”

He set down the umbrella.

“We generally handle smaller claims.”

Behind him stood rows of shallow drawers. Their brass labels read things like **WAITING FOR SOMEONE WHO DID NOT COME** and **SATURDAYS SPENT BEING REASONABLE**.

Mara pointed to a drawer marked **MISCELLANEOUS, SUMMER**.

“What’s in that one?”

“Mostly school holidays. Some excellent clouds.”

He handed her a form.

Under *Describe the missing interval*, she wrote: *An afternoon at my grandmother’s house. I was nine. It rained. Nothing happened.*

The receptionist read this carefully.

“Nothing?”

“We shelled peas. She said something funny.”

“What did she say?”

“I don’t remember.”

“Ah.”

He disappeared between the cabinets and returned carrying a saucer. On it lay a small patch of yellow light.

“Found behind a shopping list,” he said. “Happens more often than you’d think.”

Mara touched it.

The office vanished.

She was sitting at the kitchen table, her feet hooked around the chair legs. Rain ticked against the window. Her grandmother’s hands worked steadily over a chipped bowl.

One pea escaped, bounced twice, and disappeared beneath the refrigerator.

“Well,” her grandmother said, “that one’s off to university.”

Mara laughed. Her grandmother laughed because Mara did, and for a moment neither of them could manage the peas.

Then the saucer was empty.

The receptionist offered her a tissue without looking directly at her.

“Can I have it again?” she asked.

“I’m afraid we only return things once.”

“Oh.”

From downstairs came the faint whine of a dentist’s drill.

Mara folded the tissue into a small square.

“I thought there would be more,” she said.

“There may be. You can submit another form.”

She considered this, then shook her head. She had remembered how the kitchen smelled. She wanted to go somewhere quiet before she forgot it again.

At the door, she turned back.

“Do you ever lose afternoons?”

The receptionist held up the paper umbrella. One of its thin wooden ribs had come loose.

“I’ve spent most of this one on this.”

“Is it worth repairing?”

He opened it carefully. Pink paper spread above his hand.

“I haven’t decided.”

Outside, rain was beginning. Mara was late for the dentist, but there was still time to call her sister.

It began as a clerical error. Someone printed **LOST: ONE POSSIBLE FUTURE** on a municipal form, and because the form had all the proper boxes, the city was obliged to process it.

The clerk checked the shelves.

“We have the bell,” he said.

She took it home wrapped in newspaper.

A man asked for the person he might have become if he had learned to swim. The clerk explained that they couldn’t store people.

“Against the fire code?”

“Among other things.”

They found him a towel, still warm from a summer afternoon in 1983.

Not everything could be located. Whole careers were missing. So were several marriages and a remarkably specific revolution. The office had plenty of speeches, but almost none of the courage required to deliver them.

The clerk was patient. He had worked for the city for twenty-six years. Before this, he had issued parking permits.

One evening, just before closing, a little girl arrived carrying a cardboard box.

“I think this belongs here.”

Inside was an ordinary stone.

“What was it going to be?” the clerk asked.

“A moon.”

He examined it carefully.

“For what?”

She looked at him with the exhausted tolerance children reserve for adults who ask unnecessary questions.

“For the sky.”

Of course. He filled out an intake slip.

After she left, he put the stone on the highest shelf. Then he finished the day’s paperwork, turned off the lights, and stood for a moment in the doorway.

There was just enough light to see the room.

He checked the windows. He checked the green exit sign.

Finally, he climbed onto his chair and held his hand above the stone.

His palm was faintly illuminated.

The next morning, he submitted a request for a larger building.

At the end of the tram line, where the city gave up pretending to be a city and became a field with opinions, there was a shop that repaired things no one else would touch.

Not watches or shoes. There were perfectly good shops for those.

The sign in the window read:

**APOLOGIES RESTORED**  
**BAD ENDINGS ALTERED**  
**SMALL MISUNDERSTANDINGS WHILE YOU WAIT**

Underneath, in smaller letters:

**No miracles. Please stop asking.**

The proprietor was a woman named Ada, who wore a carpenter’s apron and kept her pencils in a chipped vase. Most mornings she worked on minor repairs: a joke that had landed cruelly, a goodbye spoken while looking at a phone, a birthday forgotten for reasons that were understandable but not good enough.

People brought these things in paper bags.

They often said, “It’s probably nothing.”

Ada would open the bag.

“Well,” she would say, “let’s have a look.”

One wet Thursday, a man arrived carrying nothing at all.

“I think I’ve wasted my life,” he said.

Ada glanced at the clock. It was twenty minutes until closing.

“That’s a large item.”

“I know.”

“Have you brought the whole thing?”

He looked down at his empty hands.

“I wouldn’t know how.”

She pulled out a chair.

“Start with yesterday.”

Yesterday, he told her, he had done laundry. He had answered six emails and avoided a seventh. He had eaten lunch standing up. On the way home, he had stopped to watch two men trying to get a sofa through a narrow doorway.

“Did they manage it?” Ada asked.

“I don’t know. I went home.”

“What was in the seventh email?”

“An invitation. My brother wants me to visit.”

“And do you want to?”

“Yes. But we haven’t spoken properly in years. I keep trying to write something that explains.”

Ada took a small envelope from beneath the counter and slid it across to him.

He opened it. Inside was a tram ticket.

“What does this repair?”

“Nothing yet. Your brother lives three stops from here, doesn’t he?”

“Four.”

“You’ll have to pay the difference.”

He remained in the chair for a while, turning the ticket over. Then he asked if he could borrow a pencil.

Ada gave him one from the vase. On the back of an old receipt, he wrote several sentences, crossed them out, and finally took out his phone.

“Can I come on Saturday?” he read aloud.

Ada was putting away her tools.

“You’d have to ask him.”

After he left, she found the pencil tucked behind her ear. Outside, the last of the rain dripped from the awning, and a tram waited at the edge of the field with its doors open.

**DEPARTMENT OF THINGS THAT MIGHT STILL WORK**

Below that, in smaller letters:

**Please knock. The bell is unreliable.**

People brought toasters, marriages, fountain pens, elaborate plans to learn Italian. The department accepted everything except printers, which fell under a separate and considerably darker jurisdiction.

There was only one employee, a woman named Ada, who had been meaning to retire for eleven years.

“The bath.”

“A difficult sea.”

The boy nodded.

Ada spread a cloth over her desk. She examined the boat, then took two narrow pieces of wood from a drawer.

“I can mend the mast. That seam needs drying before we glue it. Can you leave it with me?”

He kept his hands on the box.

“Will it be the same?”

“No,” Ada said. “There’ll be a little lump here. See? Where the new wood goes.”

He bent down to look.

“Will it float?”

“We’ll test it.”

“Admissions,” someone said.

“I have a question about applying.”

“For yourself?”

Ada glanced at the boat resting on its side, the two pieces of wood laid beside it.

“Yes,” she said, and pulled the form closer.

The town hired a cartographer to map the places people went when they said they were going nowhere.

It was a small commission, poorly funded. He received a bicycle, a notebook, and permission to ask impolite questions.

At first, nobody helped.

“Nowhere,” said the baker, locking the shop.

“Just out,” said a girl with a fishing rod and no hook.

“Mind your business,” said the mayor, who was carrying two pears.

So the cartographer rode his bicycle through the town and waited.

He found a bench behind the railway station where you could hear every departure but see no trains. He found a strip of grass between the cemetery wall and the hardware store, warm long after sunset. Beneath the bridge, someone had arranged seven flat stones in a circle. Nothing stood in the middle.

He marked these places carefully.

His first draft was rejected.

“These are ordinary locations,” the council said. “We already have a map of those.”

He returned to work.

This time, beside the bench, he wrote: *Where a person may reconsider a journey without buying another ticket.*

Beside the grass: *For sitting after the hardware store has closed, particularly if you have forgotten what you meant to repair.*

Beside the stones, he wrote nothing. But he drew all seven.

Slowly, people began to visit his office.

A woman told him about the third-floor landing of the hospital, where the window opened despite the notice saying it did not.

A boy described an alley where a dog would lean against your legs, provided you made no attempt to pet it.

The mayor came in after dark.

“There’s an orchard outside town,” she said. “Abandoned. I used to go there with my brother.”

“May I put it on the map?”

She considered this.

“Put the orchard on it,” she said. “Leave my brother out.”

By winter, the map was finished. The printer complained about the empty spaces, but the cartographer would not fill them.

Copies appeared in kitchens and railway offices. People penciled in corrections. One bench had been removed. The hospital window had been painted shut. Someone added a shortcut to the orchard, then crossed it out because it led through a field with a bull.

The cartographer kept that copy.

In spring, when the council offered him another commission, he asked for a week to think. He left his bicycle outside the office and walked down to the station.

For once, he took nothing to write with.

The mapmaker’s daughter discovered that her father had been adding benches to the city.

Not building them. Drawing them.

On every map he published, among the bus stops and public fountains, there were tiny green marks indicating places to sit. Most were accurate. But some marked benches that had never existed.

“There’s no bench on Wren Street,” she told him.

“There ought to be,” he said.

Her father was seventy-three and had begun treating objections as useful suggestions for other people.

“You can’t put imaginary things on a map.”

“Your grandfather put a sea serpent in the bay.”

“That was a decorative border.”

“It was a warning. He disliked sailing.”

She worked for the city’s planning office. Accuracy mattered to her. A misplaced line could put a drain beneath a foundation, a cycle lane through a loading dock. People trusted maps precisely because they could not inspect the whole world themselves.

So, one Saturday, she took his newest edition and went looking.

The first nonexistent bench overlooked the river from a steep street. She arrived breathing hard. An elderly man stood nearby, pretending to study a parking sign while he rested.

The second was outside the courthouse.

The third was halfway between the oncology clinic and the bus station.

She sat on a low wall there, holding the map in both hands.

That evening she returned to her father’s apartment.

“Well?” he asked.

“Eleven.”

“Fourteen,” he said. “You missed the industrial estate.”

She spread the map across his kitchen table. He moved his tea.

For a while, neither spoke.

Then she took a pencil from behind her ear and circled a point near the north entrance of the market.

“This one won’t work,” she said. “The pavement’s too narrow. Someone with a wheelchair couldn’t get past.”

Her father leaned over the map.

“Across the street?”

“The bakery gets deliveries there.”

They considered the intersection.

“Here,” she said at last. “Under the plane tree.”

He nodded and reached for his green pen.

“No,” she said, putting her hand over it. “Give me until Tuesday.”

The first bench took eight months, three forms, and an argument about whose budget should pay for the concrete base.

At the installation, her father examined the bolts, tested the backrest, and sat down.

“Well?” she asked.

He shifted a little to one side.

“Good,” he said. “You can see the river.”

She sat beside him. Below them, a tug was pushing an empty barge upstream. Her father watched it for a moment, then unfolded his map on his knee.

The town’s clockmaker retired on a Tuesday and left the public clock running seven minutes slow.

At first, everyone assumed someone else would fix it.

The baker phoned the council. The council phoned the clockmaker. The clockmaker, who had taken up fishing, let the phone ring in the empty shop.

By Friday, the stationmaster had posted a notice:

**THE CLOCK IN THE SQUARE IS WRONG.  
TRAINS REMAIN CORRECT.**

People missed trains anyway.

In the café, a woman arrived seven minutes late for a difficult conversation and found that the man waiting for her had already ordered her usual coffee. This annoyed her. Then it helped.

At the school, children discovered that seven minutes could be stretched considerably if you walked home with someone you liked.

The butcher began closing by the square’s clock rather than the one above his freezer. “It’s the public clock,” he said. “We pay taxes.”

Most people eventually adjusted. They looked at their phones before leaving home, then glanced up at the clock when they crossed the square, feeling faintly superior.

Only the florist continued to trust it.

“You know it’s slow,” her daughter said.

“Yes.”

“So why do you use it?”

The florist clipped a bruised leaf from a stem.

“I can see it from here.”

In November, the council sent a young technician up the tower. He opened the mechanism, made a small adjustment, and restored the missing seven minutes.

Nobody applauded. A few people complained, though they had complained when it was wrong.

That afternoon, the florist closed on time. She carried the unsold flowers to the bus stop, where the retired clockmaker was sitting beside an empty bucket.

“Catch anything?” she asked.

“No.”

She gave him three chrysanthemums.

“Clock’s fixed,” he said.

“I saw.”

He moved the bucket so she could sit down.

They watched a bus turn into the square. It was hers, but she had noticed a fish scale stuck to his sleeve, bright as a sequin.

“You caught something.”

“One,” he admitted.

“What happened to it?”

He took a while answering. The bus opened its doors, waited, and went on.

Then he held his hands apart to show her.

At the end of a narrow street, between a locksmith and a shop that had been “Opening Soon” for eleven years, there was a small office where you could retrieve things you had forgotten.

Not misplaced things. No keys, no earrings, no phones.

Forgotten things.

The name of your first teacher’s dog. The tune your father hummed while washing dishes. What you had meant to say before the conversation changed.

The woman behind the counter wore green cardigans and never asked for identification.

“You’ll know if it’s yours,” she said.

Most people came once.

A man collected the smell of his grandmother’s hallway and stood very still for several minutes. A teenager recovered an elaborate game she had invented with her brother before they learned to be embarrassed by each other. Someone came for a grudge and was gently advised to browse a little longer.

One wet Thursday, a woman arrived carrying nothing.

“I think I’ve forgotten what I wanted,” she said.

The clerk looked up.

“For lunch?”

“For my life.”

“Ah.” The clerk put down her pen. “We get that.”

She disappeared through a door behind the counter. The woman heard drawers opening, a small crash, and a muttered complaint about the filing system.

At last the clerk returned with a shallow cardboard box.

Inside were a smooth stone, a photograph of a horse, three pencils, and a paper crown.

“This can’t be right,” the woman said.

“Take your time.”

She picked up the stone.

She remembered wanting to walk beside a river until she found where it began.

The horse: wanting to be trusted by something large and easily frightened.

The pencils: wanting to make pictures good enough that other people could see what she saw.

The crown embarrassed her.

“I wanted to be queen?”

“Possibly. We don’t interpret.”

Then she remembered a birthday party. She had made crowns for everyone, even the adults. Her uncle had worn his all the way home on the bus.

She turned the paper over in her hands. There was a thumbprint in the glue.

To reach it, you had to enter the lift while thinking about something you meant to do. The birthday card still in your desk. The language you were going to learn. The shelf.

Especially the shelf.

The lift knew a great deal about shelves.

**PLEASE HAVE YOUR EXCUSES READY.**

“I didn’t know this place existed,” she said.

“That’s the most common one.” He pushed a form toward her. “What have you brought?”

“Nothing.”

The clerk glanced at her hands.

She was holding a blue notebook.

“Oh,” she said.

Inside were thirty-seven pages of a novel she had begun at twenty-three. She was forty-one now. In the intervening years she had moved six times, married once, learned to make bread, and developed firm opinions about dishwasher loading. The notebook had accompanied her through all of it, occupying increasingly inaccessible drawers.

“I suppose you’re going to tell me to finish it.”

“Good heavens, no,” said the clerk. “We’re understaffed as it is.”

He led her into the archive.

There were half-knitted jumpers sleeping on shelves. An enormous glasshouse contained gardens nobody had planted. Somewhere, an orchestra repeatedly played the first eight bars of something promising.

In one corner stood a door.

“What’s through there?” Mara asked.

“A conversation someone keeps rehearsing.”

“Does it ever happen?”

“Sometimes. Then we can use the room for storage.”

“What’s the difference between leaving it here and keeping it in a drawer?”

“The drawer charges interest.”

Mara opened the notebook.

The first sentence was terrible.

She laughed.

The second sentence was also terrible, but with ambition.

“Will I have to come back?”

“The rain,” she explained.

The clerk handed her a pair of scissors.

Every home has a small museum of unresolved possibilities.

Usually it is a drawer.

Inside: a key without a lock, a cable for a vanished device, three foreign coins, a pencil too short to hold comfortably but too long to throw away. A screw that looks important. Instructions for something that broke during a previous decade.

These objects have escaped the ordinary laws of usefulness. They survive on appeal.

*You might need me.*

And because the claim is technically impossible to disprove, they stay.

There is something tender about this. A person who would never describe themselves as an optimist will preserve a tiny metal bracket for seventeen years on the chance that one day the world will explain it.

Occasionally, the world does.

A cupboard handle comes loose. Someone searches the drawer. Beneath the dead batteries and a birthday candle shaped like a seven, the exact right screw appears.

For one glorious minute, the entire institution is vindicated.

“This,” says the keeper of the drawer, holding it up.

No further argument is necessary. The unidentified washers receive another decade of funding. The mysterious cable is granted protected status. A plastic cap, origin unknown, settles deeper into its corner.

But most objects will never have their moment. The key will remain unclaimed. The instructions will fade along their folds. Eventually someone will empty the drawer onto a table and begin making decisions.

Even then, there will probably be hesitation.

“What do you think this goes to?”

Someone will turn the little bracket over, examining its two holes and its peculiar bend. It is well made. Surely it was made for something.

“Better keep it.”

And back it goes.

The first thing the lighthouse keeper did after retiring was buy curtains.

For forty-three years, he had slept in rooms that could never be properly dark. Light climbed the walls, crossed the ceiling, and moved on. Every twelve seconds, the world looked in.

Now he lived above a bakery, forty miles from the sea.

The curtains were green. He closed them at six in the evening, though it was summer and the street was still bright, and stood in the room to see whether they worked.

They did.

For several weeks, he slept badly.

He missed the machinery’s steady turning. He missed the stairs, which had made his knees hurt but had also settled the question of what his knees were for. Most of all, he missed having one necessary thing to do.

Downstairs, the baker began work at four.

There were small noises: a door catching, trays touching, the soft, heavy arrival of flour. The keeper learned them without intending to. After a while, he could tell whether she was making the dark rye or the little round loaves before the smell reached him.

One morning, the noises stopped.

He lay awake until half past four. Then he dressed and went downstairs.

The baker was sitting on an overturned bucket with her hand wrapped in a towel.

“Cut myself,” she said. “Nothing serious. But I can’t knead.”

He looked at the pale dough waiting on the bench.

“I don’t know how.”

“I have one good hand. I can point.”

So he washed, rolled up his sleeves, and began.

He was too rough at first. Then too careful.

“It isn’t an injured bird,” she told him.

By six, his shoulders ached. By seven, the first customers had come in, bringing wet umbrellas and the day’s complaints.

He carried trays. He gave someone the wrong change. He learned that the smallest loaf belonged to a woman who would insist every morning that it had got smaller.

The baker’s hand healed.

He kept coming down.

Months later, a former colleague visited and asked whether he missed the lighthouse.

They sat at the kitchen table eating bread that the keeper had made. He considered the question.

“Yes,” he said.

His colleague waited.

Outside, the bakery sign creaked in the wind. The keeper brushed some crumbs together with the side of his hand.

“But I have to get up early tomorrow.”

At six, he closed the green curtains.

It occupied two rooms above the licensing office. Most people went their entire lives without visiting, although everyone contributed to its collection.

There were the usual items: apologies swallowed at doorways, trains missed by seconds, hands that nearly touched on cinema armrests. These arrived in gray envelopes and were filed by date.

More troublesome were the larger submissions.

A bridge never built required three cabinets.

A war narrowly avoided occupied a locked drawer that nobody was allowed to open, though on quiet afternoons the handle grew warm.

Mara had worked there for eleven years. Her job was to catalogue conversations.

Each morning she put on headphones and listened to the things people had almost said.

*Stay.*

*I know it was you.*

*Actually, I wanted to be a dancer.*

She transcribed them carefully. Department policy forbade punctuation that was not clearly audible.

One Tuesday, she received a recording containing only a kettle boiling.

She listened twice.

Behind the kettle, a chair scraped. Someone took a breath.

Then nothing.

She checked the accompanying form.

**LOCATION:** Kitchen  
**PARTICIPANTS:** Two  
**UNSAID:** Unknown

This was unusual. The department rarely admitted uncertainty on paper.

Mara took the recording to her supervisor, who was eating a pear over the wastebasket.

“Equipment fault,” he said.

“There’s a breath.”

“There usually is.”

She returned to her desk.

### The Museum of Almost

The museum stood between a pharmacy and a shop that sold replacement buttons. Most people walked past it. Those who entered usually believed they were somewhere else.

“Is this the place that repairs watches?” they asked.

“Sometimes,” said the curator.

Admission was free, though visitors were asked to leave something at the desk: a receipt, a pebble, an opinion they no longer needed. One man left a very convincing excuse. The curator put it in a drawer with the others.

Inside, the exhibits were modest.

In the first room stood a kitchen table set for a conversation that had nearly happened in 1987. Two cups. A sugar bowl. A father’s hand resting beside a spoon.

If you stood quietly, you could hear him take a breath.

In the next room, under glass, lay the first sentence of a novel abandoned after eleven pages:

*By the time the sea returned, everyone had learned to sleep through the bells.*

Visitors often asked what happened next.

“We don’t know,” said the curator. “That’s why it’s here.”

There was a gallery of missed trains, which was more cheerful than expected. One had led to a marriage. Another had prevented one. A third had given a tired woman forty minutes to eat an orange in the sun, and she had remembered those forty minutes for the rest of her life.

Children preferred the Room of Almost Animals: the deer that had nearly stepped out of the trees, the fox glimpsed as a movement in the hedge. The room appeared empty until you turned toward the exit.

At the back of the museum was a small door marked **STAFF ONLY**.

Behind it, the curator kept the things he could not bear to display.

A pair of walking shoes bought for a trip his mother had been too ill to take. A letter to his brother, revised so many times that the paper had softened at the folds.

Every evening he dusted this room himself.

One rainy Thursday, a visitor stayed until closing. She had spent a long time beside the kitchen table.

“Can anything leave?” she asked.

“The museum?”

She nodded.

“Occasionally.”

“How?”

The curator started to give his usual explanation, then stopped. She was holding a phone.

“Would you like some privacy?” he asked.

She shook her head, then nodded, and he went to fetch his coat.

When he returned, the kitchen table was bare. The cups, the sugar bowl, the spoon—all gone. Through the window he could see the woman standing beneath the pharmacy awning, still talking.

He turned off the gallery lights.

Then he went into the little room at the back, unfolded his letter, and read it once more. On the last page he crossed out three paragraphs and wrote, in the space beneath them:

*Are you free on Sunday?*

The next morning, on his way to open the museum, he bought a stamp.

There is a particular kind of quiet that belongs to a city before sunrise. Not silence: refrigerators hum behind locked café doors, a bus exhales at an empty stop, and somewhere a delivery driver argues gently with a stubborn gate. The city is awake, but it has not introduced itself.

At this hour, ordinary things seem briefly unclaimed. A bench is not a place to wait; it is simply wood holding the cold. A puddle becomes a small, unreliable sky. Even the traffic lights appear contemplative, offering their instructions to nobody with an admirable commitment to the possibility of company.

I like imagining that every day begins with this small rehearsal. The baker tests the oven. The street sweeper draws patient circles around yesterday. Someone on a balcony waters a plant that has survived three apartments and one terrible breakup. Nothing spectacular happens, which is precisely what makes it precious.

We are often told to search for meaning in extraordinary moments: departures, declarations, victories, storms. But most of a life is made from smaller materials. Clean socks. A familiar staircase. The sound of someone chopping onions in another room. A message that says nothing more than, “Did you get home?”

Eventually, the first café opens. Chairs scrape the pavement, and a spoon rings against a cup. The spell does not break; it merely changes shape. What was quiet becomes conversation. What was waiting becomes movement. Above the rooftops, the light arrives without applause, and everyone begins again, ready or not.

There should be a museum for things that almost happened. Not the grand alternatives of history, but the private branches: the train you nearly boarded, the apology you rehearsed, the yellow coat you left hanging in the shop because you thought you were not a yellow coat sort of person.

The first room would contain empty chairs. Beside each chair, a label would describe someone you might have met if rain had started five minutes later. Visitors would sit quietly, listening to recordings of conversations that never occurred. Some would laugh without knowing why. Others would suddenly feel less alone.

Upstairs, behind glass, would be all the sentences abandoned halfway through writing. Love letters would curl like dried leaves. Resignations would stand stiffly at attention. Unsent invitations would glow a little after dark, attracting moths that the curators could never entirely explain or persuade to leave through the open windows.

Of course, the museum would need a garden. There, gardeners would cultivate seeds from hobbies briefly considered: astronomy, pottery, the violin. Nothing would bloom according to season. A visitor might discover a whole orchard growing from an afternoon once spent wondering whether it was too late to learn something new.

At the exit, there would be no gift shop. Only a desk, a pencil, and a stack of blank cards. Take one, the attendant would say. There is still room in the collection. Then they would point toward the street, where ordinary life waited, unfinished, wearing its astonishing yellow coat.

At night, the city becomes an instrument nobody remembers learning to play. Pipes knock inside walls. A train draws its bow across the tracks. Somewhere, a refrigerator hums with the confidence of a creature that has never doubted its purpose. Even silence arrives carrying the faint electrical buzz of expectation.

I like to imagine that lost things hold meetings during these hours. Gloves gather beneath benches. Keys compare the doors they once opened. The names we forget sit together politely, waiting for someone to recognize them. Nothing is truly gone, they insist, only temporarily employed by an entirely different story.

Meanwhile, a baker measures flour into a bowl. Pale dust rises, then settles on the counter like weather. Bread is an ordinary miracle that wisely avoids advertising itself. Water, grain, warmth, patience. By morning, people will tear it apart and feel, briefly, that the world has kept a small promise.

Perhaps this is what hope usually looks like: not a sunrise or a speech, but somebody preparing something useful before anyone asks. A clean cup. A repaired hinge. An extra blanket folded at the foot of a bed. Small gestures making quiet room for lives they cannot predict or control.

By dawn, the city will pretend it made itself. Cars will start. Screens will glow. Everyone will hurry toward whatever seems urgent. But underneath the noise, those unnoticed kindnesses will remain, holding the day together as invisibly as stitches inside a coat. We walk warmed by work we never see.

There should be a museum of ordinary things that almost disappeared without anyone noticing. A chipped blue mug. The rubber band around a bundle of letters. A grocery list written by someone who always remembered peaches but forgot soap. Nothing valuable enough to insure, everything valuable enough to make someone pause.

The galleries would be quiet, but not solemn. Visitors could open drawers and turn handles. Somewhere, an old refrigerator would hum with the peculiar confidence of a machine that has kept milk cold through three family arguments and a birthday party nobody wanted to end.

Each object would have two labels. The first would tell you what it was. The second would tell you what it meant. “Kitchen chair, pine, approximately forty years old.” Beneath that: “The place where he sat to peel apples in one long ribbon, which his daughter believed was a kind of magic.”

Perhaps the final room would be empty except for a table and a stack of cards. You would write down something you had lost: a mitten, a recipe, the exact sound of a familiar knock. Then you would leave the card behind, not as a replacement, but as a small act of witness.

Outside, the world would look briefly rearranged. Your keys would feel heavier. The cracked button on your coat would seem less like a flaw. And when you got home, you might keep the ugly bowl another year, simply because it had been there for so many ordinary, irreplaceable mornings.

Before the city wakes, its objects seem to belong to themselves. A bicycle leans against a bakery wall, keeping its own counsel. Traffic lights change for empty streets. Somewhere, a delivery driver rests both hands around a paper cup, borrowing a little warmth before the business of the day begins.

This is my favorite imaginary hour: not quite night, not yet morning, when every window holds a different shade of blue. Even the pigeons look thoughtful. They step around yesterday’s crumbs with the solemn concentration of scholars examining a ruined civilization, occasionally discovering that history tastes faintly of sesame seeds.

Soon enough, everything will acquire a purpose. The bicycle will carry someone late to work. The bakery will sell its first loaf. The driver will navigate a difficult intersection while an impatient voice crackles through a speaker. For now, though, the world has not finished putting on its public face.

There is something merciful about that unfinishedness. We spend so much time being legible: answering messages, explaining decisions, making ourselves useful or interesting or easy to understand. An empty street asks for none of this. You can simply walk through it, carrying thoughts that have not yet learned their names.

Then a door opens. A broom whispers across a threshold. The first bus sighs at the curb, bright inside as a traveling kitchen. Someone laughs, and the sound makes the morning official. Nothing extraordinary has happened. Still, for a moment, the ordinary seems less like a category than a gift.

After the rain, the city seems to remember that it was built from things that once belonged to the earth. Brick darkens into clay. Wooden doors swell against their frames. In the cracks of the pavement, small green lives stand upright, looking less like intruders than tenants returning from holiday.

I like this brief rearrangement of authority. The traffic lights still give orders, but their reflections tremble in puddles, and nobody can make them stop. A bus passes wearing a blurred red ribbon of itself. Somewhere, water drips from a fire escape with the patience of an extremely old clock.

People emerge cautiously, then all at once. Umbrellas close like tired birds. A delivery rider shakes one sleeve and laughs at something through an earbud. Two strangers negotiate a narrow patch of dry sidewalk, performing that little dance in which each person briefly becomes the obstacle and then the solution.

Nothing important has happened, which is perhaps why everything feels available for notice. The bakery window glows. A dog examines a leaf with professional seriousness. Above the rooftops, the clouds begin to separate, revealing a blue so pale it looks newly invented, not yet tested against the weight of weather.

Soon the streets will dry, and the city will put its familiar expression back on. We will hurry again. But for another minute, there is this: a world rinsed clean of its own explanations, asking for nothing more elaborate than our attention, and giving us somewhere beautiful to place it.

I like the hour before a town fully wakes, when the streets seem to belong to their own architecture. Windows hold pale squares of sky. A delivery truck idles beside a bakery. Somewhere, behind a locked door, someone is arranging ordinary things so that strangers will feel welcomed and expected.

There is a quiet generosity in preparation. Chairs are lowered from tables. Bread is sliced. The first bus driver checks a mirror, then opens the doors to nobody yet. Most of what keeps the world livable happens without an audience, and much of it looks almost embarrassingly small from outside.

We tend to tell stories about arrivals: the victory, the discovery, the sudden declaration of love. But perhaps a life is shaped just as deeply by its repeated beginnings. Filling the kettle. Learning a difficult name. Trying again to listen without rehearsing a reply. Leaving a light on for someone.

None of this makes suffering tidy. A clean cup cannot repair a cruel system, and kindness is not a substitute for justice. Still, the scale of a gesture does not determine its worth. Sometimes the smallest act is simply the part of the world we can reach with our hands.

By morning, the town becomes noisy enough to forget its own assembly. Customers enter. Engines turn. The bakery window clouds with warmth. Yet I like imagining that first loaf placed on the counter, before anyone asked for it: a modest answer to an uncertain day, offered while the streets waited.

There is a particular kind of silence that exists just before a city wakes. It is not the absence of sound. Pipes knock inside old walls. A truck sighs at a red light. Somewhere, a baker drops a metal tray, and the noise travels farther than it has any right to.

I like to imagine this hour as the city’s rehearsal. The streets are still deciding what they will become: a shortcut, a meeting place, the setting for an argument someone will remember for years. For now, they are simply streets, holding yesterday’s rain in the shallow curves beside the curb.

A woman opens a café and sets two chairs outside. This seems like a small act of optimism. She cannot know who will sit there, whether they will be lonely or delighted, whether the coffee will accompany good news. Nevertheless, she arranges the chairs so they face each other.

Perhaps that is most of what civilization amounts to: making arrangements for people we have not met. Planting trees whose shade we will never need. Labeling the fuse box clearly. Leaving a porch light on. The grand speeches matter, but so does the person who puts a spare blanket in the guest room.

Soon the traffic gathers itself. Doors slam, phones ring, and the city begins insisting on its importance. The quiet hour disappears without complaint. Yet those two chairs remain outside the café, waiting patiently for strangers to arrive and turn an ordinary morning into something worth telling someone.

There is a particular kind of silence in a kitchen after everyone has gone to bed. The refrigerator hums with the confidence of something that has one job and intends to do it well. A spoon rests in the sink. On the windowsill, a basil plant leans toward a moon that offers absolutely no useful gardening advice.

I like to imagine that ordinary objects find this hour restorative. The chairs stop being occupied and become simply chairs. The table no longer has to host arguments, homework, or the complicated negotiations of breakfast. Even the clock seems less managerial, though it continues its little rounds.

We spend so much time asking what things are for. What is this skill for? Where is this road going? Will this afternoon amount to anything? These are sensible questions, but they can become a fence around the world. Sometimes an afternoon is for watching rain collect on a railing until one drop grows brave enough to fall.

Perhaps attention is a quieter kind of ambition. Not the desire to own more of life, but to miss less of it. To notice the flour on someone's sleeve. The brief warmth of a cup after the tea is gone. The way a familiar person becomes unfamiliar for a second when they laugh without guarding themselves.

Tomorrow, the kitchen will fill with instructions again. Find your keys. Eat something. We're late. But tonight, nothing needs improving. The basil waits. The spoon shines faintly. The refrigerator keeps its modest promise.

samples.result:
The city opened the Office of Lost Time on a Tuesday, in a building previously occupied by a discount carpet store.

For weeks, people arrived carrying clocks.

“No,” said the woman behind the counter. “Not that kind.”

They brought watches, appointment books, dead phones. One man brought a microwave that had displayed 12:00 continuously since his divorce.

“Especially not that kind,” she said.

Her name was Ruth. She had been transferred from Parking Enforcement and retained a professional distrust of elaborate explanations.

Above her desk, a sign read:

**PLEASE DESCRIBE THE TIME YOU HAVE LOST.**  
**BE SPECIFIC.**

Most people weren’t.

“My twenties,” they said.

“The best years of my life.”

“Every Monday.”

Ruth handed them the longer form.

The office could not recover years. It could rarely recover afternoons. What it found, mostly, were minutes: a little unclaimed interval behind a laundromat, forty seconds caught in a disconnected telephone line, the pause after someone said, “Well,” but before they said what they meant.

These arrived downstairs in gray envelopes.

Nobody knew who delivered them. The custodian occasionally saw a wet footprint beside the sorting table, even in dry weather. He put down a mat.

I worked in Verification.

My job was to open each envelope, experience its contents, and decide whether the claimant had identified the missing time accurately.

There were precautions. We wore gloves. We never opened two envelopes at once. We were discouraged from verifying anything lost in our own neighborhoods.

“You’ll want to improve it,” Ruth explained during my training.

“Improve what?”

“Whatever happened.”

“Can you?”

“No. That doesn’t stop people trying.”

My first assignment was seventy-three seconds belonging to a woman named Alvarez.

She remembered standing in a supermarket, holding a pear, suddenly unable to remember whether her mother liked pears.

Her mother had been dead for six years.

Inside the envelope was the supermarket: cold mist over the vegetables, a wheel squeaking three aisles away, the pear’s narrow neck resting between her fingers.

Nothing happened.

That was the time.

I approved the claim.

Mrs. Alvarez collected it on Friday. She sat in one of our plastic chairs with the envelope against her chest.

“She liked them hard,” she told me. “Practically green. I always thought that was ridiculous.”

Then she left.

By November, I had verified two hundred and twelve recoveries.

A boy reclaimed the moment before diving into a swimming pool.

A retired dentist recovered four minutes spent laughing with a stranger whose name he had never learned.

A man asked for the last ordinary breakfast before his wife became ill. We found the right morning, but the available fragment contained only his search for the car keys.

He took it anyway.

There were fraudulent claims. People requested famous concerts they had never attended. They requested the instant a lottery number was drawn, which didn’t work for several reasons.

One woman repeatedly requested “the summer I was happy.”

We found six plausible summers.

She rejected them all.

In December, an envelope arrived with my name on it.

I knew immediately that I should give it to Ruth.

Instead, I held it up to the light.

Eleven minutes, according to the label. A Saturday in March. My father’s garage.

He had been dead for nine years.

I remembered that Saturday vaguely. I had driven over to borrow a drill. We’d argued about whether I needed wall anchors. He said yes. I said I knew what I was doing.

The shelf fell down three weeks later.

I took the envelope into a verification booth.

There he was.

Not younger in any remarkable way. Just alive, wearing the blue sweatshirt with a pale smear of paint on one sleeve.

Rain ticked against the garage door.

Between us stood an old biscuit tin full of screws.

“Help me sort these,” he said.

I wanted to tell him about the hospital. I wanted to ask whether he had been frightened. I wanted to apologize for being so impatient with every story that began before I was born.

But the recovered time had its own words.

“What’s the point?” I heard myself say.

“The point is, when you need one, you can find it.”

He tipped the tin onto a sheet of newspaper.

We sorted screws.

Long ones, short ones, brass ones. Screws with ruined heads. A surprising number of nails.

“This isn’t even a screw,” I said.

“No,” he agreed. “You’ve spotted that correctly.”

I laughed.

I had forgotten that I laughed.

For eleven minutes, rain tapped the door and my father turned small pieces of metal between his thumb and forefinger. He put the bent ones aside, though he would never throw them out.

Then the booth returned.

Ruth was waiting outside.

“You’re not supposed to verify your own.”

“I know.”

“Was it accurate?”

I nodded.

She sat beside me.

“People think they want the important moments,” she said.

I waited for her to finish.

She didn’t.

Eventually she stood, straightened the neighboring chair, and went back to the counter.

I took my envelope home.

The drill was still in my cupboard. I’d never returned it. Wrapped around its handle was a strip of masking tape on which my father had written our surname, as though I might confuse it with another family’s drill.

I spent a while peeling back one loose corner, then pressed it flat again.

On Sunday, I bought wall anchors.

The hardware shop assistant asked what kind of wall I had.

I opened my mouth.

Then I closed it.

“I’m not sure,” I said.

He came around the counter to show me the different kinds.

samples.result:
The first thing they taught us at the lighthouse was how to make darkness.

Not light. Light was easy. Turn a switch, strike a match, open the furnace door. Any fool could interrupt the dark.

Making it required care.

“There are ships,” said the keeper, “that can only find their way by what isn’t there.”

I was seventeen and had taken the job because the advertisement promised a room, three meals, and no references. I assumed he was speaking metaphorically. Adults had been doing that to me for years, usually just before asking me to carry something heavy.

He handed me a bucket.

“Start with the stairs.”

***

The lighthouse stood on an island so small that, at high tide, the gulls had to queue.

Every morning I washed the salt from the windows. Every afternoon I polished the brass. At sunset, the keeper climbed the tower and lit the lamp, and the great white beam went shouldering across the water.

Then, at eleven minutes past two, we extinguished everything.

The lamp. The stove. The small green indicator on the radio.

Even our watches went into a drawer.

For nine minutes we sat opposite each other in a darkness so complete that I sometimes forgot where my hands were.

“Who are we helping?” I asked the first night.

“Depends who’s out.”

“Fishing boats?”

“Sometimes.”

He had a habit of answering questions just enough to make them worse.

***

In October, I cheated.

I brought a pocket torch upstairs and hid it beneath my sweater. At thirteen minutes past two, while the keeper sat with his eyes closed, I pressed the switch.

The light shone through my fingers.

Something struck the lighthouse.

Not hard. That was the terrible part.

It was a gentle impact, almost apologetic: the sound a person makes bumping into furniture in an unfamiliar room.

The keeper crossed the space between us and closed his hand over mine.

The torch went dark.

Outside, something dragged slowly against the glass.

We were thirty metres above the sea.

Neither of us moved until the nine minutes had passed.

In the morning there was a mark on the window: five long streaks, clean of salt.

The keeper confiscated the torch.

“Now,” he said, “you can start asking sensible questions.”

***

He showed me the logbooks.

Most entries were ordinary.

*Heavy fog. Supply boat delayed.*

*Replaced bearing in lamp assembly.*

*Cormorant in kitchen again.*

But scattered through the years were others.

*Dark interval maintained. Three passages.*

*Audible bells. No vessel visible.*

*Someone called from below in Mrs. Vale’s voice. Did not answer.*

One entry, written forty years earlier, occupied a page by itself.

*Light shown during interval. We are very sorry.*

I turned back to it twice, looking for something I had missed.

The keeper waited.

“Why not tear it out?” I asked.

“Because the next keeper has to read it.”

***

Winter reduced the world to stone, water, and deliveries that did not arrive.

We ate beans. We repaired things that were not broken because there was nothing else to repair. The keeper taught me knots, weather, and how to make bread in a temperamental oven.

He never explained the ships.

Instead, he told me what to do if I heard knocking.

“Nothing.”

“What if it sounds urgent?”

“Especially then.”

“What if someone needs help?”

He pressed a thumb into the dough.

For a long time I thought he had not heard me.

“There’s a rescue station on the mainland,” he said at last. “Radio works twenty-three hours and fifty-one minutes a day.”

***

In February, during the dark interval, I heard my brother.

He had been dead for six years.

He said my name in the exasperated way he used when I fell behind on our walks.

Then he laughed.

There are things memory cannot keep intact. I had photographs of his face and remembered a dozen things he used to say. But I had forgotten that laugh: the quick breath in the middle, as if something funnier had just occurred to him.

I stood.

Across the room, the keeper moved his chair.

He did not touch me. He simply placed it between me and the stairs.

My brother called again.

I gripped the chair back. The keeper stayed in it.

When the lamp came on, my throat hurt, though I had made no sound.

At breakfast he gave me the heel of the loaf, which was his favourite part.

We did not discuss it.

***

Spring brought a technician from the mainland.

He wore orange waterproofs and carried a tablet in a sealed case. The lighthouse was to be automated. A new system would improve efficiency, reduce costs, and eliminate human error.

“No more night shifts,” he said.

The keeper asked whether the lamp could be programmed to go dark for nine minutes.

The technician frowned.

“Why would you want that?”

“Local conditions.”

“What conditions?”

The keeper looked at me.

For the first time since I had arrived, he seemed old.

***

I wish I could say we convinced them.

We submitted reports. We made calls. The keeper travelled to the mainland in his best coat and returned with a leaflet about retirement accommodation.

On his last evening, we carried his bags down to the landing.

He gave me a key.

“What’s this?”

“Service cupboard. Below the lamp.”

“The new lock?”

He nodded.

The boat arrived before I could ask anything else.

***

I live on the mainland now. I have a different job, mostly ordinary work.

But once a week I go out to check the lighthouse.

Officially, I clean the windows.

The service cupboard contains a manual override. At eleven minutes past two, I open it and turn the handle.

Then I sit on the stairs until the nine minutes are over.

Last Thursday I heard bells.

I put them in the book.

samples.result:
On his last day as the caretaker of the public swimming pool, Leonard found a fish in lane four.

It was a small fish, the color of a spoon. It held itself halfway between the surface and the blue-tiled bottom, moving its fins with the air of someone making tiny corrections to a difficult calculation.

The pool had been closed for eleven months.

Leonard stood with his mop.

“Well,” he said.

The fish did not seem interested in how it had happened either.

For thirty-two years, Leonard had opened the building at five each morning. He knew which fluorescent tube would blink before it settled, which shower required a blow with the heel of a hand, which locker could be opened with a twenty-pence coin instead of a pound.

He knew the regular swimmers by what they forgot.

Mrs. Vale forgot her shampoo. Mr. Jenkins forgot that other people wanted to use the fast lane. A boy named Aiden forgot his towel every Thursday for six years, then became a broad-shouldered man who visited at Christmas and called Leonard “mate” with an uncertainty that embarrassed them both.

The council had built a new leisure center beside the bypass. It had a climbing wall and a café where the chairs looked permanently startled. Leonard had been offered a job there.

“Facilities experience is transferable,” the letter said.

He had put the letter beneath a leaking bottle of bleach.

Now the old pool was scheduled for demolition. The water should have been drained weeks ago, but the contractor responsible had gone bankrupt, and the contractor replacing him required a different contractor to certify the first contractor’s pipes.

So there was still a pool.

And now there was a fish.

Leonard went to the office and searched the drawers for something useful. He found three whistles, a rubber band hardened into a crescent, and a photograph of the staff at a Christmas dinner in 2004.

His wife was in the photograph.

She had never worked at the pool. She had come because Leonard disliked parties and she liked making him go to them. In the photograph, her hand was inside his jacket pocket. He remembered this with such sudden clarity that he sat down.

She had been looking for the car keys.

That was all. He had been drinking; she was driving. Her fingers had moved past his handkerchief and the folded raffle tickets.

For years he had remembered the dinner as the one where somebody knocked a candle into the gravy.

He put the photograph in his coat.

At the pet shop, a young woman with purple eyebrows asked what kind of fish he had.

“Unexpected.”

She waited.

“Silver. About this long.”

“Freshwater?”

“It’s in a swimming pool.”

Her face changed.

“Bring it in,” she said.

Back at the building, Leonard found the fish beneath the diving board. He fetched the long skimming net from the storeroom.

Catching it took forty minutes.

At first he tried from the edge. Then he took off his shoes and rolled up his trousers. Eventually he went into the changing room and put on a pair of swimming trunks from lost property, which he chose not to think about.

The water was cold enough to make him swear aloud.

He had spent most of his working life beside this pool and almost none of it in the water.

From there, the building looked different. Higher. The windows held a strip of pale winter sky. The clock above the shallow end had stopped at ten past seven, though Leonard could not remember whether this had happened in the morning or the evening.

He stood chest-deep and waited.

The fish approached his knee.

“There you are,” he whispered, and lowered the net.

The woman at the pet shop said it was a young goldfish.

“It isn’t gold.”

“Not yet.”

She tested the water from his bucket. Then she tested it again.

“How long has the pool been shut?”

“Nearly a year.”

“And nobody’s been treating it?”

“No.”

“That’s lucky for him.”

Leonard looked at the fish.

The woman explained what he would need: a proper tank, a filter, somewhere out of direct sunlight. She spoke seriously, without making him feel foolish for having arrived in damp trousers carrying a mop bucket.

He bought everything.

At home, he set the tank on the kitchen counter, then moved it because his wife had always needed that space for pastry. Then he stood with his hands against the glass.

After a while, he moved it back.

The fish hovered near the bottom.

Leonard made tea. He took the staff photograph from his pocket and propped it against the sugar jar. There were people in it whose surnames he had forgotten. One man he had disliked intensely, for reasons he could no longer retrieve.

His wife was laughing at something outside the frame.

The telephone rang. It was his daughter.

“How was the last day?”

“All right.”

“Did they do anything for you?”

“There was supposed to be a card. I left before the post.”

She was quiet for a moment.

“Dad.”

“I got a fish.”

“You got a what?”

He turned his chair toward the tank.

The fish had begun exploring. It investigated the filter, retreated, and approached it again from a different angle.

“Are you still there?” his daughter asked.

“Yes.”

“What are you going to call it?”

He considered this.

Beyond the kitchen window, rain collected on the dark square of garden. The kettle clicked as it cooled. In the photograph, his wife went on searching his pocket.

“I don’t know yet,” he said. “I’ve only just met him.”

For six years, I was responsible for turning off the stars.

It was less impressive than it sounds. There was a switch behind the planetarium desk, beside a kettle that tasted faintly of pennies. At five fifteen, after the last school group had gone, I shut down the projector, checked beneath the seats for jumpers and water bottles, and made the universe safe for the cleaners.

The stars did not disappear all at once. First went the faint ones. Then the familiar shapes unraveled. Orion lost his belt. The Great Bear became an argument about dots. Finally there was only the emergency exit sign, offering its modest green alternative to eternity.

I liked that part best.

People assumed I loved astronomy. I had put “enthusiastic amateur astronomer” on the application because my sister said employers wanted evidence of passion. Mostly I wanted a job I could walk to.

By my second year, though, I could find my way around the sky. I knew which facts made children gasp and which made their teachers check the time. Black holes were dependable. Distances were harder. Tell someone a star is four hundred light-years away and they nod politely. Tell them its light began traveling before their grandmother’s grandmother was born and sometimes they look up again.

The cleaner was called June. She arrived while I was putting the ticket money in the safe, dragging a vacuum cleaner with one wheel that refused to turn.

“Anything good up there today?” she would ask.

“Saturn.”

“Again?”

“It remains popular.”

June had cleaned the planetarium for eleven years without seeing a show. Her shift began when ours ended, and she said she wasn’t coming into work on her day off just to sit in the dark.

One wet November evening, the vacuum gave a cough and stopped.

June kicked it once, without conviction.

“That’s that,” she said.

I offered to ring maintenance.

“They’ll tell me to check the plug.”

“Have you?”

She looked at me.

While she filled in the fault report, I switched the projector back on. I was testing a new program for a group booked the following morning, but June put down her pen.

“Oh,” she said.

The stars sharpened above us.

She stood in the aisle with the vacuum hose still in her hand. Then she sat in the nearest seat.

I began explaining the winter constellations.

“No,” she said gently. “Just leave it a minute.”

So I did.

The projector hummed. Rain tapped somewhere beyond the dome. After a while I sat down too.

June watched for nearly ten minutes. When she got up, she folded the fault report into quarters and tucked it under the dead machine’s handle.

“My husband used to know all those,” she said.

I waited.

“Or said he did. Could’ve been making it up. I never checked.”

After that, we had an arrangement. On Fridays, before she started cleaning, I gave her ten minutes of sky.

Sometimes she asked for a particular place.

“What would it look like from Sydney?”

“Tonight?”

“June 1983.”

The computer could do that. It could put us almost anywhere, almost anywhen. Sydney, June 1983. Lisbon on her honeymoon. The village where she grew up, on a date she had written down on the back of a shopping receipt.

I never asked what had happened on those days. Once, when she requested an afternoon, I explained that there wouldn’t be much to see.

“I know,” she said. “Can you do it anyway?”

We sat beneath a pale blue dome.

In my sixth year, the council announced a refurbishment. The old projector would be replaced by a digital system. There would be reclining seats, interactive exhibits, a café serving things on wooden boards.

My job would become a visitor engagement role.

I could apply for it, they said.

Around the same time, my sister offered me work in her printing business. Better money. Regular hours. She needed someone who could be trusted to notice when an invitation said “pubic celebration.”

I took it.

On my last Friday, June arrived carrying two paper cups of tea from the bakery.

“Not drinking that kettle water,” she said. “Not on an occasion.”

We sat in the middle row.

“Where do you want to go?” I asked.

She thought about it.

“Here.”

“What date?”

“Now.”

I entered our location and the time. Above us appeared the sky we would have seen if the dome, the roof, and the November clouds had been removed.

For once, I didn’t recognize it immediately. There were always constellations I neglected: faint, awkward arrangements that never featured in the school show. I found one and tried to remember its name.

June leaned back, holding her tea with both hands.

“Will you miss it?”

“Some of it.”

She nodded.

We stayed until her phone alarm went off. She had other buildings to clean.

I shut down the projector. We watched the stars disappear in their usual order. Then June collected our cups, and I went to clear out my desk.

Outside, she was wrestling the vacuum into the back of her car.

“They fixed the wheel,” I said.

“Eventually.”

I helped her lift it over the lip of the boot. The machine was heavier than I expected.

June drove off. I stood beneath the streetlamp, looking for my keys, then remembered I had left the building keys on the desk, as instructed. It would take a few days to stop checking for them.

On the walk home, I passed the bakery, the closed pharmacy, the bus shelter with its cracked panel. A light rain started. I put up my hood.

Near my flat, I stopped to let a man maneuver a sofa through a doorway. He was arguing with someone I couldn’t see.

Above the rooftops was one bright point. Jupiter, probably, though I wasn’t certain.

I waited for another to appear.

Then the man asked if I could hold the door, and I said yes.
