The mountain moved on a Thursday, which gave the town something to discuss besides the school roof.

It moved only a little. Six inches, according to the surveyor. Less, according to the mayor, who owned property on that side of town.

“Mountains settle,” the mayor said.

“Down,” said the surveyor. “They settle down.”

They were standing beside a fence that had, until breakfast, been straight.

By noon, a crowd had gathered. Everyone looked uphill, expecting to catch something enormous in the act.

Nothing happened.

A boy threw a stone at the mountain.

His mother made him apologize, then looked embarrassed.

***

The following Thursday it moved another six inches.

This time there were instruments. There were cameras. A university sent three people in matching windbreakers, who installed a silver box and asked that nobody touch it.

The mountain moved while they were eating sandwiches.

On the recordings, the trees shuddered. A deer lifted its head. The entire slope advanced without spilling a stone.

The sound was disappointingly small: a scrape, like a chair being pulled toward a table.

“It appears,” said one of the university people, “to be a localized phenomenon.”

“Which part?” asked the surveyor.

***

By October, the mountain had reached the abandoned petrol station.

There was considerable argument about whether it had crushed the building or whether the building, already in poor condition, had collapsed in anticipation.

The mayor favored anticipation. It sounded less expensive.

People began selling things.

Postcards. Mountain-shaped biscuits. T-shirts that said I WAS MOVED.

For a while, the town prospered.

Tourists stood beside the police tape on Thursdays with their phones raised. Some complained afterward.

“You can barely see it,” one woman said.

The surveyor, who had spent thirty years measuring the town’s boundaries and had recently started drinking at lunch, said, “You ought to have come when it stayed still.”

***

Only Ada Bell thought to ask where it was going.

Ada drove the school bus. She knew that a thing could be large and dangerous and still have a destination.

She spread a road map across her kitchen table and marked each movement in red.

The line passed through the petrol station, the municipal tennis courts, the cold-storage warehouse, and her own house.

Beyond that lay seventy miles of farmland.

Then the sea.

She took the map to the council meeting.

“You can’t establish intent from direction,” said the mayor.

“No,” Ada said. “But I generally can tell which children are heading for the door.”

***

Winter stopped the tourists.

It did not stop the mountain.

The tennis courts vanished beneath a slow arrival of ferns and granite. A section of chain-link fence rose along the slope, carrying a sign that read PROPER FOOTWEAR REQUIRED.

The council issued an evacuation plan.

Then a revised evacuation plan.

Then a clarification explaining that the first two plans had been preliminary discussions.

People nearest the mountain packed their houses. They argued over what could be stored in their relatives’ garages. Wardrobes stood on pavements under tarpaulins. A man on Quarry Road refused to leave until the roots of a beech tree came through his pantry.

Ada packed the good plates in newspaper.

She had expected to cry over the house. Instead she cried over a pencil mark inside the kitchen doorway: her daughter’s height at eleven.

Her daughter, now forty-three, offered to cut that section out.

Ada said no.

Then she called back and said yes.

***

In March, the university people returned with a theory involving stress, groundwater, and a previously unobserved mechanism.

“Can you stop it?” asked the mayor.

They looked at one another.

“Should we?” asked the youngest.

She was not invited to dinner.

***

The first serious proposal was dynamite.

The second was a trench.

The third, submitted anonymously, was to turn off every light in town and pretend nobody was home.

Ada proposed moving the road.

“Where?” said the mayor.

“Around.”

“And after that?”

“We’ll still need a road.”

There was a long silence.

The road crew began on Monday.

***

It took fourteen years for the mountain to leave town.

Children grew up with its progress marked on a board outside the library. They learned to ride bicycles on streets that ended a little sooner each spring.

The mayor retired. The surveyor’s apprentice took over the measurements. The university’s silver box failed and was replaced by a better one, which failed differently.

Ada moved into a flat above the bakery.

Sometimes she watched the mountain from her window. From there she could see a pale rectangle on the slope where her kitchen tiles had briefly held together.

One Thursday, after a difficult night of sleep, she waved.

She checked the windows opposite afterward.

***

When the mountain finally cleared the last house, the town held a picnic on the exposed ground.

Beneath where it had stood, they found darkness, pale roots, and stones that had never been warm.

Everyone had expected treasure.

Someone brought a metal detector anyway.

Ada, eighty-one and walking with two sticks, sat in a folding chair while children carried her their discoveries.

A white beetle.

A stone shaped like bread.

A rusted spoon, which caused some debate.

Later, someone asked whether she thought the mountain would reach the sea.

“Perhaps,” she said.

“And then what?”

Below them, the road crew was lifting the temporary barriers. One worker struggled with a bolt until another came over and held the rail steady.

Ada watched them finish.

“I don’t know,” she said.

The following Thursday, the mountain moved another six inches.

The first thing my father repaired after he retired was a chair nobody liked.

It had come with the house, abandoned in the cellar by people who had also left six jars of blackened preserves and a calendar from a year in which everyone looked optimistic. The chair was too upright for comfort and too plain to be valuable. One leg ended an inch above the others.

“Firewood,” I said.

“Mostly,” my father agreed.

He carried it upstairs.

Before retirement, he had inspected bridges. He wore white shirts to work and came home with dirt on the cuffs. At dinner, he sometimes described a crack he had seen that day, drawing it on his paper napkin while my mother moved the gravy out of reach of his elbow.

We crossed bridges differently when he drove. He turned the radio down. Once, on holiday, he took a forty-mile detour and refused to tell us why until we were eating lunch.

After retirement, there were no bridges he was authorized to worry about. He began checking the cellar for water. He bought a thermometer for the refrigerator. He asked whether I had ever had the wiring inspected in my apartment.

Then he found the chair.

He set it in the kitchen and spent a morning looking at it.

My mother went around him with the vacuum cleaner.

“Is this where you work now?”

“For the moment.”

“Then your office is on the cord.”

He moved into the garage.

All winter, whenever I visited, the chair stood upside down on his workbench. He took it apart, cleaned the joints, and fitted a new piece of wood to the short leg. The original was beech. His replacement was ash.

“Won’t match,” I said.

“No.”

“You could stain it.”

“Could.”

He didn’t.

In March, he brought the chair into the kitchen. The pale extension looked like a sock on one foot.

My mother sat in it while she peeled an apple. She shifted once, then again.

“Well?” he asked.

“It’s still an uncomfortable chair.”

He pulled it out for himself and finished the apple.

After that came a lamp, a drawer that would not close, and the handle of a saucepan my mother had planned to replace. She had to buy a new saucepan anyway; he kept the old one in the garage for soaking paintbrushes.

Word spread along the street. Mrs. Alvarez brought over a fan that clicked. A boy appeared with a skateboard under his arm and stayed for two hours. Someone left a bread maker on the doorstep with a note that said SOMETIMES SMOKE.

My father wrote back: WHICH TIMES?

He would not let people simply leave things.

“Show me what happens,” he said.

They plugged things in, turned handles, pushed buttons. They made the noises themselves when the machines declined to cooperate.

Most people stayed while he worked. Mrs. Alvarez sat in the repaired chair, which had returned to the garage, and told him about her sister’s hip operation. The boy with the skateboard came back the next Saturday, although his wheels were fine.

Then my father’s hands began to shake.

At first he blamed the cold. He installed a heater. Then he blamed a batch of small screws.

“Cheap heads,” he said, holding one out to me. “Look at that.”

I could see nothing wrong with it, but I looked for a long time.

He started turning work away. He told Mrs. Alvarez her fan needed a specialist. He told the boy, now taller than either of us, that he was getting out of the business.

“You never were a business,” my mother said.

“Well, then. Easy to get out.”

One Saturday, I found him trying to thread a nut onto a bolt. The nut slipped from his fingers and landed somewhere beneath the bench.

Neither of us moved to retrieve it.

Finally he said, “You do it.”

I picked up another nut from the tray.

“Not that one. Different thread.”

I put it down.

He watched as I found the right one and fitted it.

“Don’t force it.”

“I’m not.”

“You are a little.”

We worked for an hour. It was a garden gate latch, bent out of shape by frost or impatience. He held it steady while I tightened the bolts. Then we exchanged places because he didn’t like my angle.

The following week, the boy came back. His name was Daniel. I had never thought to ask.

My father showed him how to replace the cord on a lamp. Daniel did the cutting and stripping. My father checked each connection, leaning close beneath the work light.

By summer, three people were coming regularly. My mother put a kettle in the garage and banned soldering during tea.

The chair finally broke in November.

Mrs. Alvarez leaned back to laugh at something, and one of the old rear legs split. She caught the edge of the bench. Daniel caught her elbow. Her tea went everywhere.

My father knelt beside the pieces.

“Not your leg,” I said, pointing to the pale repair.

He gave me an irritated look.

“Get a towel before she slips.”

We cleared up the tea. Mrs. Alvarez insisted she was fine, then insisted on showing us the bruise already forming on her arm.

When she had gone, my father laid the broken leg on the bench.

Daniel reached for the glue.

“Wait,” my father said. He pulled another chair close and sat down. “Let’s have a look first.”

The city employed a man to notice things.

It was an old position, established before the buses, and nobody could find the document that explained it. His salary came from a budget line called Miscellaneous Continuity. Every few years, someone proposed eliminating it. Every few years, someone else said they ought to determine what it was before they did.

His name was Mr. Vale. He had a narrow office above the public baths and a raincoat the color of weak tea.

Each morning, he walked.

He noticed which shopkeepers swept their dust into the street and which swept it into pans. He noticed the first day the swifts returned. He noticed that the stone lion outside the courthouse had gradually acquired an expression of embarrassment, though whether this was weathering or a change in the courthouse he couldn’t say.

At four, he returned to his office and wrote his report.

*April 9. The little girl at Number 18 no longer counts the steps aloud.*

*April 10. Someone has repaired the blue cup in the window of the locksmith’s apartment. Gold adhesive.*

*April 11. The butcher sang today. First recorded instance since November.*

Nobody requested these reports. He filed them anyway.

When Mr. Vale turned seventy, the city decided he should have an apprentice.

The apprentice was called Mara. She arrived carrying a tablet and wearing shoes that suggested she expected the future to involve a great deal of running.

“What are our objectives?” she asked.

“To notice things.”

“For what purpose?”

Mr. Vale considered this.

“We should leave before the market gets crowded.”

On their first walk, Mara took 213 photographs.

That afternoon, she showed him a cracked drainpipe, six examples of illegal parking, a dangerous paving stone, and a dog sitting upright in a delivery van.

“The dog is good,” said Mr. Vale.

“The paving stone is a liability.”

“Yes. Send that to Streets.”

“And the drainpipe?”

“Buildings.”

“What do we keep?”

He looked again at the dog. Behind it, in the dim interior of the van, someone had hung a small curtain.

“That,” he said, pointing.

By the third week, Mara was irritated.

They had no targets. Their records weren’t searchable. Mr. Vale sometimes spent twenty minutes watching a person choose oranges.

“We could at least establish categories,” she said.

“We had categories once.”

“What happened?”

“Too many things went under Other.”

One Thursday, they passed a woman standing outside the railway station with a cake box. She wore a green coat. Her hair had been pinned carefully, and one pin was coming loose.

Mr. Vale stopped beside a newspaper stand.

“Do we know her?” Mara asked.

“No.”

“Is something wrong?”

“I don’t know.”

They waited.

People came out of the station in loose, hurrying groups. Each time the doors opened, the woman lifted the box slightly, as if preparing to hand it over. Each time, she lowered it again.

After a while, she sat on the low wall beneath the station clock.

Mara checked the departures board through the glass.

“Perhaps the train’s delayed.”

“Perhaps.”

“Should we ask?”

“You can.”

Mara crossed the pavement. Mr. Vale watched her speak to the woman, watched the woman shake her head and smile. Mara came back.

“She says she’s all right.”

They continued their walk.

That afternoon, Mara wrote:

*May 16. Woman waiting outside station. Green coat. Cake.*

She stared at the entry.

“That’s not enough,” she said.

“No,” said Mr. Vale.

“Do you ever find out what happened?”

“Usually not.”

She added the loose hairpin, then deleted it. She couldn’t decide whether it belonged to the woman or to the report.

In June, Mr. Vale missed a day of work.

In July, he missed nine.

The office smelled different without his wet raincoat. Mara opened the window, then closed it again because she could hear the bathhouse pumps laboring below.

She walked alone.

The butcher had stopped singing, but now a boy worked beside him, and they argued companionably about football. The locksmith’s blue cup disappeared from the window. On Saturday, Mara saw it in his hand as he stood on the balcony, drinking.

She began taking fewer photographs.

Once, she followed a shadow across a square until it joined the feet of the man who was repainting the flagpole. She felt foolish, but included it in her report.

Mr. Vale returned in August to clear his desk.

There was very little to clear: a comb, spare socks, a tin of stale biscuits, and thirty-eight years of reports.

“What should I do with these?” Mara asked.

“Keep them, if there’s room.”

“And if there isn’t?”

He sat down. The walk upstairs had tired him.

“Read some first.”

After he left, Mara opened a folder at random.

*September 3. Apprentice arrived at Waterworks today. Young man, very nervous. His father shook his hand before leaving. Neither appeared accustomed to this.*

She looked at the date. The young man would be old now, if he was alive.

Below it, in different ink, Mr. Vale had added:

*September 4. Father walked past Waterworks twice.*

Mara stayed late that evening.

At six, the cleaners arrived in the square below. One held the ladder while the other took down the summer bunting. When they reached the last length, they folded it between them, bringing their hands together and walking apart, together and apart, until the whole bright summer was a small square of cloth.

Mara found her pen.

samples.result:
The town hired a man to move the bench six feet to the left.

There were reasons. The bench interfered with the sightline from the new municipal camera. Its present location encouraged congregation near the pharmacy entrance. A wheelchair user had complained—not about the bench, actually, but about the sandwich board beside it. Nevertheless, a report had been written, and the report recommended moving the bench.

The man’s name was Arthur. He arrived with a socket wrench, a cordless drill, and a sandwich wrapped in the paper his wife still bought in bulk, though she had been dead for eighteen months.

It was good paper. You couldn’t blame paper for outlasting somebody.

At nine fifteen he set two orange cones around the bench.

At nine seventeen a woman stepped between them and sat down.

“I’m moving this,” Arthur said.

“I won’t be long.”

She took a shoe box from her shopping bag and rested it on her knees.

Arthur checked the bolts. They had been painted over several times: green, black, green again. Municipal geology.

“You’ll need to get up eventually.”

“Everybody does.”

He decided not to pursue that.

Across the road, a boy in a butcher’s apron washed the shop window with a sponge. He was making it substantially wetter without making it noticeably cleaner. Arthur watched him for a while, then took out a wire brush.

The woman said, “Do you know anything about birds?”

“Not professionally.”

“This one flew into my conservatory.”

“Is it in the box?”

“Yes.”

“Alive?”

“That’s the question.”

Arthur stopped brushing.

“Have you opened it?”

“Of course I’ve opened it.”

“And?”

“It looked offended.”

“That’s usually promising.”

She lifted the lid half an inch. Arthur leaned over.

Inside, on a tea towel embroidered with lemons, sat a small brown bird. Its eyes were open. It appeared to be considering legal action.

“Probably stunned,” he said.

“That’s what my daughter said.”

“Your daughter know about birds?”

“She knows about most things since moving to Bristol.”

The woman lowered the lid.

Arthur managed to expose the head of the first bolt. It was a size he didn’t have.

This did not surprise him. In thirty-one years of maintenance work, he had rarely encountered a bolt that wanted to be removed.

“I’ll have to go to the van,” he said.

“I’ll watch your cones.”

When he returned, a second woman was standing beside the bench, looking into the box.

“Give it water,” she said.

“Don’t give it water,” said the first woman.

“My uncle kept pigeons.”

“This isn’t a pigeon.”

“Same principles.”

Arthur put the socket on the bolt and leaned. Nothing happened.

The second woman watched.

“You want some oil on that.”

“I do.”

“My uncle also worked on cars.”

“A versatile man.”

“He was, before the drinking.”

By ten o’clock the bench had acquired a small committee.

The pharmacist came out and said the bird should be kept somewhere quiet.

The butcher’s boy came across with a saucer.

A man waiting for the number eight said birds couldn’t smell, which nobody had asked about.

Arthur loosened the first bolt.

Everyone turned at the sharp metallic crack.

“That’s one,” he said, and found himself pleased by the attention.

He could not remember the last time four people had watched him accomplish something. At home, repairs had become private events. He had fixed the loose banister in February and still occasionally gripped it harder than necessary to appreciate the result.

The woman with the box introduced herself as June.

“Arthur.”

“I know. It’s on your shirt.”

He looked down. So it was.

At half past ten, he had removed three bolts. The fourth turned freely without rising.

“Nut underneath,” he said.

The committee accepted this diagnosis solemnly.

He lay down on the pavement.

Under the bench were two cigarette ends, a hair clip, and a coin pressed into a dark clot of chewing gum. Above him, people discussed whether the bird was a sparrow.

His wife would have known. Not because she knew birds, but because she would have gone into the library and come back with a book. She had trusted information that required walking somewhere.

Arthur fitted a spanner around the nut.

“Try it now,” he said.

No one moved.

“The wrench. On top.”

June held the box out to the pharmacist and bent over the bolt. Her first attempt slipped.

“Keep it level,” Arthur said.

“Like that?”

“That’s it.”

The bolt came free.

When he crawled out, June was holding it up by its clean silver end.

The butcher’s boy helped them carry the bench. Six feet to the left put it beside the library wall, where the paving sloped slightly. Arthur measured, drilled, and fitted new anchors while June sat on the wall with the box.

They were tightening the last bolt when something scratched inside it.

June took off the lid.

The bird remained still for a moment, then flew straight toward the pharmacy, swerved above the sandwich board, and disappeared over the roof.

Nobody had time to say anything useful.

The pharmacist returned to work with the empty saucer. The boy went back to his window. June folded the lemon towel and put it in her shopping bag.

Arthur collected the cones.

“Is it ready?” she asked.

He gave the bench a firm shake.

June sat down. After a moment, Arthur sat beside her and unwrapped his sandwich.

From its new position, the bench caught the sun. Unfortunately, it also offered a clear view of the butcher’s window.

“He’s missed a bit,” June said.

Arthur chewed.

“Several bits.”

Neither called across.

The first thing we disagreed about was whether the house had thirteen stairs or fourteen.

“Fourteen,” my sister said.

She was standing at the bottom with a roll of blue painter’s tape around her wrist. Behind her, the front door stood open. Everything in the house had begun to look like something being carried out of it.

“Thirteen,” I said. “I used to count them.”

“So did I.”

We counted together, touching each tread with the toe of a shoe.

There were thirteen.

“You’re not counting the landing,” she said.

“The landing isn’t a stair.”

“It is if you’re coming up.”

This was the kind of argument we had been having for three days: small enough to survive, large enough to shelter in.

Our mother had lived in the house for forty-six years. Now she lived in a room with a window overlooking a parking lot, though the brochure called it a garden-facing suite. There was a garden between the building and the cars, technically: five lavender bushes, a birdbath, something low and silver neither of us could name.

She was not dead. This made sorting her belongings feel both less urgent and more criminal.

We had her permission. She had given it impatiently.

“Keep what you want. Sell the rest.”

“What about the dining table?”

“Does somebody want it?”

“What about your sewing machine?”

“Does somebody sew?”

But when I asked about the blue bowl, she said, “Which blue bowl?” and I knew better than to describe it.

***

By noon, my sister had made six categories.

KEEP. SELL. DONATE. RECYCLE. RUBBISH. ASK MUM.

ASK MUM occupied most of the dining room.

There was a wooden duck with a chipped beak. Three keys on a pink elastic band. A photograph of two women neither of us recognized, standing in snow beside a car. A biscuit tin containing buttons, a bus ticket, and one human tooth.

“Yours,” my sister said.

“Why mine?”

“I kept mine.”

“All of them?”

“The ones that came out.”

She said this while wrapping a lamp in newspaper, as if dental completeness were a reasonable subject for sibling competition.

I carried the tooth to the kitchen. It was astonishingly small. Somewhere in its yellowed root was the pain of an afternoon I could no longer remember.

I put it back in the tin.

***

Our father’s handwriting appeared wherever we stopped looking for it.

On a fuse box: KITCHEN / BACK ROOM.

Inside a cookbook: Too much salt.

On the underside of a drawer, in pencil: sticks in damp weather.

He had been dead for eleven years. Most days that fact stayed where we put it. But there it was again, beneath the drawer.

My sister sat on the floor.

I sat beside her.

“He could have fixed it,” she said.

“The drawer?”

“He could fix anything.”

I looked at the wooden runner, dark with the grease he had rubbed into it. The drawer had been troublesome for as long as I remembered.

“Maybe he thought that counted.”

She ran her thumb over the words. Then she got up to fetch a candle. We waxed the runners the way we had seen him do and pushed the drawer back in.

It still stuck.

***

At two, our mother telephoned to ask whether we had eaten.

“Yes,” we lied, separately.

“There’s soup in the freezer.”

“We know.”

“Not the container marked soup. That’s stock.”

“All right.”

“The soup is in the ice-cream tub.”

“We’ll find it.”

A pause.

“Have you done the stairs?”

We looked at each other.

“What about them?”

“The cupboard underneath.”

The cupboard contained a vacuum cleaner, six umbrellas, and the narrow height chart our father had made from a strip of wood.

We had forgotten it.

Our names climbed its surface in alternating pencil marks. My sister’s were neat and dated. Mine lurched upward at irregular intervals. Near the top, where our father had held the pencil sideways to mark my head, the line grew thick.

At the bottom were two marks labelled with the dog’s name.

“He wouldn’t stand still,” my sister said.

“You made him.”

“You held his tail.”

We laughed so suddenly that I knocked an umbrella onto the floor.

There was nowhere in either of our homes to put the chart. My sister had glass doors and fitted cupboards. I rented, and my landlord objected to nails.

We stood it in ASK MUM.

Then she moved it to KEEP.

***

By evening, the rooms had begun to echo.

We ate the soup sitting on the kitchen counter. It was carrot, probably. The label on the tub said VANILLA in a looping blue script.

My sister said she had thought our mother would fight harder.

“About moving?”

“About everything.”

Outside, a van slowed in front of the house. The driver checked a number and continued down the street.

“She fought quite hard about the bird feeder,” I said.

“She won that one.”

“She usually does.”

We washed the bowls and left them on the draining board. Then we walked through the house turning lights off.

At the stairs, my sister stopped.

She went up slowly, counting under her breath. I listened from below.

“Thirteen,” she said, reaching the last tread.

Then she stepped onto the landing.

“Fourteen.”

I was too tired to argue. Tomorrow we would have to decide about the table, and find someone who wanted a sewing machine.

“Coming?” she said.

I put my foot on the first stair.

The lighthouse appeared in the wheat field sometime between the evening weather report and the first bus to town.

It was not an especially handsome lighthouse. Its white paint had blistered, and rust ran down from the gallery railing in long, apologetic streaks. Someone had left a mop outside the door. At its base, the wheat leaned away in a perfect circle, as though politely making room.

Our nearest ocean was six hundred miles east.

By seven, people had parked along the county road to look. By eight, someone was selling coffee. By nine, the farmer, Mr. Bell, had put up a sign:

**PLEASE DO NOT WALK ON THE CROP TO INVESTIGATE THE IMPOSSIBLE.**

I arrived at ten because the town employed me to inspect structures, and whatever else it was, the lighthouse was plainly a structure.

Mr. Bell met me at the fence.

“Is it yours?” I asked.

“Do I look like I ordered a lighthouse?”

“People order unusual things.”

“Last thing I ordered was a replacement belt for the combine. They sent the wrong belt. This is worse.”

I ducked between the wires.

Up close, the tower smelled of salt and old pennies. There was a brass knocker shaped like a fish. Beneath it, a small notice read:

**KEEPER TEMPORARILY ABSENT.  
PLEASE MAINTAIN THE LIGHT.**

The door was unlocked.

Inside stood a narrow bed, a table, a stove, and a pair of rubber boots placed neatly on yesterday’s newspaper. The newspaper was from a town I had never heard of. Its lead story concerned a missing lighthouse.

I folded it and put it in my bag.

Then I climbed.

There were eighty-three steps. I counted because counting is one of the few things you can do professionally while afraid.

At the top, an enormous lens surrounded a lamp no larger than a mixing bowl. Everything was clean. The brass shone. A logbook lay open on a stool.

The latest entry said:

*Tuesday. Fog. Nothing lost.*

Below that:

*Wednesday. Clear. Nothing lost.*

Below that, in a shakier hand:

*Thursday. Inland. Will inquire.*

I looked out across the wheat.

From that height, our town seemed both smaller and more complicated. I could see the water tower, the school roof, the pale rectangle where the grocery store had burned down. Cars collected around the lighthouse like filings around a magnet.

There was a switch beside the lamp.

I left it alone.

***

By afternoon, the mayor wanted it removed.

By evening, the historical society wanted it preserved.

The school principal wanted to know whether children could visit, and the insurance company wanted everyone to stop using the word *appeared*.

I wrote a preliminary report.

*Foundation inaccessible. Staircase sound. Electrical supply undetermined. Recommend no immediate action.*

This was not cowardice. “No immediate action” is often the most useful thing a town employee can recommend.

That night, I went back.

I told myself I wanted to check the wiring. In fact, I had been thinking about the notice on the door.

*Please maintain the light.*

There are instructions you can ignore all day that become difficult after dark.

The coffee seller had gone home. Mr. Bell’s sign moved softly in the wind. I crossed the field with a flashlight, found the door, and climbed the eighty-three steps.

Then I turned the switch.

The lamp lit without a sound.

Its beam passed over the wheat, the road, the town. It swept across the church steeple and the supermarket loading dock. It entered bedroom windows and crossed kitchen tables.

On its third circuit, my phone rang.

It was my sister.

“Are you at the lighthouse?”

“Yes.”

“Can you leave it on?”

I waited.

“Just for a while,” she said.

My sister had spent the past month packing up her house. Her husband had left in January, and she was trying to decide whether leaving town would count as starting over or merely leaving town.

“Does it bother you?” I asked.

“No,” she said. “That’s the thing.”

***

Other people called.

A nurse finishing her shift asked who had authorized it. When I apologized, she said she hadn’t complained.

A boy watching his little brother while their mother worked sent the town’s public information account a photograph of the beam crossing their ceiling.

Mr. Bell called at eleven.

“It comes through my window every forty seconds.”

“I can turn it off.”

He was quiet.

“Didn’t say that.”

I stayed until dawn.

***

The keeper returned on Saturday.

She was short, sunburned, and carrying a canvas bag full of oranges.

“Any trouble?” she asked.

“Some.”

“Usually is.”

She set the oranges on the table and inspected the stove.

“Where did you go?” I asked.

“To ask directions.”

“From whom?”

She gave me a look that suggested I was not licensed to inspect that question.

Outside, wind moved through the wheat in broad, traveling shadows.

“Will it go back?” I asked.

“Oh, yes.”

“When?”

“When we can.”

I wanted to ask what that meant. Instead I asked whether she needed anything.

“Fresh bread,” she said. “And the bottom stair has a wobble.”

***

The lighthouse vanished the following Monday.

It left a round patch of flattened wheat and one orange, which Mr. Bell found beneath his tractor.

For several nights afterward, I woke every forty seconds, or imagined I did.

My sister stayed in town. She said rent was cheaper here.

At the next council meeting, I submitted a modest proposal: replace the broken lights at the bus shelter, repaint the hospital entrance, and put a reflective marker on the dangerous bend beyond the school.

The mayor asked what had prompted this.

I said I had noticed some maintenance issues while working nights.

The motion passed, four votes to two.
